What Oklahoma's statutes do not have: (1) no duty in the Landlord and Tenant Act to comply with building and housing codes (the Act defines the term but never uses it in your duties; city codes may still apply directly); (2) no statutory warranty of habitability by that name and no statutory list of conditions that make a unit uninhabitable; (3) no minimum indoor temperature, only reasonable heat; (4) no duty to provide air conditioning or cooling, though air conditioning you supply must be kept in good and safe working order; (5) no rent-escrow or rent-withholding statute (the repair remedies above are the tenant's tools); (6) no statutory presumptions about habitability; (7) no statute requiring carbon monoxide detectors in rentals: a State Fire Marshal rule requires detectors only in occupancies with a carbon monoxide system. Oklahoma has adopted statewide the 2024 International Residential Code for building new one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses, and the 2024 International Fire Code as the minimum code for residential and commercial fire prevention, including its chapters on fire protection systems and on existing buildings; neither adoption changes those codes' alarm sections, so ask your local building or fire official whether a carbon monoxide alarm requirement reaches your building. Mold, radon and bed bugs have no Oklahoma disclosure or treatment statute either (see the separate guidance on each); smoke detectors are required.

title: The Tenant's Right to Quiet Possession
bodyText: Oklahoma's Landlord and Tenant Act does not state a covenant of quiet enjoyment by that name, but it protects the tenant's possession in specific rules. You must deliver full possession at the start of the term. During the tenancy you have no right of access except as the Act allows (consent, emergency, at least one day's notice at reasonable times) or a court orders, unless the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit. You may not remove or lock out the tenant except through the courts; a wrongful removal or exclusion lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease and recover up to twice the average monthly rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater. Unlawful or harassing entry lets the tenant get an injunction or end the lease and recover actual damages. The Act also makes it a tenant duty not to disturb other tenants' quiet and peaceful enjoyment, which is why the library's no-disturbance clause applies. Oklahoma's statutes on deeds and damages speak of a covenant of quiet enjoyment in a grant of an estate in real property; whether that reaches a residential lease is a question for the courts. The practical course is the same either way: respect the tenant's exclusive possession and handle every entry and removal by the Act's rules.

title: Shifting Repairs or Maintenance to the Tenant
bodyText:
In Oklahoma the only route for putting repairs or maintenance on the tenant is a conspicuous writing independent of the lease in which you and the tenant agree that the tenant will perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling. The statute does not limit this to any type of dwelling, does not require a rent reduction or other particular payment, and has no landlord precondition, but it does require the tasks to be specified, and the agreement must be a separate, conspicuous document rather than a clause or addendum in the lease.

As a separate contract it needs ordinary consideration, so state what the tenant receives (for example a stated rent credit, or the tenancy itself), and like every duty under the Act it must be performed and enforced in good faith. The agreement does not say it relieves you of your own duty to keep the unit fit and habitable, so treat it as moving who does the listed work, not as a waiver. The tenant's own statutory duties, such as keeping the unit clean and safe and not damaging it, need no separate agreement. Use the library's optional Tenant Maintenance Agreement, printed and signed as its own document.

title: No Pre-Set Deposit Charges
bodyText: Oklahoma has no statute that lets a lease pre-set cleaning, carpet-cleaning, painting or repair charges against the security deposit, and none that requires a special notice for one. What controls is the deposit rule: when the tenancy ends you may apply the deposit to accrued rent and to the damages you have actually suffered because the tenant did not comply with the Landlord and Tenant Act or the lease, itemized in a written statement. The tenant's cleaning duty under the Act is to keep the part of the premises the tenant uses as safe, clean and sanitary as the condition of the premises permits, so the ordinary effect of normal use is not a breach you can charge for. A figure fixed in the lease in advance as the damages for a breach (for example, a set amount if the carpets are not cleaned) is valid under Oklahoma contract law only where the actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, and cleaning and repair costs can usually be fixed from invoices. A flat move-out charge owed by every tenant whatever the unit's condition is not damages; under the Act a fee the lease requires counts as rent, and whether a court would let you take such a fee from the deposit, or treat it as a penalty or a disguised nonrefundable deposit, is a question of case law. No lease term can make the tenant give up the deposit rights the Act grants. The library does not offer a pre-set charge schedule. The cautious course: charge from the unit's actual condition, keep move-in and move-out photographs and invoices, put the real figures in the itemized statement, and treat any schedule you add after legal advice as an estimate you still have to justify item by item. If you want a fixed cleaning fee, state it in the lease as a separate fee rather than as a deduction from the deposit.

title: No Right to Pay the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute gives a tenant a right to pay the security deposit in installments or requires you to offer a payment plan. You may agree to one if you choose; if you do, write the amounts and due dates into the lease. Every installment you receive is part of the deposit: it goes into the escrow account and is applied and returned under the security deposit rules. Because the Landlord and Tenant Act's definition of rent leaves out deposits, an unpaid deposit installment is not unpaid rent, so the five-day nonpayment notice does not reach it. A missed installment is a breach of the lease; if it is a material noncompliance it is handled through the Act's noncompliance notice (a written notice that gives the tenant ten days to remedy the breach before the lease ends). Do not try to get around this by calling a deposit installment rent in the lease; whether a court would accept that label is a question of case law.

title: Deposit Refund Does Not Depend on a Move-Out Notice
bodyText: Oklahoma does not make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out or of surrendering the unit, and no statute lets the lease add that condition. The Landlord and Tenant Act sets the tenant's conditions itself: your 45-day deadline to return the balance runs only after the tenancy has ended, the tenant has delivered possession and the tenant has made a written demand for the deposit, and if the tenant makes no written demand within six months after the tenancy ends, the deposit becomes yours. A lease term that forfeits the deposit because the tenant did not give a move-out notice would make the tenant give up rights under the Act, and such a term is unenforceable. A fixed forfeiture for that breach is also enforceable under Oklahoma contract law only where actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, which lost rent usually is not. Your remedy for a tenant who leaves without the notice the lease or the law requires is your actual damages, such as rent for the notice period, itemized against the deposit like any other damages. You may ask the tenant to include a forwarding address in the written demand; the library's deposit-return clause does. The written notice needed to end a month-to-month or shorter tenancy is a separate rule and does not change the deposit refund.

title: No Deposit Standards Disclosure
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a landlord, however many units it has, to post or hand out the standards it uses to set security deposits, and none regulates using different deposit standards for different units or applicants. Oklahoma also sets no cap on the amount. The limit that does apply is fair housing: Oklahoma law makes it unlawful to discriminate against any person in the terms, conditions or privileges of renting housing because of race, color, religion, gender, national origin, age, familial status or disability, and the deposit amount is a term of the rental. Federal fair housing law applies too. If you use more than one deposit level, for example by screening result or unit type, write the criteria down, apply them the same way to every applicant, and keep the record. That is good practice, not a statutory duty.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: Oklahoma has no fast-track procedure for settling a security deposit, no shorter deadline a tenant can trigger, and no authority to charge a processing or early-return fee. There is one clock: you return the balance, with an itemized written statement of anything you keep, within 45 days after the tenancy ends, the tenant delivers possession and the tenant makes a written demand. You may always return the deposit sooner. The library does not offer a fee for early return; no statute authorizes one, and a charge that reduces the refund for doing what the law already requires is likely to be treated as an improper deduction. If you and the tenant disagree about deductions, the Landlord and Tenant Act lets you settle a claim disputed in good faith by agreement, without further payment, and either side may sue in small claims court, where the prevailing party in a case over the lease or the Act is entitled to reasonable attorney fees. Put any settlement in writing and signed by both of you.

title: Fees in Place of a Security Deposit
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute regulates a fee, insurance policy or surety bond offered in place of a security deposit. The Landlord and Tenant Act's definitions decide how the money is treated. Money you require as security that is to be returned to the tenant when the tenancy ends meets the Act's definition of a deposit, whatever the lease calls it: it goes in the escrow account and is applied and returned under the deposit rules. A nonrefundable fee the lease requires, including a monthly fee charged instead of a deposit, is not a deposit; the Act counts it as rent. A fee does not cap what the tenant owes: the tenant stays liable for unpaid rent and for damage the tenant causes, and you recover those through the usual remedies. If a third-party company sells the tenant a bond or insurance product, Oklahoma insurance law may regulate that company and product, and federal credit-reporting law governs any report it makes about the tenant (see the rent-reporting guidance for those duties). The library does not offer a fee-in-lieu clause. The arrangement is lawful as a fee, but its terms depend on the product you use. If you offer one, make it the tenant's choice, say plainly in the lease that the fee is not refundable, is not a security deposit and does not limit the tenant's liability, and have a lawyer review the product's terms before you add your own clause.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute regulates a holding or reservation deposit taken before the lease is signed: there is no cap, no deadline to refund it, and no rule that you must return it doubled if you back out. The Landlord and Tenant Act governs rights under a rental agreement, and its deposit rules cover money a landlord requires from a tenant as security to be returned when the tenancy ends, so money taken from an applicant before any lease exists sits outside them, under ordinary contract law. Once the lease is signed, money you credit to the security deposit becomes a deposit (escrow account, return rules) and money you credit to the first month's rent is rent. If you keep a holding deposit because the applicant backs out, Oklahoma contract law treats a sum fixed in advance as damages for a breach as valid only where the actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix; no Oklahoma case on rental holding deposits was reviewed. The library offers no holding-deposit agreement. The cautious course: put the terms in a short signed writing (the amount, how long you will hold the unit, what it will be credited to, and when it is refunded), keep the amount close to the rent you lose while the unit is held, refund it promptly if you decline the applicant or do not deliver the unit, apply the same terms to every applicant, and keep the money separate from your own. A licensed real estate broker or manager who takes it must hold it in an escrow account that contains only other people's money.

title: Nonrefundable Fees and Deposits
bodyText:
Oklahoma has no statute on nonrefundable deposits and requires no special notice for them. The Landlord and Tenant Act's definitions sort the money instead. A deposit is money you require as security that is to be returned when the tenancy ends, less proper deductions; every other payment the lease requires, except damages, is rent. So a sum cannot be both a security deposit and nonrefundable.

If you want to keep a charge whatever the unit's condition, make it a fee (for example a pet fee or a move-in fee), say in the lease that it is nonrefundable and what it is for, and keep it out of the deposit; the optional Nonrefundable Fees clause does this. If a payment works as security for damage or for the tenant's performance, treat it as part of the deposit, whatever it is called: keep it in the escrow account, itemize deductions and return the balance under the deposit rules. Oklahoma has no rule that reaches deposits however they are labeled, but that cautious course avoids the argument.

Fair housing law bars charging an additional nonrefundable fee, or an unreasonable deposit, to a blind, deaf or disabled person for a guide, signal or service dog, though the tenant remains liable for damage the dog does.

title: No Separate Notice for Nonrefundable Fees
bodyText: Oklahoma does not require a separate written notice, apart from the lease, telling the tenant that a fee or part of a deposit will not be refunded. Under the Landlord and Tenant Act a deposit is money held as security and returned when the tenancy ends, less proper deductions, so there is no such thing as a nonrefundable part of a deposit to give notice of; a nonrefundable charge is a fee, which the Act counts as rent. State each nonrefundable fee, its amount and its purpose in the lease itself (the optional Nonrefundable Fees clause does this), and do not describe any part of the security deposit as nonrefundable.

title: Collecting Rent Does Not Shed the Duty to Maintain
bodyText: Putting someone else in the landlord's seat does not free the owner of the duty to maintain. Under the Landlord and Tenant Act, any agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument that authorizes a person other than the beneficial owner to act as landlord does not relieve the beneficial owner of the duty to comply with the Act and with any other law, code, ordinance or regulation on maintaining and operating the premises. That reaches management agreements, assignments of rents to a lender, and mortgages or deeds of trust that let a lender or receiver collect the rent. The person who collects the rent does not escape either: a manager who does not give the tenant the Act's written disclosure of the owner, the manager and the person authorized to accept notices becomes a landlord under the Act, responsible for the landlord's obligations and for using the rents collected to meet them. A lease cannot make the tenant give up the Act's maintenance rights. If you sell or otherwise lose your interest, you are relieved of obligations for events after you give the tenant written notice of the change, and your successor takes them on. Check rent-assignment language in loan and management documents with this in mind.

title: Utility Deposits and Unpaid Utility Charges
bodyText: Oklahoma has no separate rule for a utility deposit a landlord collects. If you require money from the tenant as security for utility charges and it is to be returned at the end of the tenancy, it is a deposit under the Landlord and Tenant Act: keep it in the escrow account with the security deposit and apply and return it under the same rules. Unpaid utility charges the lease makes the tenant pay to you are rent, because the Act defines rent as every payment due to you under the lease other than deposits and damages; you may apply the deposit to them as accrued rent, itemized in your written statement. If you resell electricity, gas, water or sewer service bought from a city to a residential tenant, you may not charge more than 10% above your cost for each billing cycle and must show the per-unit cost and each fee on the bill, so deduct only what you could lawfully bill. A deposit the tenant pays directly to a utility is between the tenant and the utility: a city utility issues any refund within 30 days after service ends, and a Corporation Commission-regulated electric, gas or water utility applies the deposit to unpaid charges when service is discontinued and returns the balance within 30 days. You do not hold or return those deposits.

title: Paying to Stop an Eviction
bodyText: Oklahoma gives a tenant no general right to stop an eviction for nonpayment by paying what is owed after the deadline. The tenant's chance to pay comes with your written demand: you may end the lease for unpaid rent only if the tenant does not pay within five days after written notice of your demand. After that, no statute requires you to accept late rent, to accept a payment a charity or agency makes for the tenant, or to stop the eviction if the tenant pays before trial or before the writ is carried out, and no statute prescribes wording for accepting a partial payment. Whether taking money after the deadline waives your right to go ahead is a question of case law; if you accept any payment, give the tenant a written statement that you accept it without waiving the termination or the eviction, and decide each case on its facts. One narrow cure is written into the law: if rent went unpaid because of the tenant's good-faith claim that you failed to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, and the tenant gave written notice of that claim (or actual notice to your agent for collecting rent) within ten days after the rent was due, the court's order must state that the tenant can avoid the writ, cure the breach and stay by paying the judgment, including court costs and attorney fees, in cash or by cashier's check within 72 hours. A tenant who appeals and posts a supersedeas bond must keep paying current rent into the court clerk's office while the appeal is pending.

title: No Rent Reporting Rule
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to offer positive rent reporting, lets a tenant opt in or out of it, requires you to tell a tenant before you report late rent to a credit bureau, or sets up a state rent-reporting program a tenant could be required to join. Whether and how you report rent payments is a business choice. Federal law (the Fair Credit Reporting Act) sets duties for anyone who reports to a credit bureau: do not report information you know or have reasonable cause to believe is inaccurate; if you regularly report and find something you reported was incomplete or inaccurate, promptly correct it with the bureau; if a tenant disputes an item with you, report it only with notice that it is disputed; and when a credit bureau sends you a dispute, investigate it and correct, delete or block anything inaccurate or unverifiable. Check the reporting service's terms too before you report. If you use a reporting service, say in the lease or a separate signed form what you will report, to whom, and how a tenant can dispute an entry.

title: No Property Tax Rent Statement
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to tell tenants what share of their rent goes to property taxes, to give an annual rent certificate, or to certify rent received for a tenant's tax credit. Oklahoma's property tax relief for people 65 or older or totally disabled is limited to owners who occupy their own home and pay ad valorem tax on it, so renters do not claim it through their rent and you have no statement to provide. If a tenant asks for proof of rent paid for some other purpose, you may give a simple statement of the amounts received.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Statute
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute bans or regulates using software or an algorithm to set rents or lease terms. Oklahoma's general antitrust law still applies: every agreement, combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade within the state is illegal, the law is read consistently with federal antitrust law, a person injured by a violation recovers three times the damages plus costs and attorney fees, and some violations are felonies. Sharing nonpublic rent, occupancy or lease data with competing landlords through a common pricing service, or agreeing to follow its recommendations, can create antitrust risk under state and federal law; how courts treat those services is a question of case law. If you use pricing software, base it on your own and public data, keep the final decision on each rent your own, and get legal advice before joining a service that pools competitors' data.

title: No Rent Ledger or Record Retention Rule
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to give a tenant a rent ledger or account history on request, to include one in a nonpayment notice, or to keep tenant files for a set period. The records the Landlord and Tenant Act does require are specific: the written itemized statement of deposit deductions, the written disclosure of the owner, manager and person authorized to accept notices, and the written notices the Act calls for. Keep a running ledger of every charge and payment anyway, together with the lease, move-in and move-out records and copies of notices, for at least as long as a claim could be brought; it is your best evidence in a rent or deposit dispute and in an eviction case.

title: Protecting Applicant and Tenant Data
bodyText: Oklahoma's Security Breach Notification Act reaches landlords. If you or your company own or license computerized data that includes a person's name together with a Social Security number, driver license or other government identification number, a financial account or card number with the code needed to use it, an electronic identifier or routing code with the code needed to reach a financial account, or biometric data, and an unauthorized person gets unencrypted and unredacted copies in a way that causes, or that you reasonably believe has caused or will cause, identity theft or other fraud, you must notify each affected Oklahoma resident without unreasonable delay (a delay is allowed while law enforcement says notice would impede an investigation). If 500 or more Oklahoma residents are affected, you must also notify the Attorney General within 60 days after notifying them. If a vendor such as a screening or property-management software company holds the data for you, it must notify you. The Attorney General or a district attorney enforces the Act: penalties can reach $150,000 per breach, but a landlord who used reasonable safeguards and gave the required notice faces no civil penalty, and one who gave notice without reasonable safeguards faces actual damages and a $75,000 penalty. Reasonable safeguards, scaled to your size and the data you hold, include risk assessments, technical and physical layered defenses, employee training and an incident response plan. Oklahoma has no separate statute requiring a written information security program or limiting how a landlord collects Social Security numbers. Collect only what you need for screening, encrypt or redact stored numbers (no more than five digits of a Social Security number, or the last four of a license or account number), and shred paper files you no longer need. The Act applies to breaches on or after January 1, 2026. Separately, a new consumer data privacy law takes effect January 1, 2027, but it applies only to a business that, in a calendar year, controls or processes personal data of at least 100,000 Oklahoma consumers, or of at least 25,000 and gets over half its gross revenue from selling personal data; few landlords meet that threshold.

title: No Fee-Transparency or All-In Rent Law
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to advertise or state rent as one all-in figure that includes mandatory fees, to put fees on the first page of the lease, to copy a statutory fee notice into the lease, or to itemize fees in any set form. Oklahoma's only all-in price rule of this kind applies to motor vehicle rental companies, and its rule on automatically renewing contracts applies to rentals of goods, not homes. There is no special format rule for subsidized tenancies, because there is no format rule at all. Three rules still shape how you handle fees. First, if you resell electricity, gas, water or sewer service that you buy from a city to a residential tenant, each bill must separately show your per-unit cost and the dollar amount of every fee or charge, and your markup is capped (see the utility resale row). Second, the Landlord and Tenant Act defines rent as the payments the tenant must make to you under the rental agreement, which means the lease and any valid rules adopted under the Act; a charge that appears in neither is not rent under that definition. Third, the Consumer Protection Act covers transactions in real property and treats as unlawful a misleading omission, a false or misleading statement about price, and knowingly charging a consumer for services the consumer did not authorize in advance; a consumer can recover actual damages and attorney fees. Whether and how that Act reaches a residential lease is a question of case law. The cautious course: list every fee the tenant must pay in the lease, with its amount or how it is calculated and when it is due; include mandatory fees when you quote or advertise the monthly cost; and do not collect any charge the signed lease or a valid rule does not provide for.

title: Fees for Services You Do Not Provide
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute specifically bars you from charging a fee for a service or amenity you do not actually provide, and no statute specifically bars a separate fee for work the Landlord and Tenant Act already makes your duty. Three rules still point the same way. First, the Act makes these your duties during the tenancy: repairs needed to keep the unit fit and habitable; keeping common areas clean, safe and sanitary (except for a single-family residence); keeping supplied facilities and appliances in good and safe working order; trash receptacles and frequent removal (except for one- or two-family residences or where a government provides it); and running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat (except for a single-family residence or separately metered service). A lease cannot make the tenant give up rights under the Act, and a tenant can take on specified repairs or maintenance only in a conspicuous writing separate from the lease. Whether a separate fee for doing your own statutory work is treated as shifting that duty is a question of case law. Second, if you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service the lease or the Act requires, the tenant, after giving you written notice, can end the lease, buy the service and deduct its cost from rent, recover damages for the reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing and pay no rent for that period. Third, the Consumer Protection Act treats as unlawful a misleading omission or practice and knowingly charging a consumer for services the consumer did not authorize in advance; whether it reaches a residential lease is a question of case law. The cautious course: charge a service or amenity fee only for something the tenant actually receives, describe it and its price in the lease, stop or credit the fee for any period the service is not available, and do not charge a separate fee for repairs or services the Act requires you to provide.

title: No Statutory Late Fee Limit
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute caps or regulates late fees on residential rent. There is no maximum dollar amount or percentage, no required grace period, and no rule on daily late fees. Oklahoma has no separate mobile home park statute: a rented manufactured or mobile home lot is a dwelling unit under the Landlord and Tenant Act, so the same rule applies. The only statutory late-fee figure for a rental is in the self-storage law, which treats a storage late fee of the greater of $20 or 20% of the unpaid rent as reasonable; it does not apply to homes and is not a guide for them.

The Consumer Credit Code's limits on delinquency charges apply to consumer credit sales, consumer loans and leases of goods, not to a lease of a home. What does limit a late fee is Oklahoma contract law: a penalty for non-performance is void, an amount fixed in advance as the damages for a breach is valid only when, from the nature of the case, the actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, and damages must always be reasonable. How Oklahoma courts apply those rules to residential late fees is a question of case law.

A late fee the lease requires is also rent under the Act's definition, but whether an unpaid late fee can support the five-day nonpayment notice and an eviction is likewise case law. The cautious course: set a modest fee tied to a reasonable estimate of what a late payment really costs you, state the amount and any grace period in the lease, keep a record of how you set it, and avoid daily or compounding fees.

The library's Late Fee clause is built for this.

title: Oklahoma's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: These are the money limits Oklahoma statutes set for a residential tenancy. Not capped: the security deposit, late fees, application and screening fees, pet fees and other lease fees, and rent in ordinary times. Cities may not regulate the amount of rent on private rental property, except property the city owns, subsidized properties under an agreement, and properties assisted with federal Community Development Block Grant funds. Contract law still voids penalties and requires any fixed charge to be reasonable (see the penalties row). Caps and fixed measures: (1) Emergencies. During a declared emergency (by the Governor or the President) and for 30 days after it, you may not rent or offer a dwelling unit in the emergency area for more than 10% above the price you charged just before the declaration, and the same 10% limit on dwelling units runs for another 180 days, unless the increase is attributable to petroleum and natural gas price increases or only to factors unrelated to the emergency that add no profit. An increase a government agency approves is allowed. (2) Reselling utilities. If you buy electricity, gas, water or sewer service from a city and resell it to a residential tenant, you may not charge more than 10% above your cost for each billing cycle; a willful violation is a misdemeanor and makes you liable for treble damages. (3) Interest. Where no rate is agreed, the legal rate is 6% a year. A lease may agree a rate only as the law authorizes. The Constitution makes a contract rate above 10% a year usurious where no statute fixes a maximum, and the Consumer Credit Code's rates cover loans and credit sales, which an overdue-rent debt is not as the Code defines them. Knowingly charging usurious interest forfeits all the interest, and a tenant who paid it may recover twice the interest paid by suing within two years after the debt matured. The library offers no interest clause; if you add one after advice, keep it at or below 10% a year. (4) Holdover. If a tenant's holdover is willful and not in good faith, you may recover up to twice the average monthly rent, prorated daily, for each month or part of a month; an older statute also makes double rent the measure where a tenant gave notice of leaving and then stays. (5) Possession and lockouts. A willful, bad-faith failure to deliver possession costs up to twice the monthly rent, prorated daily, for each month or part of a month. If you wrongfully remove or exclude a tenant, the tenant recovers up to twice the average monthly rent or twice the actual damages, whichever is greater. (6) Tenant repairs. A tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy is limited to repairs costing no more than one month's rent. (7) Deposits. There is no deposit cap and no multiplier for wrongful retention: the tenant recovers the deposit and any prepaid rent. Misappropriating a deposit from the escrow account is a crime punishable by up to six months in county jail and a fine of up to twice the amount misappropriated. (8) Property left behind. If you store it in the vacated unit, the storage cost may not exceed the unit's fair rental value. (9) Assistance animals. If a tenant obtained an accommodation by a knowingly false claim or fraudulent documentation, a landlord who wins the eviction may be awarded court costs and fees plus damages of up to $1,000. (10) Consumer Protection Act. If a violation is also unconscionable, the consumer may recover a civil penalty of up to $2,000 per violation; whether the Act reaches leases is a question of case law. (11) Court. Small claims covers money claims up to $10,000, not counting attorney fees and costs; an eviction joined with a claim for rent or damages within that amount goes on the small claims docket; and in an uncontested small claims case attorney fees are limited to 10% of the judgment, or up to 25% on a documented application. There is no statutory limit on a returned-payment fee for rent (see the bad checks row).

title: No Rule on Which Fees the Lease Must List
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute requires the lease to list every fee with its purpose, to state a charge for accepting a partial payment, to give the tenant a set number of days' notice before a new fee, or to show rent plus mandatory fees as one labelled total. No statute bars a fee for maintaining common areas. What Oklahoma law does say: a fee the lease requires counts as rent under the Landlord and Tenant Act, because rent means every payment, other than deposits and damages, that the tenant must make under the rental agreement; and a rule you adopt after the tenant signs that substantially changes the tenant's bargain binds the tenant only with the tenant's written consent, so adding a new charge mid-lease generally needs the tenant's signature.

If you resell electricity, gas, water or sewer service bought from a city, your charge may not exceed your cost plus 10% for each billing cycle, and each bill must show your per-unit cost and every fee in dollars and cents. Any fixed charge must also survive Oklahoma's penalty rules (a reasonable estimate of your real cost is the cautious course). The library's Fees and Charges clause lists every fee in one place and promises no new fee during the term without the tenant's written agreement; using it is good practice, not a legal requirement.

title: Government Fines and Nuisance Costs
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute bars you from passing to a tenant a government fine or nuisance-abatement cost the tenant caused, and none requires the tenant to pay it unless the lease says so. By default these costs fall on you as the owner. A city may clean trash and mow weeds on your property after notice to the owner, bill the owner the actual cost, and have the cost collected with property taxes and made a lien on the property; city code fines, penalties and abatement costs can likewise become liens on the property.

A city may also make it an offense for an owner or a person in possession or control of property to let trash accumulate or weeds grow, so a tenant can be cited directly. Oklahoma's nuisance statute makes a later owner who neglects to abate a continuing nuisance created by a former owner liable for it; it has no rule shifting that liability to a tenant. If you want the tenant to bear a fine caused by the tenant, the tenant's household or guests, say so in the lease: the library's optional clause treats the tenant-caused condition as a breach of the lease and the amount you paid as your actual damages for that breach. It is not written as an indemnity, because a lease term making either party indemnify the other for liability for damage or injury to persons or property caused by either party's acts or omissions in operating or maintaining the unit or the premises is unenforceable in Oklahoma, and no court decision was reviewed on how far that rule reaches.

Never charge the tenant for a fine caused by a condition that is your duty to fix, and keep a copy of the citation and proof of what you paid.

title: Passing Local Government Fees to the Tenant
bodyText:
Oklahoma cities may not require registration of real property, and may not enforce a registration requirement through fees, civil fines or criminal penalties, so there is no rental registration fee to pass through. A city may keep a list of owners or their designees, and to deal with nuisances and dilapidated property it may require contact information for the person responsible for emergencies and maintenance and for a person to receive notices, but it may not charge a fee for collecting that information. Other local fees and occupancy-standard rules are not barred by that law.

No Oklahoma statute authorizes or bars making the tenant reimburse a local government fee on the property; if you want that, it must be in the lease from the start (the library's optional Local Government Fees clause), because adding a new charge in the middle of a lease generally needs the tenant's written agreement. A reimbursement the lease requires counts as rent under the Landlord and Tenant Act. Do not pass through fines or penalties assessed against you this way; see the government fines row.

title: No Smoke Detector Tampering Fee
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute or State Fire Marshal rule authorizes a lease fee for removing or tampering with a smoke detector, or sets an amount for one. What the law does say: anyone who tampers with, removes, destroys, disconnects or removes power from an installed smoke detector, except while inspecting, maintaining or replacing it, commits a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of $50 to $100; that fine goes to the state, not to you. You must explain to the tenant how to test the detector, and the tenant renting a one- or two-family dwelling or an apartment is responsible for checking that it works; in apartment houses of three or more units, hotels, motels, dormitories and rooming houses, the Fire Marshal's rules make the owner or management responsible for maintenance where the occupant is not the owner. If a tenant, or someone the tenant lets in, damages, disables or removes a detector, you may recover the actual, reasonable cost of repairing or replacing it as damages, including from the deposit with an itemized statement. A flat tampering fee set in advance is different: Oklahoma voids contract penalties, and an amount fixed in advance as damages is valid only where the actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, which a detector's replacement cost is not. So charge the documented cost, not a fixed fee. The library's Smoke Detectors clause records your explanation and the tenant's checking, reporting and no-tampering duties, and the Damage Caused by Tenant clause covers the cost of repairs. No Oklahoma statute requires carbon monoxide alarms in rentals; a State Fire Marshal rule requires carbon monoxide detectors only in occupancies with a carbon monoxide system (see the habitability guidance).

title: Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute lets you require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, sets a condition for requiring it, or limits carpet or paint charges by the age of the carpet or paint. What controls is the deposit rule and the tenant's own duty. The tenant must keep the part of the premises the tenant uses as safe, clean and sanitary as the condition of the premises permits, and must not deliberately or negligently damage it; so soiling or damage beyond what ordinary use causes is a breach, and you may apply the deposit to the actual damages, itemized in your written statement. A carpet that is simply worn or lightly soiled from ordinary living is not a breach you can charge for. Requiring the tenant to have the carpets professionally cleaned is a different thing: it is a maintenance task, and in Oklahoma the landlord and tenant may agree that the tenant performs specified maintenance tasks only in a conspicuous writing separate from the lease. The library therefore does not put a carpet-cleaning requirement in the lease. If you want one, list it as a task in the separate Tenant Maintenance Agreement; whether a deposit deduction can rest on that separate agreement is a question for the courts, so the cautious course is to deduct only the documented, reasonable cost of cleaning that goes beyond ordinary use, supported by move-in and move-out photographs and receipts. A flat carpet-cleaning charge fixed in advance is treated in the deposit charges row.

title: Collection Fees Are Not Offered
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute authorizes, caps or bars a lease charge for the cost of collecting unpaid rent or other money the tenant owes, such as a collection-agency fee or a percentage collection charge, and Oklahoma has no general collection-agency licensing law. Such a term is not expressly barred, but the library does not offer one, for two reasons. First, a lease may not make the tenant agree to pay the landlord's attorney fees, and a term is unenforceable if it does; a collection charge that covers lawyer work, or a collector's fee when the account goes to a lawyer, risks being read that way. Second, a collection charge fixed in advance is a stipulated amount of damages, which Oklahoma enforces only where the actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, and contract penalties are void; how Oklahoma courts treat collection charges in leases is a question of case law. Where the Legislature wanted contract collection fees allowed, as for certain student loans, it said so expressly. What the law gives you instead: in a suit for breach of the lease or to enforce the Landlord and Tenant Act, and in an eviction case, the court awards the winning side a reasonable attorney fee; and money claims up to $10,000 can be filed in small claims court, although a collection agency or someone you assign the claim to may not file there. A collection agency you hire is also subject to federal debt-collection law, which bars it from collecting any fee or charge beyond the debt unless the agreement creating the debt expressly authorizes it or the law permits it; that federal law generally does not reach you when you or your employees collect your own rent in your own name. If you still want a collection-fee term, add your own clause after legal advice, tie it to costs you actually incur, and keep attorney fees out of it.

title: Notice and Filing Fees Are Not Offered
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute authorizes, caps or bars a lease charge for preparing, posting or serving a notice (for example a five-day demand for rent or a notice to cure) or for filing an eviction. Such a term is not expressly barred, but the library does not offer one. Serving the notices the Landlord and Tenant Act requires is part of using your own remedies: the Act sets how they are served (personally, to a family member over 12 living with the tenant, or by posting plus certified mail) and puts no charge on the tenant for it. A notice or filing fee fixed in advance is a stipulated amount of damages, which Oklahoma enforces only where the actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, and contract penalties are void; the cost of a notice or a filing is easy to document. A lease also may not make the tenant agree to pay your attorney fees, so a fee that covers a lawyer's notice or filing work is unenforceable. What the law gives you instead: when you win an eviction or a suit on the lease, the court awards a reasonable attorney fee and allows court costs. No Oklahoma court decision on notice or filing fees in leases was reviewed. If you still want such a fee, add your own clause after legal advice, limit it to out-of-pocket costs you can document, and keep attorney fees out of it.

title: Late Fees and the Subsidy Portion of Rent
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute addresses late fees on the part of the rent that a housing subsidy pays. For a Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) tenancy, federal rules settle the main point: the family is not responsible for paying the part of the rent covered by the housing assistance payment, and the housing authority's failure to pay it is not a violation of the lease, so during the lease you may not end the tenancy for the authority's nonpayment. Do not charge the tenant a late fee, or count a payment as late, because the subsidy arrived late. A late fee on the tenant's own share is governed by your lease and Oklahoma's ordinary rules (no statutory cap, but a fixed fee must be a reasonable estimate of your real cost; see the late fee row). The HUD tenancy addendum must be added word for word to a voucher lease and controls over any other lease term, so check that your late-fee clause does not conflict with it. If the housing authority pays its share late, the HAP contract must provide for a late-payment penalty against the authority, but only if such penalties follow local practice for tenants' late rent, you charge them to assisted and unassisted tenants alike, and you charge your tenant a penalty for late payment of the tenant's own share; HUD can excuse the authority when the delay was beyond its control. Other programs (project-based Section 8, public housing, tax-credit properties and other rental assistance) have their own rules; follow the program's required lease terms.

title: No Lockout for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Oklahoma does not allow you to lock out a tenant for unpaid rent, and a lease cannot give you that right. There is no opt-in lockout procedure with advance notice and key access like some states have. You may not remove or exclude a tenant from the unit except through the court eviction process. If you wrongfully remove or exclude a tenant, the tenant may recover possession in court or end the lease, and either way recover up to twice the average monthly rent or twice the tenant's actual damages, whichever is greater; if the lease ends you must also return the deposit and all prepaid and unearned rent. A lease term allowing a lockout would be a waiver of the tenant's rights under the Landlord and Tenant Act, which a lease cannot contain, and it is unenforceable. Using or helping someone use force to enter or keep possession of another's property, except as the law allows, is a misdemeanor. Cutting off heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service you are required to supply gives the tenant its own remedies, including ending the lease or recovering damages. The lawful route for unpaid rent is a written demand for payment, then termination if the tenant does not pay within five days, then an eviction case; after judgment the sheriff removes the tenant under the court's writ. The sheriff's quick removal procedure for squatters does not apply to current or former tenants. Two separate rules are not lockouts: an older statute lets a landlord re-enter, after ten days' notice to quit, when a tenant for a term of two years or less assigns without the landlord's written consent (it does not cover unpaid rent, and how it fits with the Landlord and Tenant Act is a question for the courts); and the landlord's statutory lien on some of the tenant's property has its own rules (see the landlord's lien row).

title: Requiring Renter's Insurance
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute regulates a lease requirement that the tenant carry renter's insurance. There is no rule that the tenant may choose the insurer, no procedure or fee limit for coverage you buy on the tenant's behalf if the tenant does not, no required statement that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings, and no renter's or flood insurance notice before signing.

A lease may therefore require the tenant to carry insurance; the library's Tenant's Property and Renter's Insurance clause does that for Oklahoma without any term limiting your own liability, because a lease term limiting either party's liability for damage or injury to persons or property caused by either party's acts or omissions in operating or maintaining the unit or the premises is unenforceable in Oklahoma.

Points to keep in mind: (1) Let the tenant buy from any licensed insurer. Oklahoma's insurance code forbids requiring, as a condition of a sale of property or a loan, that insurance be bought through a particular agent or insurer; it does not mention leases, but following it is the cautious course. (2) Do not sell or offer policies to tenants yourself for compensation unless you hold an insurance producer license; Oklahoma created a special limited license only for self-storage operators.

(3) If the lease lets you buy coverage when the tenant fails to, a charge you then pass on to the tenant counts as rent under the Act, and you should charge only the actual premium, since no statute authorizes an added administrative fee and fixed charges must survive Oklahoma's penalty rules. (4) If you know the unit flooded in the past five years, the lease must say so prominently in writing (see the flooding disclosure).

title: Online Tenant Portals
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute regulates online tenant portals or bars you from requiring that rent be paid through one. Three rules still shape how you use a portal. First, electronic records and signatures count only between parties who have agreed to do business electronically, and a tenant who agreed may later refuse to conduct further transactions electronically; that right cannot be waived in the lease. So you may offer the portal for notices and signatures, but you cannot make it the only way the tenant may give you a notice, and an electronic record you send counts as a writing only if the tenant can print or store it.

Second, where a statute requires a notice to be delivered a particular way, it must still be delivered that way: notices ending a tenancy must be served personally, on a family member over 12 living with the tenant, or by posting and certified mail, not through the portal. Third, if the portal adds a surcharge when the tenant pays by credit card, follow Oklahoma's surcharge statute, which reaches anyone doing business in any sale, service or lease transaction: post the surcharge clearly where the tenant starts and completes an online payment (on the portal's home page and its payment page), keep it to the lesser of 2% of the payment or your actual card-processing cost, and charge no surcharge at all if the portal accepts only credit cards.

No court decision on whether that statute reaches rent was reviewed, so follow it. The library's optional Online Tenant Portal clause keeps notices by portal voluntary and promises a fee-free way to pay when the portal is down.

title: No Rule on Charging Separately for Parking
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to offer parking separately from the unit ("unbundled" parking), to let a tenant decline a parking space and pay less rent, or bars you from including parking in the rent or charging a separate parking fee. You may do either; the lease decides. A parking fee the lease requires counts as rent under the Landlord and Tenant Act, so list it with the other fees, state which space or area the tenant may use, and keep any parking rules reasonable and applied fairly to all tenants. Towing from your lot has its own statutory rules (see the towing row). Local zoning codes can set parking requirements for buildings.

title: Insurance Claims Against the Tenant
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute protects a tenant from a claim by you, or by your insurer after it pays you, for a fire or other loss the tenant caused, and no statute treats an accidental fire specially. Under Oklahoma's standard fire policy, your insurer may require you to assign it your right of recovery against anyone responsible for the loss, to the extent it pays. Whether the tenant is liable is a matter of ordinary law: the tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or let anyone else do so, and the Landlord and Tenant Act's casualty and repair rules withhold the tenant's own remedies when the damage was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a family member, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal there with the tenant's consent. A lease cannot shift this in either direction. A lease term limiting or excusing either party's liability for damage to property caused by either party's acts or omissions in operating or maintaining the unit or the premises is unenforceable in Oklahoma. A clause in which you agree to look only to your own insurance, give up your insurer's right to pursue the tenant (a waiver of subrogation), or make the tenant an insured so the insurer cannot recover from the tenant, risks being unenforceable for that reason; no court decision on such clauses was reviewed, and the library offers none. The practical protection for both sides is the tenant's own renter's insurance with liability coverage, which a lease may require.

title: Deadlines to Sue
bodyText: Oklahoma has no special deadline for landlord-tenant lawsuits; the general limitation periods apply, counted from when the claim arose. A suit on a written lease (for unpaid rent, damages under the lease, or other breach) must be filed within five years. A suit on an oral lease, or on a liability created by statute other than a penalty or forfeiture, must be filed within three years. A suit for injuring or taking personal property, for trespass on real property, or for fraud (counted from discovery of the fraud) must be filed within two years. A suit on a statute for a penalty or forfeiture must be filed within one year unless that statute sets its own period; whether the Landlord and Tenant Act's double-rent remedies count as penalties for this purpose is a question for the courts, so treat those claims as subject to the one-year period. Partial payments restart the clock: in a case founded on contract, if any part of the principal or interest is paid, or the tenant acknowledges the debt or promises to pay it, you may sue within the full period counted from that payment, acknowledgment or promise, but an acknowledgment or promise counts only if it is in writing and signed by the tenant. Time does not run while the tenant is out of the state or hiding, unless the tenant can be served by a method that reaches people outside the state. If a timely suit fails other than on the merits, a new suit may be filed within one year. Once a claim is barred, it can be used only as a counterclaim or setoff. A lease term shortening the time to sue is void. Separately, a tenant who does not make written demand for the deposit within six months after the tenancy ends loses it, and a debt collector may not threaten to sue on a time-barred debt.

title: No State Confidentiality Duty for Victim Information
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a private landlord to keep confidential the fact that an applicant or tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking, or the protective order or other papers the tenant gives you, and no Oklahoma statute bars you from asking for the protective order the tenant must give you to end a lease early as a victim. Oklahoma's Address Confidentiality Program, run by the Attorney General, lets a certified victim use an address designated by the Attorney General in place of the real one. The law requires state and local agencies, not private landlords, to accept that substitute address, and it bars agency employees, not landlords, from disclosing a participant's real address. Oklahoma also makes certain records confidential in the hands of public utilities (a victim's certification letter for a utility deposit waiver) and of certified domestic violence programs; those rules do not reach landlords. Federal law is different for some properties: if your property is in a federal covered housing program (for example public housing, the Housing Choice Voucher program or a low-income housing tax credit property), you must keep any information a tenant or applicant submits to claim protection as a victim, including the fact of being a victim, in confidence, may not put it in any shared database, and may not disclose it unless the person asks or consents in writing, it is required in an eviction proceeding over the protections, or other law requires it. The cautious course for every landlord: keep protective orders and victim documents in a restricted file, share them only with staff who need them to act, never tell the abuser, other residents or outside callers where the victim lives, which unit is theirs, or that they have reported abuse, and do not list a victim's status in screening or tenant databases.

title: No Special Deposit Rule After a Victim Ends the Lease
bodyText: Oklahoma has no special security-deposit rule for a tenant who ends a lease as a victim of domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking. The ordinary deposit rule applies: after the tenancy ends, the tenant delivers possession and the tenant makes a written demand, you may apply the deposit to accrued rent and to damages caused by the tenant's noncompliance, itemized in a written statement, and must return the balance within 45 days; if the tenant makes no written demand within six months after the tenancy ends, the deposit reverts to you. Because the victim may end the lease without penalty, do not deduct an early-termination fee, a reletting charge or rent for the rest of the term. The law does not say whether a victim's termination ends the lease for co-tenants who stay, or whether the 45 days for a shared deposit wait until every tenant has moved out, and no Oklahoma case was read on either point. The cautious course: when a victim leaves and a co-tenant stays, get a written agreement signed by all tenants saying whether the deposit stays in place for the remaining tenants or how it is divided now, and if they will not agree, account to the departing victim for that tenant's share within 45 days of the victim's written demand rather than waiting for the others to leave. Oklahoma's separate rule waiving initial utility deposits for victims applies to public utilities, not to landlords.

title: Victims Cannot Be Evicted for the Violence
bodyText: You may not deny, refuse to renew or terminate a tenancy because an applicant, tenant or household member is a victim or alleged victim of domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking, whether or not there is a current protective order, and you may not deny a tenancy to or retaliate against someone because they earlier ended a lease as a victim. This means you should not file an eviction or end a tenancy because of the violence itself, because police were called to the unit, or because of crimes committed against the tenant. Oklahoma separately makes criminal activity by a tenant, a household member or a guest that threatens other residents grounds for immediate termination; that rule has no victim exception in its own words, and no Oklahoma case was read on how the two rules fit together, so the cautious course is never to use the criminal-activity ground against a tenant for violence of which the tenant or a household member was the victim. You may still end a victim's tenancy for reasons that have nothing to do with the violence, such as unpaid rent, on the same terms as any other tenant. Oklahoma has no statute letting you split (bifurcate) a lease to remove only the abuser: if the abuser is a tenant on the lease, any eviction must go through the courts against that tenant for that tenant's own breach, and a protective order that orders the abuser to stay away from the residence is enforced by the police and the court, not by you. If your property is in a federal covered housing program (public housing, Housing Choice Vouchers, low-income housing tax credit and other listed programs), federal law adds its own protections: the violence is not good cause or a serious lease violation, you may bifurcate the lease to evict the abuser while keeping the victim, you may ask in writing for documentation, and you must give the federal notice of rights, with the certification form, to an applicant you turn down, to a tenant at admission, and with any eviction or termination notice.

title: No Victim Lock-Change Statute
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute gives a victim of domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking a right to have the locks changed, requires you to change them, says who pays, or voids a lease term on lock changes. The general rule against lockouts still applies: if you wrongfully remove or exclude a tenant from possession, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to twice the average monthly rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater. A protective order changes the picture for the person it restrains. Every Oklahoma protective order tells the restrained person to avoid the protected person's residence, and the sheriff will help put the protected person in possession of the residence on request; violating the order is a crime. No statute says whether a landlord who changes the locks to keep out a co-tenant named in such an order has "wrongfully" excluded that co-tenant, and no Oklahoma case was read on it. The cautious course: when a tenant gives you a protective order that requires a household member to avoid the residence, change or rekey the locks promptly at the protected tenant's request, give new keys only to the protected tenant and other tenants the order does not restrain, refuse the restrained person a key while the order is in effect, and let the police handle any visit to collect belongings. Do not change locks against a co-tenant on the strength of an accusation, an expired or dismissed order, or an order that does not cover the residence; in that case the remedy is the court. Agree with the tenant in writing who pays for the lock change before doing the work, and charge no more than your actual cost.

title: Domestic Violence Law Citations Current in Oklahoma
bodyText: Oklahoma's victim protections for tenants sit in the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (the early-termination right and the ban on denying, refusing to renew or ending a tenancy because someone is a victim). Those provisions do not cross-refer to the protective-order law, so no cross-reference in them can go stale; they simply say "protective order" without defining it. The protective-order law is current and still sits where it always has: the Protection from Domestic Abuse Act at the start of Title 22 (Criminal Procedure), sections 60 to 60.20, with the Uniform Interstate Enforcement of Domestic Violence Protection Orders Act right after it (sections 60.21 to 60.29). Two sections in that run were renumbered by the editors to fix duplicate numbers, so older forms and articles may cite the wrong number: the Address Confidentiality Program is now section 60.14 (formerly 60.13), and the section on police duties and emergency temporary orders when court is closed is now section 60.16 (formerly 60.14). The old sections 60.13 and 60.15 are repealed. The orders a tenant may show you go by several names: emergency temporary order, emergency ex parte order, final protective order, and victim protection order (VPO). All are orders under the Protection from Domestic Abuse Act, valid statewide and nationwide, and an order from another state or a tribal court is presumed valid. Final orders usually last up to five years and some are continuous. Treat any of them as a protective order unless a court has vacated it. The Address Confidentiality Program moved from the Secretary of State to the Attorney General in 2008; apply to or check with the Attorney General's office.

title: What Proof a Victim Must Give
bodyText: Oklahoma's two victim protections for tenants ask for different proof. To end a lease early without penalty, a victim of domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking must give you written notice and a protective order of an incident of that violence within 30 days of the incident. The 30 days run from the incident, not from the date the order was issued, and you may waive the time limit. The statute names no other document: a police report, an advocate's letter or the tenant's own statement does not trigger the early-termination right by itself, although you may always agree to release a tenant. The Act does not define "protective order"; Oklahoma's protective-order law issues emergency temporary orders, emergency ex parte orders and final orders, and treats orders from other states and tribal courts as valid. The cautious course is to accept any of them, and a copy is enough unless you have a real reason to doubt it. The ban on denying, refusing to renew or ending a tenancy because someone is a victim needs no document at all: it applies whether or not there is a current protective order, and to alleged victims too, so do not demand proof before deciding not to treat someone worse because of the violence. Other Oklahoma laws accept more kinds of proof (for example, public utilities must waive a victim's initial deposit on a protective order, a statement from law enforcement, or a certified domestic violence program's certification letter), but those rules do not apply to landlords. If your property is in a federal covered housing program, federal law lets you ask in writing for documentation and gives the tenant 14 business days; acceptable proof includes the HUD self-certification form, a statement signed by a victim service provider, attorney, medical or mental health professional, or a police, court or agency record, and you may accept the tenant's own statement.

title: No Separate State Ban on Protected-Class Questions
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute separately forbids a landlord to ask an applicant or tenant about race, color, religion, gender, national origin, age, familial status or disability, or to keep records of those traits. Oklahoma's fair housing law reaches questions in two other ways. First, it is unlawful to make, print or publish any notice, statement or advertisement about renting housing that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on a protected class; an application form or a spoken question that signals such a preference can fall within that ban. Second, refusing to rent, or setting different terms, because of a protected class is unlawful, and asking about a protected trait is strong evidence of the reason for a decision. Federal fair housing law applies too, and its rules on questions are stricter for disability: federal regulations treat it as unlawful to ask whether an applicant or anyone who will live with them has a disability, or about its nature or severity, with narrow exceptions (for example, asking all applicants whether they can meet the requirements of tenancy, or whether they qualify for housing reserved for people with disabilities). The same federal rule lets you ask every applicant, whether or not they have a disability, whether they currently use or are addicted to a controlled substance illegally, and whether they have been convicted of illegally making or distributing one. Federal rules also say the statement ban covers spoken statements and written documents, application forms included. The cautious course: ask every applicant the same written questions, limited to what you need to decide (identity, income, rental history, references, the number of occupants, and any criminal-history criteria you apply to everyone); do not ask about religion, national origin, pregnancy or plans to have children, marital status or medical conditions; ask about disability only when the applicant requests an accommodation or modification and the disability or need is not obvious; and keep any accommodation papers separate from the tenant file. Oklahoma also bars employers and public agencies, not landlords, from requiring disclosure of sealed protective-order records.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText:
Both Oklahoma and federal fair housing law require you to make reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices and services when a person with a disability needs one to have an equal opportunity to use and enjoy a home, including common areas (for example, a reserved parking space near the unit, or an assistance animal despite a no-pets rule). Both also require you to allow reasonable modifications of the premises that a person with a disability needs, made at that person's expense. You may ask for a reasonable description of the work and assurances that it will be done well and with any required permits.

Restoration: where it is reasonable, you may make permission conditional on the tenant restoring the inside of the unit at the end of the tenancy, apart from normal wear and tear; you cannot require the tenant to undo changes that would not get in the way of the next tenant (such as a widened doorway or wall reinforcement). Oklahoma's law adds that the tenant must provide a surety bond guaranteeing restoration where restoration is needed to make the unit suitable for tenants without disabilities.

Federal law does not mention bonds; it forbids raising the security deposit and allows, only where necessary to be reasonably sure money will be there, an agreement for the tenant to pay a reasonable amount, not more than the restoration cost, into an interest-bearing escrow account, with the interest going to the tenant. Because federal law applies in Oklahoma too, the cautious course is to ask for a bond or escrow only when restoration will really be needed and costly, and to let the tenant choose the escrow instead of a bond.

No Oklahoma or federal statute requires the lease itself to state your right to require restoration; the library's optional clause does so if you want it. Buildings of four or more units first occupied after March 13, 1991 must meet accessible design requirements: every unit if the building has an elevator, and the ground-floor units if it does not. You need not rent to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property. Small landlords exempt from Oklahoma's act may still be covered by federal law.

title: No Criminal Penalty for Refusing an Assistance Animal; Civil Remedies Apply
bodyText: Oklahoma has no criminal penalty aimed at a landlord who refuses to rent, or ends a tenancy, because of a tenant's guide, signal, service or assistance animal. The penalties that do exist are civil. Under Oklahoma's fair housing law, refusing to rent to a blind, deaf or disabled person because of a properly trained guide, signal or service dog, or charging an extra nonrefundable fee or an unreasonable deposit for the dog, is a discriminatory housing practice; a court can award actual and punitive damages, attorney fees and court costs, and in a pattern-or-practice case brought by the Attorney General can add a civil penalty of up to $50,000 for a first violation and $100,000 for a later one. Refusing a reasonable accommodation for an assistance animal is also discrimination under Oklahoma and federal law. The Landlord and Tenant Act separately says you may not deny or end a tenancy because of a guide, signal or service dog; its old exception for leases signed before November 1, 1985 no longer matters. Oklahoma's guide-dog access law does carry a criminal penalty (a misdemeanor), but it protects access to public transportation and places open to the public, such as hotels, motels and other lodging, college dormitories, government buildings and buildings to which the general public is invited. It does not list apartments or other rental homes, and its penalty refers only to that access law, not to the housing rule. A leasing office, model unit or clubhouse that you open to the public could fall within it, so let anyone with a guide, signal or service dog in. It is also a crime for anyone to willfully interfere with a service animal's work or to let their own animal attack or interfere with one, which matters if another tenant's pet threatens a service animal.

title: Tenant Information: No Disclosure Statute, but Breach and Disposal Rules
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute specifically bars a landlord from disclosing a tenant's or applicant's information, or says what consent is needed before you share it. Three general rules still govern what you hold. First, Oklahoma's Security Breach Notification Act: if you own or license computerized data that includes a person's name together with a Social Security number, driver license or other government ID number, a financial account or card number with its access code, or biometric data, and that data is accessed and acquired without authorization in a way that causes, or that you reasonably believe has caused or will cause, identity theft or other fraud, you must notify the affected Oklahoma residents without unreasonable delay. If 500 or more Oklahoma residents are affected, you must also notify the Attorney General within 60 days after notifying them. Since January 1, 2026, a business that used reasonable safeguards (risk assessments, layered technical and physical defenses, staff training and an incident response plan) and gave the required notice is shielded from civil penalties; one that did not use them faces damages and penalties. Second, federal law requires anyone who keeps information from tenant screening or credit reports to dispose of it properly, for example by shredding paper and wiping or destroying electronic files. Third, Oklahoma's new consumer data privacy law takes effect January 1, 2027, but it applies only to businesses that control or process personal data of at least 100,000 Oklahoma consumers a year (or 25,000 if more than half their revenue comes from selling personal data), so it will reach only very large management companies. The cautious course: collect only the identification and financial data you need, keep it encrypted or locked away, limit who can see it, do not share tenant files except with the tenant's written consent, your own agents and service providers, or as law or a court requires, answer reference requests with facts you can document, and shred screening reports once you no longer need them.

title: No Statutory Tenant Organizing Right
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute gives residential tenants a right to form or join a tenant association or union, to meet in common areas, or to distribute literature or canvass door to door in a rental property, and none bars a landlord from retaliating against tenants for organizing. Oklahoma's Landlord and Tenant Act has no general anti-retaliation section; its only retaliation rule protects people who ended an earlier lease as victims of domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking. The Oklahoma Constitution's right to assemble peaceably and petition the government is a limit on government, and no Oklahoma case was read applying it to private rental property. Federal fair housing law does make it unlawful to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with anyone for exercising, or helping others exercise, fair housing rights, so acting against tenants who organize around discrimination complaints carries federal risk. If your property receives federal housing assistance, federal program rules may give tenants organizing rights. The cautious course: apply your common-area, posting and solicitation rules the same way to tenant groups as to everyone else, adopt any such rules through the Act's rules procedure, and do not single out organizers for nonrenewal, rent increases or reduced services.

title: No Religious or Cultural Display Statute
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute gives a tenant a right to display a religious or cultural item (such as a mezuzah on the door frame, a cross, a wreath or holiday decorations) against a landlord's rules, and none limits a landlord's rules on such displays. Oklahoma's Religious Freedom Act and the Constitution's guarantee of religious toleration restrain government, not private landlords, and no Oklahoma case was read applying them to a lease. Fair housing law is the real limit. Oklahoma and federal law forbid discriminating because of religion in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental or in services and facilities, so a rule that targets religious items, or is enforced against one faith's items but not others or not against secular decorations, carries risk. The cautious course: write display and decoration rules in neutral terms (size, placement, fire safety, damage to doors and walls, items in hallways), apply them the same way to religious, cultural and secular items, and allow small items fixed to the door frame of the tenant's own unit, such as a mezuzah, unless they cause real damage or a safety problem. Adopt any such rule through the Act's rules procedure.

title: No Political Access or Sign Law; Association Flag Rule
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute gives candidates, campaign workers or petition circulators a right to enter an apartment building or gated rental community to canvass, and none gives tenants a right to post political signs or limits a landlord's rules on them. The criminal trespass law cuts the other way: a person working on behalf of a candidate for political office, or conducting a poll, may enter another's land unless the owner or lawful occupier forbids it orally or in writing, so a canvasser who has not been told to stay away is not trespassing. You may forbid canvassing on property you control by posting or telling the person; whether a tenant may invite a canvasser to the tenant's own door over your objection is a question for the courts. Your lease and rules may therefore control signs, banners and door-to-door solicitation, as long as they are applied evenly and adopted through the Act's rules procedure. Oklahoma's only display statute of this kind is about the U.S. flag, and it binds associations, not landlords: an owners association, condominium association, cooperative association or residential real estate management association may not adopt or enforce a policy, or enter into an agreement, that stops a member of the association from displaying the U.S. flag at a reasonable height of no more than 20 feet on residential property in which that member has a separate ownership interest or a right to exclusive possession or use.
