Membership in an owners association belongs to the recorded owners of lots, so if you own a rented home in an association, you as the member are protected; the statute does not say whether it protects your tenant's flag. The cautious course: let a tenant fly the U.S. flag at a reasonable height in a way that does not damage the property, and if the home is in an association, follow the association's lawful rules (see the association compliance clause). Federal rules on satellite dishes and antennas are a separate topic.

title: No Statutory Guest Rights; Lease May Set Reasonable Limits
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute gives residential tenants a right to have guests, caregivers, home health aides or delivery and service providers come to their home, bars a landlord from charging a fee for guests, or makes such a right non-waivable. Instead, the Landlord and Tenant Act lets the lease set reasonable limits on use of the unit and premises by a tenant or an occupant. A tenant is responsible for guests' conduct in several ways: the tenant must not let anyone on the premises with the tenant's permission disturb other tenants' quiet enjoyment, must not let any person damage the premises, and criminal activity by a guest or other person under the tenant's control is a ground for terminating the lease.

An occupant who breaches a lease condition that would bind the tenant must leave on your written request, and one who refuses within a reasonable time commits a trespass. Limits still apply. A guest rule must be reasonable, apply fairly to all tenants and be adopted through the Act's rules procedure. Fair housing law requires reasonable accommodations, so a rule that keeps out a disabled tenant's caregiver or aide may have to bend. A residents' right to receive visitors does exist in group homes for people with developmental or physical disabilities, but that law governs those homes, not ordinary rentals.

The cautious course: set a clear guest-stay limit in the lease, never charge a fee simply for having guests, and make exceptions for caregivers a tenant needs because of a disability.

title: Barring Non-Tenants and Criminal Trespass
bodyText:
Oklahoma has no trespass statute written for rental housing, but several general rules let you keep people off your property. The criminal trespass law makes it a trespass to enter another's garden, yard, pasture or field after being expressly forbidden, or without permission of the owner or lawful occupant (fine up to $250). People making deliveries, selling, polling or working for a political candidate may enter unless the owner or lawful occupier forbids them orally or in writing, and police, government employees on duty, and emergency and utility workers are exempt.

A business that offers goods or services for sale may give written or personal notice barring a person convicted of a crime on its property, and that person then commits trespass by entering. Whether these laws reach apartment hallways, parking lots and other common areas, and whose permission counts when a tenant has invited the person, is a question for the courts. Two landlord-tenant rules are clearer.

An occupant living with a tenant who breaches a lease condition must leave on your written request, and a person living in the unit without any rental agreement must leave on demand; either commits a trespass by refusing within a reasonable time. Squatters can be removed through the sheriff's verified-complaint process, which does not apply to current or former tenants. The cautious course: bar a non-tenant only for documented conduct on the property that threatened safety or damaged property, give the person a dated written notice (in person if you can) describing the property and the ban, keep a copy, post your property, and call the police rather than removing anyone yourself.

Because a tenant's invitation may undercut a ban, use the optional barred-person lease clause so that admitting a barred person is a lease breach. Never use a ban to remove a tenant, or to penalize a tenant because they are a victim of domestic violence.

title: No Statute on Family Child Care in Rentals
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a landlord to let a tenant run a family child care home, and none sets conditions such as insurance, liability waivers or notice for one. Oklahoma licenses child care through the Department of Human Services: a family child care home cares for seven or fewer children for part of the day, and a large family child care home for eight to twelve. State law limits cities and counties (they may not cut a licensed home's capacity or impose stricter fire and life-safety rules than the state guidelines), but those limits do not bind you as a landlord. The default under the Landlord and Tenant Act favors you: unless you agree otherwise, using the unit for any purpose other than as the tenant's home is a breach and grounds to end the lease. No Oklahoma case was read on whether caring for other people's children at home counts as such a use, so if you are willing to allow it, say so in writing with conditions (a current license, compliance with association rules, liability insurance, and no alterations without consent), using the optional home-business permission clause; if not, rely on the residential-use clause. Two cautions. A lease term that makes the tenant release you from, or indemnify you for, liability for injuries caused by your own or the tenant's acts or omissions in operating or maintaining the unit or premises is unenforceable, so do not rely on a waiver for injuries to children in care; require insurance instead. And a licensed family child care home creates a 2,000-foot zone in which registered sex offenders may not newly move, though a registrant already living nearby need not move.

title: Home Businesses: Not Allowed Unless the Lease Allows Them
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute makes a home-based business a permitted use of a rented home or limits a landlord's power to forbid one. The Landlord and Tenant Act sets the default: unless you and the tenant agree otherwise, the tenant's use of the unit for any purpose other than as the tenant's home is a breach of the lease and grounds to end it. So a lease may ban business use outright (the residential-use clause) or permit a particular business on conditions (the optional home-business permission clause).

No Oklahoma case was read on how much business activity, such as remote office work, turns a home into a use other than as a home; the cautious course is to state in the lease what is allowed. Other rules still matter: county housing codes may regulate mixing business and living uses, cities regulate home occupations through zoning, and a homeowners or condominium association's recorded restrictions may limit businesses. A home child care business has its own licensing rules.

title: Student Housing: Dormitories Are Outside the Act
bodyText: Oklahoma has no landlord-tenant rule written for student housing. Its one student-housing provision is a scope rule: the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not govern residence at an institution, public or private, when the residence is incidental to the institution's educational service (a college dormitory, for example), or occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization in a building run for the organization's benefit (many fraternity and sorority houses), unless the arrangement was set up to avoid the Act. A privately owned apartment building that leases to students, even one marketed as student housing, is not residence at an institution, so the Act applies to it in full. Whether a building a school master-leases from a private owner and assigns to students is covered is a question for the courts; if you are the private owner, treat your lease with the school as a commercial lease and expect the Act to govern any direct lease you sign with a student. There is no state cap, exemption from a rent rule, or special notice for student tenants, because Oklahoma has no rent cap or just-cause rule to exempt them from. Ordinary rules apply: individual or joint leases, guarantors, and deposit rules work the same as for other tenants, and a tenant who is a minor needs care (see the minor-tenant row). Colleges have their own duties for on-campus housing (such as meningococcal vaccine information), which do not reach private landlords.

title: No Employee Background-Check Rule for Landlords
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a landlord to run background checks on apartment employees, maintenance workers or leasing staff, or bars hiring anyone because of a criminal record. Two related rules exist. First, a person who manages or leases property for someone else generally needs an Oklahoma real estate license, and every license applicant must submit to a national criminal history record check before the license issues, which the Real Estate Commission then reviews; the license requirement does not apply to an owner managing its own property, or to its employees doing so as part of managing the owner's property, or to a resident manager who lives on the premises of an apartment building or complex. Second, Oklahoma's mandatory background checks for care workers apply only to nursing facilities, assisted living centers, home care agencies and similar licensed care providers, not to rental housing. Because your staff may enter tenants' homes, the cautious course is to screen anyone who will hold keys or enter units, using a consumer reporting agency and the federal consent and adverse-action steps for employment reports, and to apply the same written criteria to every applicant.

title: No Work Cards for Senior Housing Staff
bodyText: Oklahoma has no work-card, licensing or background-check requirement for employees of apartments or other housing for people 55 and older. Housing for older persons matters in Oklahoma law only as a fair housing exemption: the familial-status rules do not apply to housing designed for elderly persons under a government program, housing for persons 62 and older, or housing operated for occupancy by at least one person 55 or older per unit as the Attorney General's rules provide (federal law adds its own 80 percent, policy and verification conditions). The state's mandatory criminal background checks for workers apply to licensed care settings such as nursing facilities, assisted living centers, residential care homes and home care agencies, so if your senior property also provides care or supportive services it may need a license and those checks; a plain age-restricted apartment community does not. The cautious course is to screen staff who enter units, as for any rental property.

title: No Key-Control Mandate
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a landlord, or a large apartment complex, to adopt a key-control policy, keep a key log, limit master keys, rekey between tenants, or background-check employees who hold keys. The nearest rule is old and narrow: the proprietor or operator of a hotel, apartment hotel or inn must fit guest-room doors with night latches, chains or bolts on the inside that cannot be opened from outside by key or otherwise; that rule is about lodging guest rooms and does not reach ordinary apartments. Your own lease can control keys (the library's keys clause covers issuing keys, returning them and charging for rekeying when keys are not returned), and you remain bound by Oklahoma's entry rules when you or staff use a key to enter a unit. The cautious course for any landlord with staff: keep master and unit keys locked and logged, limit who holds them, collect keys and codes when an employee leaves, change locks or codes between tenants, and screen anyone who will hold keys.

title: No Landlord Registration, and Cities May Not Require It
bodyText: Oklahoma has no statewide landlord registration, rental license or rental registry, and no Oklahoma statute requires you to register a rental with the county assessor or any other office before you rent it. Cities and towns may not require registration of real property, and an ordinance that does is void and unenforceable against owners and lessees. A city may still keep a list of owners or their designees and, to deal with nuisances and dilapidated property, may require you to give contact information for the person responsible for emergencies and maintenance and for a person who receives notices and legal papers. It may not charge a fee for collecting that information, and the information is confidential. A city may also require the owner of a property in an abatement process to name a contact person, without charge, and may enforce occupancy standards set by ordinance and state law. Whether a city "rental license" or "rental permit" counts as a forbidden registration is a question for the courts, so if your city asks for one, get local advice before refusing. The ban names cities and towns, not counties; no Oklahoma statute provides for county rental registration. Separately, your lease must name in writing a person to receive notices and legal papers and the manager and the owner or a person authorized to act for the owner (see the owner disclosure clause).

title: Who Needs a Real Estate License to Rent or Manage for Others
bodyText: You do not need a license to rent out, lease or manage property you own or lease yourself, and the partners, officers or employees of a company that owns the property don't need one to rent or manage it for that company. Anyone else who, for a fee, commission or other pay, rents or leases real estate for someone else, negotiates or lists rentals, solicits tenants, or controls the acceptance or deposit of rent from a resident of a single-family home must hold an Oklahoma real estate license; acting as a licensee without one is unlawful. Exceptions include a resident manager who lives on the premises of an apartment building, duplex, apartment complex or court and leases it as part of that job, an attorney-in-fact completing a specific lease for the owner, a court-appointed receiver or trustee, a tenant paid a small referral fee of up to $100, managers of furnished rooms rented daily for less than 30 days, and employees of a licensed broker leasing subsidized affordable-housing units to eligible households. Oklahoma's landlord law does not require an out-of-state owner to hire an Oklahoma broker or keep an in-state agent for tenant communications; every landlord must instead give tenants in writing the name and address of the manager, of the owner or a person authorized to act for the owner, and of a person to receive notices and legal papers. A broker based outside Oklahoma needs an Oklahoma nonresident license to manage property here. Before you hire a manager, check that the manager is licensed. Business-registration duties for an out-of-state company are not covered here.

title: Government Inspections of Rentals
bodyText:
Oklahoma has no statewide rental inspection program, and no Oklahoma statute requires a rental to be inspected before it is let or during a tenancy. No Oklahoma statute bars local inspections either. Cities may enforce occupancy standards and health ordinances (through a city health officer), may condemn and remove dilapidated buildings, and in counties with a metropolitan area planning commission a city or the county may adopt a housing code that is enforced by systematic inspection. The State Department of Health may get an administrative warrant from a district judge to enter premises to inspect under the Public Health Code.

Your lease cannot authorize an inspector to enter on its own. You may enter with the tenant's consent, which the tenant may not unreasonably refuse, to inspect, repair, supply services or show the unit, at reasonable times and after at least one day's notice, except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable, and you have no other right of entry during the tenancy except as the Landlord and Tenant Act provides or a court orders. An inspector who wants to come in needs the tenant's agreement at the time or whatever legal process the agency has, such as a warrant.

The library's optional Government Inspections clause asks the tenant to cooperate and tell you if they refuse an inspector, without making the lease the tenant's consent.

title: Recording a Lease with the County Clerk
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to record or register a residential lease, and recording does not change any right or duty under the Landlord and Tenant Act. A lease is binding between you and the tenant whether or not it is recorded. Recording matters only against third persons such as a later buyer or lender: a lease for one year or less is good against them without recording if the tenant is in actual possession, but any longer lease, or a lease whose tenant has not yet taken possession, is not valid against them unless it is acknowledged (signed before a notary) and recorded with the county clerk. A recorded lease is notice of its contents to later buyers and lenders. If you rent out property that is your exempt homestead, a lease of more than one year must be in writing and signed by both spouses if both are living and not divorced or legally separated. Oklahoma has no special rule about leases to the owner's relatives. Most residential leases are one year or less and are not recorded; consider recording (or recording a short memorandum of the lease, which no Oklahoma statute regulates) only for a long lease or an option you need to protect against a sale or foreclosure, and get advice on the form.

title: No Good-Cause Notice Rule
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires good cause to end or not renew a residential tenancy, requires a termination notice to state a reason, or requires a lease or notice telling the tenant whether a good-cause law covers the unit. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date without notice unless the parties agreed otherwise, and a periodic tenancy ends on written notice (at least 30 days for month-to-month or at will, at least 7 days for a shorter period), served the way the Landlord and Tenant Act requires. Oklahoma's ban on local rent control covers only the amount of rent, and its ban on local registration covers only registration, so neither expressly forbids a city good-cause rule; whether a city could limit the termination rights the Act gives is a question of local-power law. Federal programs differ: in a Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) tenancy you may end the tenancy during the lease term only for a serious or repeated lease violation, a violation of law tied to the tenant's occupancy or use of the unit, or other good cause, and you must give the tenant a written notice stating the grounds (and the housing authority a copy of any eviction notice). Other subsidized programs have their own rules. Other limits still apply to every tenancy, such as fair housing law and the protections for victims of domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking.

title: No Required Rights and Responsibilities Guide
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to give a tenant a state-published guide or summary of landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities, at signing or at renewal, or to get a signed acknowledgment of one, and no statute directs a state agency to publish one for that purpose. The Oklahoma Real Estate Commission publishes a general information sheet for owners and tenants and a pamphlet on the Landlord and Tenant Act, which you may hand out voluntarily. If a licensed real estate broker manages your property, the Commission's rules do not require the broker to hand tenants a guide either; they treat property management as licensed work, require the broker to keep tenants' damage or security deposits in an Oklahoma escrow account at a federally insured institution, and make the broker owe tenants honesty and reasonable skill and care without becoming the tenant's broker unless that is agreed in writing. The disclosures Oklahoma does require (the person to receive notices, the manager, and the owner or the owner's authorized agent, known flooding, known methamphetamine use, and the federal lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing) are covered in their own rows.

title: No State Limit on Renting Homes in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute limits renting a home in a single-family zone, requires the owner to live on the lot before renting, or regulates short-term rentals, and Oklahoma has no state lot-split or two-unit program with owner-occupancy or minimum-rental-term conditions. Zoning is local: cities may divide their area into districts and regulate the use of buildings and land for residence and other purposes, and the density of population. Oklahoma's ban on local rent control covers only the amount of rent, and its ban on local registration covers only registration; neither stops a city from regulating land use, occupancy standards or rentals through zoning, and a city may enforce occupancy standards set by ordinance and state law. Before you rent a home, especially as a short-term or room-by-room rental, check the city or county zoning code. Separate state rules on who may live in a home still apply, such as the limits on registered sex offenders living together.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute deals with accessory dwelling units (garage apartments, backyard cottages and similar second units on a lot). State law neither allows them by right nor stops cities from limiting them, and it sets no owner-occupancy requirement or minimum rental term for them. Whether you may build or rent one is a matter of local zoning: cities may regulate the use of buildings and land for residence and the density of population. Oklahoma's ban on local rent control covers only the amount of rent and does not reach zoning. Renting an accessory unit as a home is covered by the Landlord and Tenant Act like any other dwelling.

If the unit shares heating, hot water or another essential facility with the main house, or lacks direct access to a street or thoroughfare, it does not meet the Act's test for a unit deemed a single-family residence, and no Oklahoma case was read on how that test applies to accessory units, so treat your duties to keep shared areas clean and safe and to supply running water, hot water and reasonable heat (unless the unit is independently metered) as applying.

The library's optional accessory dwelling unit clause describes the unit and its shared areas.

title: Local Health Departments and Rentals
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute sets health-department rules for rental housing, requires you to give tenants a copy of local health rules on request, or directs tenants to a health department for rental complaints. Oklahoma's public health system is organized by county, district, city-county and city: each city's governing board serves as its board of health, appoints a health officer, and may adopt health ordinances that are not inconsistent with state law or State Board of Health rules; a county board of health may adopt regulations only to protect public health in emergencies, subject to the State Commissioner's approval and no stricter than state law; and a city-county board of health recommends ordinances to the city and county. In counties that use a metropolitan area planning commission, a city or the county may also adopt a housing code covering sanitation, heating, ventilation and similar standards, administered with the city and county health departments. The State Board of Health's own rules do not fill the gap: none of their chapters covers housing or rental sanitation, and the state lodging rules do not regulate living quarters where permanent residents live. One state health law does reach many apartment properties: a swimming pool or spa used by residents (other than a pool at a private home or one run by a homeowners association for its members) is a public pool, which needs a State Department of Health construction permit before it is built and an annual license, must be open to Department inspection, and must be kept sanitary and safe. Check them before renting. Your own sanitation duties under the Landlord and Tenant Act are in the landlord duties row.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate for Rentals
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a lead-safe or lead-free certificate for a rental, an inspection or clearance test before renting, or a certificate attached to the lease. For housing built before 1978, the federal lead-based paint disclosure and the federal pamphlet are required (see the lead-based paint disclosure clause). The Department of Environmental Quality's lead rules say that nothing in the Act or the rules requires a property owner to inspect or test for lead-based paint or to reduce or abate it. What Oklahoma regulates is the work: anyone who performs or offers lead-based paint services (hazard evaluation, detection, reduction, renovation, remodeling, abatement or on-site testing) on pre-1978 housing or child-occupied facilities must be certified by the Department, and the Department applies the federal renovation, repair and painting rules, which it adopts by reference. The owner's exemption for work in a home you own lasts only while no one but you and your immediate family lives there and no child living in the building has been identified as having an elevated blood lead level, so paint-disturbing work in an occupied pre-1978 rental is covered: the firm doing it must be a certified renovation firm using certified renovators, and no more than 60 days before starting it must give the owner and an adult occupant the federal renovation pamphlet and keep proof of delivery. Small jobs (generally no more than 6 square feet of painted surface per room inside or 20 square feet outside, without window replacement, demolition or banned practices) and emergency repairs are treated differently. The federal rule speaks of renovations done for compensation; no text read settles whether an owner's own staff working on its rental fall outside that, so the cautious course is to use a certified firm, or have your own company and staff certified, for paint-disturbing work in older rentals. The Department publishes a lead hazard pamphlet that recommends a lead evaluation before leasing pre-1978 housing; that is advice, not a duty.

title: Dilapidated Buildings, Code Liens and Receivership
bodyText: Oklahoma has no receivership law for substandard rental housing: no statute lets a city, tenant or court appoint a receiver to collect rents and make code repairs, and no special rule applies to buildings with two or more units. (A court may still appoint a receiver in the general cases the civil procedure code allows, such as a mortgage foreclosure.) What Oklahoma does have are local enforcement powers that can reach a rental. After at least 10 days' notice to the owner and any mortgage holder and a hearing, a city may order a dilapidated building torn down and removed (including a building unfit for human occupancy for lack of repairs), board up and secure an unoccupied unsecured building, and treat a building that is unoccupied and has been declared dilapidated or unsecured as an abandoned building; the costs become a lien on the property, equal in priority to property taxes, and the owner's personal debt. A building occupied by a lessee is not an unsecured building. In a county that has adopted a building or fire code, the county building inspector, in an emergency that in the inspector's opinion involves imminent danger to life or health, may have an unsafe building made safe or removed and may vacate its occupants, and those of adjacent buildings; large counties may also remove dilapidated buildings in unincorporated areas. Since November 1, 2025, a city that adopts the Municipal Code Lien Enforcement Act may foreclose in court on code-violation fines, penalties and abatement costs of $1,500 or more against property that is not owner-occupied, which includes most rentals; a city must wait at least six months after recording the lien, and copies of the petition are mailed to the occupants. Oklahoma's ban on local registration expressly lets cities require the name and contact information of the person responsible for a dilapidated property or one in an abatement process, without a fee, so it does not limit these powers.

title: No Duty to Disclose Code or Condemnation Orders
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to tell a tenant or prospective tenant about outstanding inspection reports, code-violation notices, or dilapidation, condemnation or vacate orders on the property. The disclosures Oklahoma does require are the owner and notice contact, known flooding, known methamphetamine use, and the federal lead-based paint disclosure. Orders are not secret, though: before a city tears down a dilapidated building it must post notice on the property and file a notice of dilapidation and lien with the county clerk, and a city foreclosing a code lien must mail the petition to the property's occupants and post a notice on it. The Oklahoma preemption laws do not change any of this. Even without a disclosure statute, renting a unit you know is subject to a demolition, vacate or similar order invites claims, and you still owe a fit and habitable unit from the start of the tenancy, so the cautious course is to fix the problem or tell the applicant in writing before signing. No Oklahoma case on concealment of code orders was reviewed.

title: Rent When a Unit Is Condemned or Ordered Vacated
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute expressly bars you from collecting rent after a unit is condemned, declared dilapidated or ordered vacated, and none of Oklahoma's preemption laws touches the question. The Landlord and Tenant Act's remedies do much of the same work. If your failure to keep the unit fit and habitable makes it uninhabitable or an imminent threat to health and safety and you do not fix it as promptly as conditions require, the tenant may end the lease at once by written notice; for other breaches that materially affect health or safety the tenant may give notice ending the lease in at least 30 days unless you remedy the breach within 14 days. If you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant may, among other remedies, move to reasonable substitute housing and is excused from paying rent while the failure lasts. If fire or other casualty substantially impairs the unit, the tenant may (unless the impairment was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with the tenant's consent) move out at once and end the lease by giving you written notice within one week after moving out (the lease ends on the date of moving out), with deposits and unearned prepaid rent returned, or, if continued occupancy is possible, stay in the usable part and pay rent reduced in proportion. The repair and essential-service rights do not arise until the tenant gives you written notice, and do not arise if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with the tenant's consent. The cautious course: do not charge or collect rent for any period in which a government order or the unit's condition stops the tenant from lawfully living there, and refund any rent paid for that period. If the government takes the property by eminent domain, state acquisition policies call for scheduling projects, as far as practicable, so that no lawful occupant must move from a dwelling without at least 90 days' written notice, but the statute says those policies create no enforceable rights; what happens to the lease and any award is not settled by statute. A clause allocating a condemnation award or ending the lease on a taking is lawful, but the library does not offer one; you may add your own after advice.

title: No Hardship Stay of Eviction; No Moratorium Law
bodyText: Oklahoma has no statute that lets a court delay an eviction because of the tenant's hardship, no statewide eviction moratorium, and no statute that either authorizes or forbids a city or county moratorium. Once you win a forcible entry and detainer case, the court issues the writ on your request; a motion for a new trial (which must be filed within 3 days of judgment) does not stay it, and the writ is carried out after a 48-hour notice to the tenant. A tenant can delay possession only by appealing and posting a supersedeas bond within 2 days of judgment (a judge may extend that to 7 days), and must keep paying current rent into the court clerk's office while the appeal is pending; failing to pay is treated as abandoning the appeal. Federal law adds one hardship stay: if the tenant is a servicemember (or a servicemember's dependent), the unit is their residence and the monthly rent is under the federal limit, you need a court order to evict during military service, and the court must, on request of a servicemember whose ability to pay is materially affected by service, stay the case for 90 days (or another period the court finds just) or adjust the lease obligation. A tenant's bankruptcy filing generally stays an eviction under the federal automatic stay, with exceptions, for example where you obtained a judgment for possession before the filing (subject to the tenant's limited cure-and-deposit procedure) or the eviction is based on endangerment of the property or illegal drug use and you file the required certification; get advice before acting after a filing.

title: No Required Landlord Liability Insurance
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, to prove insurance to a city, or to tie insurance to a rental registration (and cities may not require registration of real property in the first place). Insurance is still prudent, and your lender, an association or a housing program may require it. Your lease may not shift to the tenant, or exempt you from, liability for injury or damage caused by your own or your agents' acts or omissions in operating or maintaining the unit or premises, so insurance, not the lease, is how you protect yourself against that risk. Separately, the owner of a dangerous dog (which can include your tenant) must register it with the city or county animal control authority and show liability insurance or a surety bond of at least $50,000.

title: No Rent-Cap or Just-Cause Exemption Notice
bodyText: Oklahoma has no statewide rent cap, just-cause eviction law or tenant right to buy the building, so there is no exemption from such a law to claim and no statute requiring a lease to say a property is exempt. Cities may not regulate the amount of rent on private rental property (with narrow exceptions for city-owned property, subsidized properties under agreement, and properties assisted with federal Community Development Block Grant funds). The only statewide rent limit is the emergency price rule, which applies to everyone renting in a declared emergency area and has no exemption notice. Do not add an exemption statement copied from another state's lease.

title: No Tenant Protection Act Notice
bodyText: Oklahoma has no tenant protection act of the kind some states have: no statewide cap on rent increases, no just-cause requirement for ending a tenancy, no right for tenants to buy or get first refusal when you sell, and no notice of such rights that a lease must carry. Cities may not regulate the amount of rent on private rental property. The one statewide rent limit applies during a declared emergency: while a Governor's or Presidential emergency declaration lasts and for 30 days afterward you may not rent or offer a dwelling unit in the emergency area for more than 10% above what you charged just before the declaration, and the same limit on dwelling units continues for 180 days after that, unless the increase comes only from factors unrelated to the emergency (with no added profit) or from petroleum and natural gas price increases; no tenant notice is required (see the rent increase row). A periodic tenancy can be ended by written notice without a reason.

title: No Tenant Protection Law on a Repeal Clock
bodyText: No Oklahoma tenant-protection statute is set to expire on a fixed date. The Landlord and Tenant Act and the state ban on local rent control have no sunset. One rule turns on events rather than dates: the emergency rent limit applies only while a Governor's or Presidential emergency declaration covers the area, for 30 days after it, and, for dwelling units, for another 180 days, so check for a current or recent declaration before raising rent in an affected county (see the rent increase row).

title: Rules That Depend on How Many Units You Own
bodyText: Oklahoma's Landlord and Tenant Act applies the same way whether you own one rental or hundreds; it has no small-landlord exemption and no duties that start at a portfolio size. A few rules do turn on numbers. (1) Fair housing: Oklahoma's housing discrimination law does not apply to renting a single-family house you own only if all of these are true: you own no more than three single-family houses (or interests in them) at one time, you rent without using a licensed real estate broker or agent (or the services of an owner of a five-family-or-larger building), and you do not publish a discriminatory notice or advertisement; and if you were not the most recent resident, the exemption covers only one sale or rental in 24 months. Separately, renting rooms or units in a building of no more than four families where you live in one unit is exempt; because the statute makes its whole exemption list subject to the no-broker and no-discriminatory-notice conditions, treat those conditions as applying here too. Read these limbs together: failing any one of them means the law applies. Federal fair housing law has similar exemptions with its own conditions, and its ban on discriminatory advertising applies even to exempt owners. (2) Accessibility design rules for new multifamily construction first occupied after March 1991 cover every unit in a building of four or more units that has an elevator, and the ground-floor units in other buildings of four or more units. (3) Some building-size rules affect owners of small rentals: from January 1, 2027, owners of residential rental properties of four or fewer units may do their own roofing without registering as roofing contractors if they provide all material supervision themselves and install roofing materials according to the adopted building code or the manufacturer's installation instructions, and suppliers and subcontractors on a residential project of four or fewer units none of which is owner-occupied need not send the owner a pre-lien notice before filing a mechanic's lien. (4) A third-party manager needs a real estate license no matter how many units, while an owner managing its own property needs none.

title: Code Variances and Your Tenants
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to give tenants a copy of a sanitary, housing, building or health code variance or exception, or to attach one to the lease. Oklahoma has no statewide sanitary or housing code for rentals with a variance procedure aimed at landlords. Variances that do exist in state law are for construction work: state plumbing, electrical, mechanical and roofing installation code variance and appeal boards can approve a particular installation, and in a county that has adopted a building or fire code the board of county commissioners may, on appeal from the building inspector, vary a code provision in a specific case to avoid practical difficulties or unnecessary hardship (a variance is not an amendment or waiver of the rest of the code). If you rely on a variance for a rental, keep a copy with your property records; telling the tenant about any condition it allows is a sensible practice but not required by statute. The State Board of Health's own rules have no housing or rental sanitation chapter, so they offer no rental variance either.

title: Housing Authority Inspections of Voucher Units
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute deals with refusing, or failing, a housing authority inspection of a subsidized unit, and Oklahoma law does not require you to accept housing vouchers in the first place (see the source of income row; fair housing rules still apply). If you do rent to a Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) family, federal rules control. The housing authority may not approve the tenancy or sign the housing assistance payments (HAP) contract until it has inspected the unit and found that it meets the federal housing quality standards, unless it uses the alternative inspection option described below, or a non-life-threatening deficiencies option under which a unit that has no life-threatening deficiencies may be approved before the other items are fixed; its time to inspect is suspended while the unit is not available for inspection, so making the unit available is in your interest. Under the alternative inspection option, if you and the family agree, the authority may approve the tenancy and sign the contract on the strength of a passing inspection done for another program, such as HOME or tax-credit housing, in the last 24 months; it must still do its own inspection within 30 days of the tenancy request and generally pays nothing until the unit passes (if it also uses the option for minor deficiencies, payments can start while non-life-threatening items are fixed), and once you correct any deficiencies in time it pays back to the contract's start. During the tenancy you must keep the unit up to those standards; after written notice of a deficiency you must correct a life-threatening one within 24 hours and others within 30 days (or an approved extension). If you do not, the authority may withhold and then must abate the assistance payments, and it terminates the HAP contract if the unit is not brought up to standard within 60 days (or a longer period it sets) after abatement; you are not paid for abated periods once payments resume, and you may not end the family's tenancy because the authority withheld or abated payments. For your own inspections, Oklahoma's entry rules apply: the tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry on one day's notice. Federal rules require the family to let the housing authority inspect the unit at reasonable times after reasonable notice; what the authority may do to a family that refuses (such as ending its assistance) is set by a federal rule and the authority's plan.

title: Abated Subsidy When a Voucher Unit Fails Standards
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute prorates rent or a housing subsidy when a subsidized unit is unfit. Oklahoma's general rules apply to every tenancy: if fire or other casualty substantially impairs the unit, a tenant who stays can vacate the unusable part and owes rent reduced in proportion to the drop in fair rental value (unless the impairment was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with the tenant's consent), and the repair and essential-service remedies can reduce or excuse rent after written notice (see the tenant remedies row). For a Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) tenancy, federal rules decide what happens to the subsidy. If you do not correct a housing quality deficiency in time after written notice, the housing authority may withhold and then must abate its assistance payments; you get no payment for the abated period even if you later make the repairs, and the authority terminates the HAP contract if the unit is still not up to standard 60 days (or a longer period it sets) after abatement. You may not shift the abated subsidy to the family: the family is not responsible for the part of the rent covered by the assistance payment, and you may not end the tenancy because payments were withheld or abated. During abatement the family may end the tenancy by notifying you and the authority. If the authority finds the family caused a deficiency beyond ordinary use, it may waive your duty to fix it, and then it may not withhold or abate your payment. Other subsidy programs have their own rules.

title: Submetering and Billing Tenants for Electricity
bodyText: How you may bill tenants for electricity depends on who sells it to you. If your electric supplier is regulated by the Oklahoma Corporation Commission (an investor-owned utility, or a rural electric cooperative that has not voted to exempt itself from Commission regulation), the Commission's rules say that, except as those rules allow, no customer may separately meter and separately bill another customer for electricity. You may always include the cost of electricity in the rent. The statewide standard for apartment complexes and other multiple residences is one utility meter per residence, billed to the occupant at the residential rate. A building served through a single utility meter may instead use a submeter system owned by you only if the Commission approves it, on a joint letter from you and the utility to the Commission's Public Utility Division Director or, if that is denied or not made, on a formal application; the Commission considers whether the system encourages conservation of energy, efficient use of utility facilities and equitable rates, and the building then pays the utility's commercial rate. If you use approved submeters, you must: use submeters that meet the current ANSI C12 standard or an equivalent ANSI standard as later amended; read them within three business days after the utility reads its meter; keep, for each tenant served, the readings, consumption, amount billed and payments; divide the utility's bill among tenants in the manner approved by and on file with the Public Utility Division Director; on a tenant's request, give a clear and concise statement of that tenant's actual consumption for each billing period of the prior year; test a submeter when a tenant demands it, on the same terms a utility follows; and refund or back-bill for fast, slow or faulty submeters within the same limits a utility must follow. A utility that learns a customer is reselling electricity must report it to the Commission. If you buy electricity from a city-owned utility, these Commission rules do not apply; instead state law caps what you may charge a residential tenant at 10% above your cost for each billing cycle and requires your bill to show your per-unit cost and each fee in dollars and cents (see the resale row). A cooperative that has voted to leave Commission regulation sets its own terms of service; ask it before submetering. No Oklahoma case was read on whether a landlord who submeters becomes a regulated utility; the Commission's rules treat you as a customer using customer submeters, and the safe course is to submeter only with Commission approval and to follow the duties above.

title: Charging Tenants for Utilities Not Separately Metered
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute makes a lease term unenforceable just because it has the tenant pay for a utility that is not separately metered to the unit. What you may do depends on the utility and who supplies it. Electricity from a Corporation Commission-regulated utility: you may include its cost in the rent, but you may not separately meter and separately bill tenants for it unless the Commission has approved a submeter system for the building (see the submetering row). Natural gas from a Commission-regulated utility: you may include the cost of gas in the rent, and you may use any formula to compute the energy part of the rent, as long as that part is not separately metered and billed as "gas". Submetering gas and billing tenants for it is not allowed, and a customer who does so can have its gas service terminated by the utility; reselling gas at all needs a Commission-approved tariff or special contract. Newly built apartment buildings must be individually metered for gas unless the Commission approves otherwise. Water from a Commission-regulated water utility: the utility may not sell water to you for resale unless a Commission-approved tariff authorizes resale and you yourself have Commission-approved tariffs, rate schedules, rules and regulations covering the resale (or are exempt by law from that requirement). Electricity, gas, water or sewer service bought from a city and resold to a residential tenant: you may not charge more than 10% above your cost for each billing cycle, and your bill must show the per-unit cost you paid and each fee or charge in dollars and cents; a willful violation is a misdemeanor and makes you liable for treble damages. Reselling water can also affect how the Department of Environmental Quality classifies your property: a multi-family dwelling that buys water from a permitted system is kept out of the "public water supply system" class only if it is built, inspected and maintained under an approved plumbing code and does not treat or resell the water, so a building that bills tenants for water and has 15 or more service connections or regularly serves 25 or more people should ask the Department whether it needs a permit. No Oklahoma case was read on whether dividing a city master-meter bill among tenants by a formula is a "resale"; the cautious course is to charge no more than your cost plus 10% and to show the per-unit cost and every fee on each bill. Utility charges the lease makes payable to you are rent under the Landlord and Tenant Act. The library does not offer a ready-made clause for billing tenants by submeter or allocation formula, because whether and how you may do it turns on who supplies the utility, on Commission approval and on the resale cap; billing tenants this way is lawful in some arrangements, and you may add your own clause after getting advice. City utilities and cooperatives that have left Commission regulation set their own terms of service.

title: No Landlord Shutoff of Submetered Utilities
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute or Corporation Commission rule gives a landlord who submeters or otherwise supplies a utility its own right to shut that service off for nonpayment. The Commission's disconnection rules (written notice periods, weather limits, medical and payment-plan delays) bind utilities, not landlords; the submetering rules govern meters, records, billing and testing, not shutoffs. Under the Landlord and Tenant Act, if, contrary to the lease or your statutory duties, you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant may give you written notice and then end the lease, buy reasonable amounts of the service and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from rent, recover damages for the reduced rental value, or move to reasonable substitute housing and be excused from paying rent while the failure lasts. These rights do not arise if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with the tenant's consent. Except in a single-family residence, you must supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat unless the service comes through a direct and independently metered utility connection to the unit. No Oklahoma case was read on whether a landlord's own submeter is such a connection; the cautious course is to treat yourself as responsible for those services in a submetered building. A landlord who wrongfully removes or excludes a tenant is liable for up to twice the average monthly rent or twice the tenant's actual damages, whichever is greater; no Oklahoma case was read on whether cutting off utilities counts, so do not use a shutoff to collect. Utility charges the lease makes payable to you are rent: collect them with the five-day written demand for unpaid rent and, if needed, an eviction case. If the utility itself moves to disconnect a master-metered building, it must also post the notice in a common area at least ten days before disconnection and may contract with tenants directly for service (see the landlord-held account row).

title: Utility Disconnection Rules
bodyText: A tenant's own utility shutoff is between the tenant and the utility, but it helps to know the rules. Electric, natural gas and water utilities regulated by the Oklahoma Corporation Commission must follow its disconnection rules. For a residential customer behind on the bill, the utility must mail written notice at least 10 days before disconnecting, and from November 15 through April 15 it must also give a second notice at least 48 hours (two business days) before disconnecting; this is an added notice, not a winter ban. The utility may disconnect only on the date in the notice or within 30 days after it, during business hours, not in the last two hours of the business day, not on a holiday, and not from noon Friday until Monday morning. The utility must hold off when the National Weather Service forecasts a temperature below 32 degrees Fahrenheit within the next 24 hours and the service is used for heat, or a heat index of 101 degrees or more is forecast for the day of disconnection (or is actually reached) and the service is used for cooling. The Commission may also order a temporary ban on disconnections during extremely severe weather or other dangerous conditions; no Oklahoma statute bars disconnection during a declared storm or other emergency by itself. Other delays: at least 20 days for a customer awaiting financial assistance; 30 days (extendable once by 30 days) for a certified life-threatening medical condition with electric or gas service; five more business days, at the Commission's request, for a registered customer who is 65 or older or has a qualifying disability; and a deferred payment agreement the utility must offer before disconnecting (for water, on balances over $50). A utility may not disconnect a customer for a previous occupant's unpaid bill unless that person still lives there or uses the service. If a master-metered building is to be disconnected, the notice must also be posted in a common area at least 10 days before, and the utility may contract with tenants directly. These rules do not bind city-owned utilities, rural water districts, or electric cooperatives that have voted to leave Commission regulation, which set their own terms. One statute does reach owners: where a public entity providing sewer service asks the public water provider to cut off water for a delinquent sewer account, it must give the account holder and the property owner at least 30 days' notice of the proposed date, under notice-and-hearing procedures it must adopt. To hear about a tenant's pending shutoff, ask the tenant to name you to receive disconnection notices (see the notice designee row).

title: Naming the Landlord to Receive Utility Shutoff Notices
bodyText:
Oklahoma Corporation Commission rules require every regulated electric, natural gas and water utility to let a residential customer designate a consenting individual or agency to receive the customer's disconnection notices. Electric utilities also recognize a "consumer representative" the customer designates under the utility's terms of service to handle billing, payment and disconnection matters. Only the account holder can make these designations: if the tenant holds the account, you cannot sign yourself up, but the tenant can name you and you can consent.

The library's optional clause has the tenant authorize you to be listed as a contact for disconnection notices and sign the utility's form, and authorize the utility to confirm whether service is connected and in the tenant's name; it does not make you responsible for the tenant's bills or oblige any utility to notify you. For electricity, a utility may release a customer's account information to a third party when the customer gives written consent, so a signed authorization also helps there.

City-owned utilities, rural water districts and electric cooperatives that have left Commission regulation are not bound by these Commission rules; ask them whether they offer third-party notice. No Oklahoma statute requires a landlord to be told of a tenant's pending shutoff. Where a city sewer provider asks a separate water provider to cut off water for a delinquent sewer account, the property owner is entitled to 30 days' notice by statute (see the disconnection rules row).

title: Utilities in the Landlord's Name
bodyText: When a utility account for the rental is in your name (for example a master-metered building, or a utility you include in the rent), these rules apply. If, contrary to the lease or your statutory duties, you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant may give you written notice and then end the lease, buy reasonable amounts of the service and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from rent, recover damages for the reduced rental value, or move to reasonable substitute housing and be excused from rent while the failure lasts. These rights do not arise if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with the tenant's consent. Except in a single-family residence, you must supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat unless the unit has its own direct and independently metered utility connection. Closing or letting lapse an account you hold, to pressure a tenant, invites these remedies and a wrongful-exclusion claim. If a Corporation Commission-regulated electric, gas or water utility moves to disconnect a master-metered apartment complex, building or trailer court, it must also post the disconnection notice in a common area at least 10 days before disconnecting, and it may contract with tenants directly for residential service. A regulated utility may not disconnect a customer for a previous owner's or occupant's unpaid bill unless that person still lives there or uses the service, and an electric utility may not make a new customer pay another person's bill as a condition of service except where that person remains an occupant or user; so your unpaid account should not follow a tenant who opens service in the tenant's own name. If a tenant refuses the utility access to its meter, the utility is to try to notify you as property owner before disconnecting. Where a public sewer provider asks a separate water provider to cut off water for a delinquent sewer account, it must give you as property owner, and the account holder, at least 30 days' notice. No Oklahoma statute or Commission rule lets tenants petition for a receiver because the landlord did not pay a utility, sets damages for failing to identify tenants to a utility, or requires a master-meter owner to give the utility a tenant list. City utilities, rural water districts and cooperatives that have left Commission regulation set their own terms.

title: Moving Utility Accounts Between Landlord and Tenant
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute requires a tenant to move utility accounts into the tenant's name by a deadline, or lets a landlord cut off service the tenant did not transfer; the lease decides who holds each account (see the optional transfer clause). Corporation Commission rules for regulated electric, gas and water utilities fill in the mechanics. A customer closing an account may have to give up to five days' notice and pays for service until then. An electric utility may leave service on between occupants if it reads the meter at both ends, but a new occupant who uses the service without applying is liable for it at the applicable rate and may be disconnected after at least 24 hours' written notice. A utility may not disconnect a new occupant for a previous occupant's unpaid bill unless that person still lives there or uses the service. If service you agreed to provide, or a tenant's service you control, is cut off because of a transfer dispute, the tenant may have remedies under the Landlord and Tenant Act for a willful or negligent failure to supply essential services; do not use a shutoff to force a transfer. In a protective-order case, a court may, after notice and hearing, order a public utility provider to transfer a household utility account to the protected person, who then becomes responsible for it. City utilities, rural water districts and cooperatives that have left Commission regulation set their own account rules.

If natural gas for the property comes from a utility the Corporation Commission regulates, make the gas account the tenant's responsibility from the start of the term rather than keeping it in your name and billing the tenant back: no Commission order or Oklahoma case decides whether passing a regulated gas bill through to a tenant is gas resold by a consumer under the Commission's rules.

title: Caps on Rebilling Utilities to Tenants
bodyText:
If you buy electricity, natural gas, water or sewer service from a city and resell it to a residential tenant, Oklahoma caps what you may charge: no more than 10% above your cost for each billing cycle. The law speaks of buying from a municipality; no Oklahoma case was read on whether service bought from a city's public utility trust counts, so the cautious course is to follow the cap there too. Each bill you give the tenant must separately show the per-unit cost of what you bought and the actual amount of each fee or charge in dollars and cents.

A willful violation is a misdemeanor, and you are liable to the tenant for treble damages, based on the total of each bill that exceeded the cap; the Attorney General enforces the law. The cap does not apply to commercial leases of electricity or gas. Service from a Corporation Commission-regulated utility is different: you may build its cost into the rent, but you may not separately meter and bill tenants for electricity without Commission approval, and you may not separately meter or submeter and bill tenants for gas at all (see the utility apportionment row).

Under the Commission's rules, selling electric vehicle charging from a charger that a regulated utility does not own is not treated as reselling electricity. No Oklahoma statute limits a utility allowance, the amount you agree to cover, or requires a particular way of passing on usage above an allowance. The library offers an optional allowance clause for a utility whose meter serves only the rental, with tenant reimbursement of the excess at actual cost and the bill details above.

title: No Required Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a residential lease to carry a utility disclosure attachment, such as a statement of who pays each utility, average utility costs or the unit's past usage. Your lease should still say plainly which utilities you provide and which the tenant arranges and pays (the library's utility clauses do this), because the Landlord and Tenant Act's essential-service remedies turn on what the lease promises. Disclosure duties that do exist are about billing, not the lease: if you resell city-bought electricity, gas, water or sewer service to a residential tenant, each bill must show your per-unit cost and each fee in dollars and cents; and if you run a Commission-approved electric submeter system, you must divide the utility bill among tenants in the approved manner on file with the Commission and give a tenant, on request, a statement of the tenant's consumption for the prior year. If the tenant uses a Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8), federal rules require the lease itself to specify which utilities and appliances the owner supplies and which the family supplies.

title: No Meter-Attached Conservation Charge Rule
bodyText: Oklahoma has no statute or Corporation Commission rule that puts an energy-efficiency or conservation repayment charge on a utility meter so that later customers at the same address keep paying it, and none that requires a landlord to warn a new tenant about such a charge or to cut the rent instead. The nearest program is different: counties may set up commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) programs for properties other than single-family residential property; the law treats any property not classified or zoned as single-family residential as commercial, which can include a multifamily rental. A PACE loan for permanently affixed energy-efficiency, energy, water-conservation or resiliency improvements is repaid through annual assessments that, once the assessment contract is recorded, are a lien running with the property with the same priority as property taxes; the owner needs written consent from any mortgage holder first. The obligation is the owner's, and no Oklahoma statute addresses passing a PACE assessment through to tenants; if your lease passes property taxes or assessments through, get advice before treating a PACE payment that way. Submetered water is not separately regulated by statute; if you buy water or sewer service from a city and resell it to a residential tenant, the cost-plus-10% cap and per-unit-cost bill disclosure apply (see the rebilling caps row).

title: No Lien for a Tenant's Unpaid City Utility Bills
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute makes a tenant's unpaid city water, sewer or trash service charges a lien on your property, puts them on your property tax bill, or makes you as owner liable for them. Cities set water charges and penalties by ordinance, and some may require the owner to hold the account or have other collection rules; check your city's utility ordinance. What state law does provide: where a public entity providing sewer service asks a separate public water provider to cut off water for a delinquent sewer account, it must give the account holder and you as property owner at least 30 days' notice of the proposed date, under notice-and-hearing procedures it must adopt. A city utility refunds a customer's deposit within 30 days after service ends, and must waive initial deposit requirements for a customer shown to be a victim of domestic violence, stalking or harassment. Liens that can reach your property are for other things: special assessments for sewer or water line construction in an improvement district; a city's cost of cleaning trash or mowing your property after notice to you, which is certified to the county treasurer and becomes a lien equal to taxes; a health officer's cost of removing a health nuisance after a written order to the owner or occupant, added to the property taxes (and a city may instead add nuisance-abatement costs to its utility bills); and, in cities that adopt the Municipal Code Lien Enforcement Act, housing and building code fines, penalties and abatement costs on property that is not owner-occupied, enforceable in court against the property once they total $1,500. Keep the property clean and in code even when the tenant controls it day to day.

title: Getting Tenants' Energy Usage Data
bodyText:
Oklahoma's Electric Usage Data Protection Act controls who may get a customer's electricity usage data. An electric utility (an investor-owned utility or a cooperative, but not a city-owned utility) must give its customer the customer's own standard usage data on request, may charge a reasonable fee for nonstandard data, and must keep customer information confidential. It may release a customer's identifying information and usage data to a third party, such as a landlord, when the customer gives written consent, and it may share aggregate data from enough customers that no one household's habits can be deduced, without consent. So if the tenant holds the electric account, you need the tenant's written consent to get the unit's usage data from the utility.

No Oklahoma statute requires a tenant to consent, requires a landlord to collect or report building energy data, or governs release of gas or water usage data; ask those providers what authorization they accept. The library's optional energy usage data authorization clause has the tenant authorize release for benchmarking, audits and efficiency programs, sign the utility's own form, limit your use of the data, and lets the tenant withdraw.

title: No Recycling Notice Requirement
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a landlord to provide recycling or to tell tenants where and how to recycle. State policy encourages recycling: every city over 5,000 people is urged to run a recycling program, and local governments may require those who generate recyclable materials to separate them for collection, so your city or trash contract may impose recycling rules. The state duty that does apply is trash removal: except for one- and two-family residences or where a government provides the service, you must provide and maintain appropriate receptacles and conveniences for removing ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste from the units and arrange for frequent removal. If you offer recycling, telling tenants how to use it in your rules or a move-in notice is good practice, not a legal requirement.

title: Rental Wells: When Testing and Notice Rules Apply
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute, and none of the state Department of Environmental Quality water-system rules read, requires you to test a well that serves only one rental home, or to give that tenant well-test results. A well that serves more than one dwelling, or a multi-family building, is different. If it has fewer than 15 connections and serves fewer than 25 people, the Department of Environmental Quality treats it as a minor public water supply system, unless each home or unit has its own well or the water is bought from a permitted water system. You need the Department's authorization before using a well that way; you must have the water tested by a laboratory for coliform bacteria once a year; and you must immediately tell everyone who uses the water to boil it or stop using it when repeat samples test positive for coliform, and tell them of any result that exceeds drinking water standards and the precautions to take. A well with 15 or more service connections, or that regularly serves an average of 25 or more people at least 60 days a year, is a public water supply system: it needs a Department permit and must follow the federal drinking water regulations the Department adopts, including monitoring, public notice and annual water-quality reports; get the Department's advice before renting from such a system. Separately, the Landlord and Tenant Act requires you to keep the unit fit and habitable, keep plumbing and other facilities you supply in good and safe working order, and, except in a single-family residence or where water comes through a direct and independently metered utility connection, supply running water; no Oklahoma case was read on whether unsafe well water breaches these duties, so the cautious course is to test a single-home rental well periodically too and fix problems promptly.

title: Which Building and Fire Codes Apply to Your Rental
bodyText: Oklahoma sets statewide minimum building and fire codes through the Oklahoma Uniform Building Code Commission, and cities, towns and counties must meet them, though they may adopt stricter codes. As of September 14, 2026 the state codes are the 2024 International Fire Code (the minimum code for fire prevention and fire protection systems in residential and commercial buildings, including its chapter on existing buildings), the 2024 International Residential Code (new construction of one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses), the 2024 International Building Code (all other new construction, which under the Commission's definitions includes apartment buildings) and the 2024 International Existing Building Code (alterations to those other existing buildings), each with Oklahoma amendments. A permit is needed before you build or make a major alteration; where your city or county issues no permits, the State Fire Marshal does. State Fire Marshal rules also say a building whose use or occupancy classification changes, or that stays unoccupied or vacant for at least 180 days, must be brought up to current code requirements for the occupancy classifications and situations the model codes identify; ask the local building or fire official how that applies before you re-rent a long-vacant building. The State Fire Marshal, the local fire chief (or the mayor where there is no fire department), the chief of a fire protection district and the sheriff may enter and inspect buildings at reasonable hours. If they find a building especially liable to fire, or combustible material or other dangerous conditions, they can order repairs, removal or demolition against the owner, lessee, agent or occupant, and wilful failure to comply is a misdemeanor with a fine for each day. Oklahoma's Landlord and Tenant Act does not itself list code compliance among your duties, but you must keep the unit fit and habitable and keep supplied facilities in good and safe working order, and a city code may apply to you directly. Ask your local building or fire official which editions and local amendments apply to your building.

title: Fire Sprinklers: When Oklahoma Requires Them
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to add fire sprinklers to an existing rental building. Sprinklers come from three narrower rules. First, every high-rise building (more than 75 feet tall, measured from the lowest level fire-fighting equipment can reach) built after May 27, 1975 must have a water sprinkler system (or an equivalent high-rise life protection system that meets a nationally recognized building code), and the record owner owes a $100 penalty for each day of violation. Second, the state residential code for new construction requires sprinklers in new townhouses unless a two-hour fire-resistance-rated wall separates the units, and does not require them when existing townhouses without sprinklers are added to or altered. Oklahoma has removed the model code's sprinkler requirement for new one- and two-family dwellings from the state code; a city or county may still adopt it by ordinance. Third, apartment buildings and other buildings outside the residential code are built under the state's adopted International Building Code and maintained under the International Fire Code; the fire code's existing-building chapter, as Oklahoma amended it, requires interior openings that connect three to five stories to be enclosed in one-hour fire-resistant construction or the building to be sprinklered throughout, except in small residential buildings classed as Group R-3 and in a few other cases. If your building has a sprinkler system, you must keep it in good and safe working order like any other facility you supply. Ask your local building or fire official what applies to your building.

title: No Fire Sprinkler Disclosure Rule
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to tell a tenant, in the lease or anywhere else, whether the building has fire sprinklers, and Oklahoma statutes offer no tax credit, grant or loan for adding sprinklers to a rental. The only sprinkler disclosure in Oklahoma statutes is on the seller's property condition form used when a home is sold, not leased. You may still state the building's sprinkler status in the lease or a building information sheet, and anything you tell a tenant about fire safety should be accurate. If the property has a sprinkler system, keep it in good and safe working order like any other facility you supply.

title: Heat and Heating Equipment
bodyText: You must supply reasonable heat at all times during the tenancy, together with running water and reasonable amounts of hot water, unless the unit is a single-family residence or the service comes through direct and independently metered utility connections to the unit. A unit with common walls still counts as a single-family residence if it has direct access to a street or thoroughfare and shares no heating, hot water or other essential facility or service with another unit. Whoever pays for the fuel, you must keep any heating facilities you supply, or are required to supply, in good and safe working order, and the lease cannot waive this duty (though you and the tenant may agree, in a conspicuous writing separate from the lease, that the tenant will perform specified repairs or maintenance tasks). No Oklahoma statute sets a minimum indoor temperature; the state-adopted model building codes may set heating-capacity standards for new construction, so ask your local building official. If you wilfully or negligently fail to supply heat you owe, the tenant may give you written notice and then end the lease on written notice, buy reasonable heat and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from rent, recover damages for the reduced rental value, or, on written notice, move to reasonable substitute housing and be excused from paying rent for the period you are out of compliance. Those rights do not arise until the tenant gives you written notice, or if the problem was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with the tenant's consent. The tenant must use heating equipment in a safe and nondestructive manner. If your apartment building has six or more family units and is heated by a steam or hot water heating boiler covered by the state boiler law, the boiler needs periodic state inspection and a certificate of operation from the Department of Labor; operating it without one is a misdemeanor for each day.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute sets a maximum or minimum water heater temperature for rentals or requires you to reset the water heater before a new tenant moves in. Your duty is to supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times (unless the unit is a single-family residence or is independently metered for the service), and to keep any water heater you supply in good and safe working order. Ordinary household water heaters are outside the state boiler inspection law. The plumbing and residential codes the state has adopted may set temperature or scald-protection rules for new installations. A sensible practice is to check that the water heater works and is set at a safe temperature at each turnover, and to tell the tenant how to report a problem.

title: Window Guards and Security Bars
bodyText: Oklahoma has no statute requiring child window guards or window stops in rentals, and no window-guard notice for the lease. What Oklahoma does regulate is security bars: in any residential occupancy built or retrofitted after November 1, 2005, bars, grills, covers, screens or similar devices placed over emergency escape and rescue openings, bulkhead enclosures, windows or window wells must be releasable or removable from the inside without a key, a tool, or more force than it takes to open the opening normally. If you add bars to a rental, use a type with an inside release, and show the tenant how it works.
