The state fire code, as Oklahoma amended it, also requires emergency escape and rescue openings in apartment buildings and other residential occupancies, in basements and in sleeping rooms below the fourth story, with exceptions (for example where a sleeping room has a door straight to the outside, or in some sprinklered buildings); do not block those openings. Ask your local building or fire official.

title: Common-Area Lighting
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute sets a lighting standard for hallways, stairways, parking areas or other shared areas of a rental. Your general duties cover it: except in a single-family residence, you must keep all common areas of your building, grounds and facilities clean, safe and sanitary at all times, and in every rental you must keep the electrical facilities you supply in good and safe working order. A shared area that is dark because fixtures are broken or unpowered can breach those duties, and the tenant then has the repair and termination remedies the Landlord and Tenant Act gives.

A city or county housing code may set specific lighting standards, and the state-adopted fire and building codes set means-of-egress lighting rules for shared exits; ask your local building or fire official. If shared-area lights are wired to a tenant's own electric service, the lease may make that tenant pay for the power (see the optional common-area lighting clause), but the duty to keep the areas safe and the equipment working stays with you, and you are not reselling electricity when the tenant pays the utility directly.

title: No Lock, Deadbolt or Rekeying Statute
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to install deadbolts, door viewers, window latches or other security devices in a rental, to rekey or change locks between tenants, or to change locks at a tenant's request. The one lock statute is old and narrow: the operator of a hotel, apartment hotel or inn must fit guest-room doors with inside night latches, chains or bolts; ordinary transient lodging is outside the Landlord and Tenant Act, and whether an apartment hotel includes any residential rental is a question for the courts. A few building and fire rules still touch locks. The state residential code for one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses, as Oklahoma amended it, requires the egress door to be readily openable from the inside without a key or special knowledge or effort, so avoid a double-keyed deadbolt on that door. Security bars over escape windows must release from inside. Installing an access-controlled entrance or exit system needs a State Fire Marshal permit. If you hire someone to install or rekey locks, they generally must hold an Oklahoma locksmith license. You still must keep the unit fit and habitable and keep supplied hardware in good working order, and courts may weigh security in negligence cases. The cautious course: provide a working deadbolt and secure window latches, rekey or change locks between tenants, and repair broken locks promptly.

title: No Duty to Provide a Stove or Refrigerator
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to provide a stove, oven or refrigerator in a rental. If you do supply one, or the lease says you will, you must keep it in good and safe working order like any other appliance you supply, and the tenant must use it in a safe and nondestructive manner. List the appliances you supply in the lease (see the appliances clause) so it is clear which ones you maintain. A tenant's refrigerator is one of the items your statutory landlord's lien cannot reach. If you take an old refrigerator out of a unit, do not leave it where children can get to it with its door or lid latch intact: anyone who abandons or discards such a refrigerator, icebox or ice chest in a place accessible to children, and an owner, lessee or manager who knowingly lets one stay there, is negligent as a matter of law and commits a misdemeanor. The model building codes adopted in Oklahoma may require kitchen facilities in new dwellings.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to install covers or guards on steam or hot water radiators, to offer them on request, or to add a radiator notice or rider to the lease. If your building has radiators, you must keep that heating equipment in good and safe working order, and a hot, exposed radiator can be a safety issue under your general duty to keep the unit fit and habitable. If an apartment building of six or more units is heated by a steam or hot water heating boiler covered by the state boiler law, the boiler itself needs state inspection and a certificate of operation (see the guidance on heating). Covering radiators where young children live is a sensible precaution.

title: Pools and Spas at Your Rental
bodyText: Which pool rules apply depends on the kind of rental. Apartment and other shared pools: the State Department of Health regulates public pools and spas, and its rules treat a pool limited to the people living or staying on the property and their guests as a public bathing place that is not open to the general public. Such a pool needs a construction permit before it is built (with plans by a licensed professional engineer) and an annual operating license; the Department may inspect it, and you, your managers and attendants are responsible for keeping it sanitary and safe. An outdoor pool of this kind must be enclosed by a barrier at least 4 feet high, with self-closing, self-latching gates and a clear view of the pool (a decorative barrier may have no open spaces over 4 inches); where existing construction makes that impossible, the owner must instead file an operating procedure with the county or state health department that keeps animals and unattended small children out. An indoor pool must be in a room whose doors can be locked whenever the pool is not in use, or have a barrier like an outdoor pool's. The rules define no separate semi-public class beyond excluding baths meant for cleansing the body. A lifeguard or attendant is recommended (and a lifeguard is required whenever the pool is open and in use if it has a diving board or platform higher than one meter); if no lifeguard or attendant is on duty during all hours, post a sign at the entrance reading "NO LIFEGUARD OR ATTENDANT ON DUTY". You must also post pool rules (including that children under 12 must be accompanied by a responsible adult where no attendant is on duty), the bathing load, spa warnings and a sign by the telephone to dial 911, lock the gates when the pool is closed, and secure the pool when it is not in season. Tell the Department if you sell or lease the pool's premises to a new operator. The statute excludes pools at private residences and homeowners' association pools limited to the owners and their nonpaying guests; no Oklahoma case or Department guidance was reviewed on whether a pool shared by the tenants of a rental complex can fall outside the statute, so treat it as covered and check with the Department. Single-family rentals: the Department does not regulate a pool at a private residence, but a new residential pool, spa or hot tub that needs a permit must be completely enclosed by a fence or barrier at least 4 feet high or by a screen enclosure (unless the lot is over 2 acres, or the pool has a power safety cover or the spa a safety cover meeting ASTM F 1346), and pedestrian gates must be self-closing and self-latching unless the gate has a locking device. No Oklahoma statute requires a pool safety notice in the lease.

title: Asbestos in Rental Buildings
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to test a rental for asbestos or to disclose asbestos to a tenant. Oklahoma regulates asbestos removal instead. Under the Oklahoma Asbestos Control Act, anyone who removes, encapsulates or encloses friable asbestos material (material with more than one percent asbestos that can be crumbled or powdered by hand) in any facility other than a private residence or an apartment house of fewer than six family units must hold an asbestos abatement license from the Commissioner of Labor and use certified workers; that includes your own staff if they do the work. Violations are misdemeanors, with each day a separate violation, and the Commissioner can inspect, issue orders and seek injunctions. Smaller rentals are outside the licensing law, but federal asbestos rules for demolition, renovation and worker safety may still apply. Before renovating or demolishing an older building, have suspect materials inspected, use a licensed abatement contractor where the law requires one, and keep tenants away from the work area. If you know of damaged asbestos material in a unit, it can affect your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable.

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires periodic inspection of balconies, decks, exterior stairways or other elevated elements of a rental building, or any engineer's report on them. Your general duties still reach them: you must make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to keep the unit and premises fit and habitable, and, except in a single-family residence, keep common areas such as shared stairways and walkways clean, safe and sanitary. Balconies and decks are part of the premises, so a rotted joist or a loose railing is yours to fix, and a tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage them. The state building and fire codes set guard and railing requirements for new construction. A sensible practice for older wood balconies and decks is a periodic visual check, with a qualified inspector for anything that looks unsound.

title: Smoke Drift and Smoking in Shared Hallways
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute deals with smoke drifting between rental units, requires you to disclose it, or sets up a smoke-drift waiver. Oklahoma's smoking law does reach some shared spaces. Subject to a list of exemptions (such as stand-alone bars, some hotel rooms, owner-only workplaces and workplaces within private residences), the Smoking in Public Places and Indoor Workplaces Act bars smoking tobacco or marijuana, and vaping marijuana, in any indoor workplace, which expressly includes hallways and other spaces used or visited by employees, and in any public place, meaning an enclosed indoor area where people other than employees are invited or permitted.

Enclosed common hallways, lobbies, laundry rooms and offices of an apartment building that staff work in or visit are therefore likely covered. A private residence is not a public place (except areas used as a licensed child care facility during its hours of operation), so the Act does not stop a tenant smoking inside a unit; your lease can (see the smoking policy).

Where smoking is prohibited by law, the owner or operator must post a smoke-free sign at each entrance and ask anyone seen smoking to stop, though the law does not make you liable for a non-employee's violation. The library does not offer a clause in which the tenant waives claims for smoke drift. A lease may not make a tenant give up the Landlord and Tenant Act's rights or remedies, or excuse your liability for harm from your own operation or maintenance of the premises, and a broad smoke-drift waiver could do both; you may add your own clause after legal advice.

A plain statement that the building is not smoke-free and that smoke from other units or outdoor areas may reach the unit is lawful notice.

title: No Portable Air Conditioner Rule
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute gives a tenant a right to install a portable or window air conditioner or other cooling device, or limits a lease term that restricts them. Oklahoma also does not require you to provide air conditioning; but air conditioning you supply, or must supply, has to be kept in good and safe working order, and the tenant must use it safely. You may therefore set reasonable rules in the lease, such as requiring consent for window units, approving the type and installation, and making the tenant responsible for damage the tenant causes (see the alterations clause). Installing a portable, self-contained, ductless air conditioner does not need a state mechanical license. Do not approve a window unit that blocks a required emergency escape window in a sleeping room.

title: Leaving Appliances You Will Not Maintain
bodyText: Oklahoma requires you to keep in good and safe working order the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances you supply or are required to supply, and the lease cannot waive that duty (though you and the tenant may agree, in a conspicuous writing separate from the lease, that the tenant will perform specified repairs or maintenance tasks). No Oklahoma statute presumes that everything left in a unit is supplied by you, and none says how a lease may exclude an item. Some items cannot be excluded at all: unless the unit is a single-family residence or the service is independently metered to the unit, you are required to supply heat, running water and reasonable hot water, so the equipment that provides them is yours to maintain. For other items, no Oklahoma case was reviewed on whether an appliance you leave in the unit but declare "not included" counts as one you supplied, so the library does not offer an exclusion clause. The cautious course is to remove any appliance you do not intend to maintain, or to list it as supplied and maintain it (see the appliances clause). If you remove an old refrigerator, icebox or ice chest with a latching door, do not leave it where children can reach it. You may add your own exclusion clause after legal advice.

title: Notice Before Pest Control Treatments
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute or State Board of Agriculture rule requires you to give tenants notice before ordinary pest control in or around a rental. Oklahoma leaves notification and posting for pesticide applications to the Board's rules and bars cities and counties from adopting stricter local rules on them. The Board's rules require notice only for fumigation of a building with gas: an apartment in a multi-unit building may be fumigated only after the apartments beside, above and below it are vacated, every dwelling within 10 feet of a building being fumigated must be told in writing in advance and vacated, and warning signs go on the entrances of the fumigated space and of adjacent units; spot and restrictive treatments inside a building are excepted from those notice, vacating and sign rules, but during the ventilation period of a spot or restrictive fumigation no one but the fumigator may occupy the premises.

The pest control company must give you, as its customer, a copy of its contract. Anyone who does pest control as a business must hold a state applicator's license for that category, though a person applying pesticides to his or her own property is exempt from that licence; an employee who uses restricted-use pesticides on property for an owner or manager must be certified as a noncommercial applicator.

The cautious course: use a licensed pest control company, give tenants written notice before any treatment inside a unit or in shared areas (with the product, the date and any preparation or re-entry instructions from the label or the applicator), and give at least the one day's notice the Landlord and Tenant Act requires before entering a unit except in an emergency or where that is impracticable.

Local ordinances on pesticides are preempted to the extent they are stricter than the Board's rules.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure Rule
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to have, show or disclose a certificate of occupancy before renting a unit, or to mention one in the lease. Certificates of occupancy come from the building codes and local permit offices: you need a permit before building or making a major alteration, and the state building codes Oklahoma has adopted, together with your city or county, decide when a certificate of occupancy is issued. Two state rules are worth knowing. State Fire Marshal rules say a building whose use or occupancy classification changes, or that stays unoccupied or vacant for at least 180 days, must be brought up to current code requirements for the occupancy classifications and situations the model codes identify, which can matter when you convert a building to rental use or re-rent a long-vacant one. And cities and counties must ask an applicant for an occupancy permit for proof of state tax registration. Ask your local building official whether your property needs a certificate of occupancy before tenants move in.

title: Elevators, Trash and Other Facilities You Supply
bodyText: You must keep in good and safe working order all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances you supply or are required to supply, and the Landlord and Tenant Act names elevators expressly. Except in one- or two-family residences or where a government provides the service, you must also provide and maintain appropriate trash receptacles and arrange for frequent removal of garbage, ashes and other waste. The tenant must use those facilities, including elevators, in a safe and nondestructive manner. Elevators also fall under the Elevator Safety Act (Department of Labor). The owner or lessee of every elevator in service must register it; elevators, escalators, platform lifts and stairway chairlifts must be inspected by a licensed elevator inspector for a certificate of operation (the Act says the owner must have conveyances inspected annually and also sets other intervals by type, such as up to two years for two-to-four-floor elevator units); violations noted in an inspection report must be corrected within 30 days or a longer period the Commissioner allows; and only a licensed elevator mechanic working for a licensed elevator contractor may install, repair or maintain an elevator. The Commissioner can order an unsafe elevator out of service. The Act does not apply to an elevator in an existing owner-occupied private residence, among other exemptions, so an elevator in a rented home is covered. No Oklahoma statute regulates garage door openers, laundry rooms or other amenities in rentals; amenities you promise in the lease must be kept as promised and in safe condition.

title: When the Law Lets a Tenant End the Lease Early
bodyText: Apart from what your lease allows and anything you agree with the tenant, the Oklahoma statutes researched give a tenant these rights to end a residential lease early, most of them triggered by something the landlord does or fails to do. (1) You fail to deliver possession at the start: rent abates and the tenant may end the lease by written notice, and you must return all prepaid rent and the deposit. (2) Material breach of the lease, or a breach of your statutory maintenance duties that materially affects health or safety: the tenant may give written notice naming the breach and a termination date at least 30 days after you receive it, and the lease ends on that date unless you adequately remedy the breach within 14 days. (3) You willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service: after written notice the tenant may end the lease immediately on written notice. (4) A breach that makes the unit uninhabitable or poses an imminent threat to an occupant's health and safety, not remedied as promptly as conditions require: the tenant may end the lease immediately by written notice naming the problem. (5) Fire or other casualty substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit: the tenant may vacate at once and give written notice within one week, and the lease ends as of the vacating date; you return all recoverable deposits and prepaid, unearned rent. (6) You wrongfully remove or lock out the tenant: the tenant may end the lease after notice and recover up to twice the average monthly rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater. (7) You enter unlawfully, enter in an unreasonable manner, or harass the tenant with repeated unreasonable demands for entry: the tenant may end the lease by written notice and recover actual damages. The repair, essential-service and uninhabitability rights arise only after the tenant's written notice to you, and none of them, nor the casualty right, arises if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with the tenant's consent. (8) A victim of domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking may end the lease without penalty by written notice with a protective order within 30 days of the incident, unless you waive that time limit (see the domestic violence row). (9) A servicemember may end a residential lease under the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act after entering military service, or after receiving qualifying permanent change of station or deployment orders (90 days or more), or, where the lease was signed on receipt of such orders, a stop-movement order of at least 30 days or of indefinite length that prevents the servicemember or dependents from occupying the unit, by written notice with a copy of the orders; you may not charge an early termination fee, though unpaid rent for the period before the termination takes effect is owed on a prorated basis, and other unpaid lease obligations, including reasonable charges for excess wear, remain payable; you must refund rent paid in advance for any period after the termination takes effect within 30 days, and before the termination date in the notice you may apply to a court to modify the servicemember's relief as justice and equity require. Where the right comes from entry into service or from change-of-station or deployment orders, a lease with monthly rent ends 30 days after the next rent due date following delivery of the notice, and any other lease on the last day of the month after the month the notice is delivered; where it comes from a stop-movement order, the lease ends when the notice and orders are delivered. Oklahoma applies the same federal protections to members of the state military forces ordered to state active duty or Title 32 active duty, except where state law gives more. The federal act also lets a spouse or dependent end the lease within one year after a servicemember's death in service, and covers catastrophic injury or illness. Fraud and other contract grounds: Oklahoma's general contract law lets a party rescind a contract in listed cases, among them consent given by mistake or obtained through duress, menace, fraud or undue influence by or with the connivance of the other party, a failure of consideration through the other party's fault, the consent of all parties, and the other party's violation of the Consumer Protection Act. The party must rescind promptly on discovering the facts and restore, or offer to restore, everything of value received. No statute gives tenants a separate lease-termination right for a landlord's misrepresentation. No Oklahoma statute requires a lease to state these termination rights or releases a tenant from rent if the lease leaves them out. Outside these situations, a tenant who leaves a fixed-term lease early stays liable for rent, subject to your duty to make reasonable efforts to re-rent.

title: No Early Termination for Age, Illness or a Move Into Care
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute lets a tenant end a lease early because of age, illness, disability or incapacity, or because the tenant moves into a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility, and no Oklahoma statute says that a month-to-month or at-will tenancy ends on notice that a party has died or lost the capacity to contract. Unless your lease says otherwise, a fixed-term lease keeps running; a month-to-month or at-will tenancy ends on at least 30 days' written notice from either side. If such a tenant leaves early, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent the unit, and the tenant (or the estate) owes the rent or the shortfall only for the rest of the term. If a tenant asks to leave early because of a disability, treat the request with care under fair housing law, and consider agreeing to a release in writing. A servicemember who suffers a catastrophic injury or illness during military service has a separate federal termination right (see the statutory early termination row).

title: Holdover Charge: Not Offered
bodyText:
The library does not offer a lease clause setting a daily or monthly charge for a tenant who stays after the lease ends. Oklahoma voids contract penalties and any contract term that fixes in advance the damages for a breach, except a pre-set amount that is valid when, from the nature of the case, it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage. The loss from a holdover is usually the rental value of the unit for the extra days, which can be measured, so a fixed holdover rate risks being void; no Oklahoma statute sets or caps a lease holdover rate.

A holdover-rate clause is not barred outright, and you may add your own after getting legal advice. Without one, the law already gives you remedies: you may sue at once for possession and damages when a tenant stays without your consent; if the holdover is willful and not in good faith, you may also recover up to twice the average monthly rent, computed and prorated daily, for each month or part of a month the tenant stays.

Two older statutes also make double rent the measure where a tenant who gave notice that he would leave fails to give up the premises, and double the yearly value of the property for the time of withholding, plus compensation for the harm caused, where a tenant willfully holds over after the term ends and after notice to quit has been duly given and possession demanded; how those older statutes fit with the Landlord and Tenant Act has not been settled here. If you accept rent after the term ends, a renewal or a month-to-month tenancy may result, so do not take rent from a holdover tenant unless you intend that.

title: No Bar on Demanding Rent for a Unit Needing Repairs
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute forbids you to demand or collect rent because a unit has been cited for code violations or is substandard, and no Oklahoma statute requires you to make a demand before rent becomes due. Rent is payable at the time and place you and the tenant agree; unless you agree otherwise, the whole rent for a term of a month or less is payable at the dwelling unit at the start of the term, and for a longer term one month's rent is payable at the start of each month. If rent is not paid when due you may sue for it at any time; to end the lease for nonpayment you must give the tenant written notice of your demand for payment, and the lease may be ended if the tenant does not pay within five days after that notice. What Oklahoma does instead is let the tenant reduce or stop paying rent in specific cases: rent abates until you deliver possession; if you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant may, after written notice, buy reasonable amounts of the service and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from rent, or, on written notice, move to reasonable substitute housing and be excused from paying rent while the failure lasts, or recover damages for the reduced rental value; for a breach that materially affects health and that can be repaired for no more than one month's rent, the tenant may give you written notice and, if you do not comply within 14 days (or as promptly as an emergency requires), have the work done and deduct the cost from rent after giving you an itemized statement; and after a fire or other casualty a tenant who stays in the usable part owes rent reduced in proportion to the drop in fair rental value. These rent remedies do not arise if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with the tenant's consent, and the repair and service remedies require the tenant's written notice first. In an eviction for unpaid rent, a tenant who withheld rent on a good-faith claim that you failed to provide essential services, and who gave written notice of the claim, or actual notice to your agent for collecting rent, within ten days after the rent was due, can avoid the writ, cure the breach and stay by paying the judgment, including court costs and attorney fees, by cash or cashier's check within 72 hours.

title: Criminal Activity: Immediate Termination, but No Special Court Track
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute sets a special or faster court procedure for evictions based on criminal or drug activity, and no statute lets a prosecutor or city evict a tenant. One old criminal statute does void the lease itself: every lease under which the tenant uses the premises for illegal gambling is wholly null and void, and a lease becomes void when the tenant is convicted of allowing prohibited gambling devices or games there; in either case you recover possession through an ordinary eviction (forcible entry and detainer) case.

No similar Oklahoma statute voids a lease for drugs, prostitution or other crimes. What Oklahoma does have is a ground for ending the lease without a chance to cure: criminal activity by the tenant, a member of the tenant's household, a guest or another person under the tenant's control that threatens the health, safety or right of peaceful enjoyment of the premises by other tenants, or that is a danger to the premises, and any drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises by any of them, is grounds for immediate termination of the lease.

Separately, if a tenant's breach causes or threatens imminent and irremediable harm to the premises or to any person and the tenant does not remedy it as promptly as conditions require after having notice of it, you may end the lease by immediately filing an eviction case. Either way, possession is decided in the ordinary eviction case, which is already quick: trial is set five to ten days after the summons issues, and possession is tried without a jury. You may not end or refuse to renew a tenancy because a tenant or household member is the victim of domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking.

How Oklahoma courts carry out an immediate termination (for example, whether a written notice must still be given first) is a question of case law; the cautious course is to give the tenant a written notice of termination stating the conduct before you file. If the property has a federally backed mortgage or is in a covered federal housing program, the federal 30-day notice to vacate may also apply (see the federal CARES Act row).

Renting a place to someone when you know, or have reasonable cause to believe, that the renter means to use it for prostitution, or knowingly renting a place for setting up prohibited gambling devices, is a crime, and an owner who knowingly lets property be used for illegal gambling faces a civil penalty that becomes a lien on the property. Separately, repeated use of a property for illegal drug distribution, prostitution or human or sex trafficking makes it a public nuisance that public officials can act to abate, and a later owner who neglects to abate a continuing nuisance created by a former owner is liable for it in the same way as the one who created it; how far a landlord answers for a nuisance a tenant creates is a question of case law, so act on credible reports promptly.

title: Your Remedies When the Lease Ends: Possession, Rent and Damages
bodyText: You can pursue possession, money, or both. If rent is unpaid when due you may sue for the rent at any time, without ending the lease; to end the lease for nonpayment you give written notice demanding payment, and if the tenant does not pay within five days the lease may be terminated. In the eviction case itself you may also claim unpaid rent, damage to the premises and other claims under the Landlord and Tenant Act, but no other kinds of claims. An eviction judgment settles only the issues actually decided and does not bar a later suit by either side. If the tenant could be served only by posting and mailing, the court can award possession but no money unless the tenant appears, and you may sue for the rent and other money afterward. If the tenant abandons the unit during the term, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent, and the tenant owes the rent, or the difference in rent, for the rest of the term only if those efforts fail; if you do not try to re-rent, or accept the abandonment as a surrender, the lease is treated as ended by you on the date you learned of the abandonment. If you end the lease yourself for a breach, both sides' duties under the lease end on the termination date; whether you can then recover, as damages, rent lost for the rest of the term is a question of case law, and any damages are subject to your duty to mitigate. If a tenant stays without your consent after the lease ends or is terminated, you may sue at once for possession and damages, plus up to twice the average monthly rent, prorated daily, for each month or part of a month of a willful, bad-faith holdover. The prevailing party in an action on the lease or the Act is entitled to a reasonable attorney fee. Which court: evictions are heard in district court. An eviction where the total amount sought, not counting attorney fees and costs, is within the small claims limit goes on the small claims docket, and a district court may by court rule send any eviction there to decide possession. A claim for money alone, such as unpaid rent or damage, may be brought under the small claims procedure if it does not exceed $10,000, not counting attorney fees and costs; the plaintiff gives up a jury there, but where the claim, counterclaim or setoff exceeds $1,500 either side may demand a jury by written notice to the clerk and a $50 deposit at least two working days before the defendant's appearance date, and on the defendant's motion the case may be moved to the regular docket (it must be moved if the claim is $7,500 or more); in an uncontested case the attorney fee is limited to 10% of the judgment, or up to 25% on application with documentation. A collection agency or assignee may not use small claims. A company, LLC, partnership or trust may appear in small claims, or in an eviction on the small claims docket, through an officer, member, manager, partner, trustee or regular full-time employee. Larger claims go on the regular district court docket, where either side may ask for a jury on the money claims (possession is always tried without a jury). Sue within five years on a written lease, or three years on an oral one; a claim for the statutory double rent for holding over may fall under a shorter period (three years, or one year if a court treats it as a penalty), so bring such a claim within one year.

title: Environmental Events: No Statutory Termination Right, Optional Clause Offered
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute lets you, or a tenant, end a residential lease just because of an environmental or public-health event, such as contamination, a chemical spill or a government order to vacate.

The rules that do apply:
- if fire or another casualty substantially impairs the unit, the tenant (not you) may vacate and, by written notice within one week, end the lease, or stay in the usable part at a proportionally reduced rent
- if your failure to keep the unit fit and habitable makes it uninhabitable or an imminent threat to health and safety and you do not remedy it as promptly as conditions require, the tenant may end the lease at once by written notice
- if you know or have reason to know that the unit was used to make methamphetamine you must tell a prospective tenant before the lease starts (unless testing shows contamination at or below the statutory level).

None of these rights arises if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with the tenant's consent. Because the law gives you no right of your own to end the lease after such an event, the library offers an optional clause that lets you end it by written notice when a government authority orders the unit vacated or declares it unfit or unsafe because of an environmental or public-health condition you did not cause by failing to meet your obligations; the lease then ends on the date stated in your notice or, if earlier, the date the tenant moves out, and the tenant owes rent only through that date and gets back prepaid rent and the deposit as the law provides.

Fire and other physical damage are handled by the separate Fire or Casualty clause. A historic state program paid relocation assistance to tenants and landlords in the Superfund lead-mining area in northeastern Oklahoma; it is not a termination right.

title: Leases After a Declared Disaster
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute ends a lease, suspends or abates rent, or stops evictions just because the Governor or the President has declared a disaster or emergency, and no statute deals with rent while a unit is merely inaccessible. What happens to the lease depends on the damage. If fire or another casualty substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may vacate at once and, by written notice within one week, end the lease as of the move-out date, or vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the drop in fair rental value; if the lease ends you return all recoverable deposits and prepaid, unearned rent, accounting as of the date of the casualty. These rights do not apply where the damage was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with the tenant's consent. The statute gives you no right of your own to end the lease after a casualty; the library's optional Fire or Casualty clause adds one. Your ordinary duties continue: if the disaster leads you to fail, willfully or negligently, to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant's essential-service remedies apply after written notice. Price limits: during a declared emergency and for 30 days afterward, you may not rent, or offer to rent, a dwelling unit in the emergency area (the affected counties, any area named in the declaration, and all neighbouring counties) at more than 10% above what you charged for it just before the declaration, and for the next 180 days the same 10% limit applies to renting or leasing a dwelling unit there, unless the increase is due to petroleum and natural gas commodity price increases, or only to factors unrelated to the emergency and not to added profit; an increase approved by the appropriate government agency is not a violation. A violation is a violation of the Consumer Protection Act, and an action may be brought within one year after the declaration ends.

title: No Rule on Housing Disaster-Displaced Guests
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute lets a tenant take in people displaced by a disaster or evacuation in spite of the lease's guest or occupancy limits, and none limits how you respond. Your lease may set reasonable limits on use of the unit by the tenant and by occupants, and a limit of two persons per bedroom is presumed reasonable (a child born to the tenants during the lease does not count against it). If an occupant breaches a lease condition that could be enforced against the tenant, you may demand in writing that the occupant leave; an occupant who wrongfully fails to leave within a reasonable time commits a trespass. In practice, consider agreeing in writing to a short, dated stay for displaced family or friends rather than treating it as a default. If you yourself let your property be used, voluntarily and without charge, to shelter people during an actual or impending emergency, you are not civilly liable for negligently causing death, injury or property loss to a person there that is caused by or incidental to that use, but you remain liable for gross, willful or wanton negligence. During a declared emergency the 10% limit on rent increases also applies to any dwelling unit you rent in the emergency area (see the disaster row).

title: When the Property Is Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute says what happens to a residential lease or to the rent when the property is taken by eminent domain: none ends or reduces the rent, lets the court in the condemnation case cancel the lease, defers to what the lease says about a taking, or provides for the owner and tenant to file an agreement dividing the award. The statutes speak mainly to the owner. A person whose property is taken or damaged for public use is entitled to just compensation: the value of the property taken plus any injury to the part not taken (for a partial taking, the drop in the whole tract's fair market value). Where public funds are used, the law states acquisition policies, including that projects be scheduled, as far as practicable, so that no lawful occupant must move from a dwelling without at least 90 days' written notice (assuming a replacement dwelling will be available) and that rent charged to an owner or tenant allowed to stay on short-term or terminable terms not exceed the fair rental value to a short-term occupier; but the statute says those policies create no rights or liabilities. If the acquiring entity requires buildings or other improvements to be removed, or determines that they will be adversely affected by the use to which the land will be put, it must acquire them too, and a tenant who owns an improvement is paid the greater of what it adds to the property's value or its value for removal, but only if the owner disclaims all interest in the tenant's improvements; the tenant may refuse that payment and seek compensation under other law. Relocation payments made under the federal Uniform Relocation Act go to the displaced person and are not compensation for the real property. How Oklahoma courts treat a lease, the rent and a tenant's share of the award after a taking is a question of case law; the cautious course is to treat the lease as ended when the tenant must give up possession, apportion rent to that date and refund prepaid rent and the deposit as the law provides. The library does not offer a condemnation clause for Oklahoma; such a clause is lawful and you may add your own after legal advice.

title: No Cold-Weather Notice Rule
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute requires a tenant to tell you before leaving the unit empty in cold weather, to keep the heat at a minimum setting, or to give notice of an extended absence. The Act's general tenant duties help: the tenant must use the heating, plumbing and other facilities in a safe and nondestructive manner, must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises, and must report as soon as practicable any defective condition the tenant has reason to believe you do not know about.

Your own duties also run in winter: unless the unit is a single-family residence or has its own independently metered utility connections, you must supply reasonable heat, and you must keep the heating and plumbing you supply in good and safe working order. You may enter without the tenant's consent in an emergency, such as a burst or freezing pipe; otherwise give at least one day's notice and enter at reasonable times.

The library's shared cold-weather clause is not offered for Oklahoma as written, because its exception for heating failures covers only systems you have agreed to maintain, while Oklahoma makes you maintain the heating facilities you supply in every case; a lease term that shifts to the tenant losses caused by your own failure to maintain the premises would be unenforceable. The library offers an Oklahoma version limited to the tenant's own failures: the tenant keeps any heat the tenant controls at 55 degrees or more from October 1 through May 1, gives you written notice before an absence of more than three days in that period, reports heating failures and leaks promptly, and answers only for freeze damage the heat or notice would have prevented, never for damage caused by your failure to supply heat or maintain the heating or plumbing.

title: Tenancies at Will and Month-to-Month Tenancies
bodyText:
Oklahoma law presumes that anyone in possession of real property with the owner's consent is a tenant at will unless the contrary is shown, and for a residential unit covered by the Landlord and Tenant Act a tenancy without a written definite term is month-to-month (week-to-week for a roomer or boarder who pays weekly). If a tenant stays after a fixed term ends and you consent, a month-to-month tenancy is created unless you agree otherwise. Either you or the tenant may end a month-to-month tenancy or a tenancy at will by written notice served at least 30 days before the date it is to end; the 30 days run from the date the notice is served.

A tenancy shorter than month-to-month (for example week-to-week) ends on written notice served at least seven days before the end date. Serve the notice personally; if the tenant cannot be located, deliver it to a family member over 12 who lives with the tenant; otherwise post it conspicuously on the unit and mail a copy by certified mail (or through the Post Office's Firm Mailing Book). In counting days, leave out the day of service, count the last day, and skip a last day that is a legal holiday.

Rent is owed through the end date, and the tenant also remains liable for rent for the one-month (or one-week) period if the tenant abandons without notice and you cannot re-rent despite reasonable efforts. Older general statutes outside the Act (used, for example, for property the Act does not cover) also make a tenant at will of anyone holding with the owner's assent, require 30 days' written notice to end a tenancy at will or from period to period of three months or less (or a notice as long as the rent interval where rent is due more often than every 30 days), require three months' written notice before the end of a year-to-year tenancy, and need no notice to quit for a tenant at will who commits waste or a tenant by sufferance.

A person who never had a rental agreement and whom you never accepted as a tenant is not a tenant at will under the Act (see the unauthorized occupant row).

title: No Special Rules for Seasonal or Vacation Rentals
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute sets special rules for seasonal, vacation or short-term residential rentals: none sets their notice, ending date or deposit rules, or takes them out of the Landlord and Tenant Act as such. A seasonal lease is handled like any other: a lease for a definite term expires on its ending date without notice unless the lease says otherwise, and if there is no written definite term the tenancy is month-to-month (week-to-week for a roomer or boarder who pays weekly), ending on 30 days' (or seven days') written notice. Unless an arrangement was created to avoid the Act, transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or other similar lodging is outside the Act regardless of the length of the stay, but no statute says when a vacation home rented by the night or week counts as similar lodging; if you rent a home for a season, use a written lease with a definite term and assume the Act applies. Occupancy of premises used primarily for agricultural purposes is also outside the Act. Sales and lodging taxes on furnishing rooms are covered in the rent tax row.

title: Curing a Default and Redeeming the Lease
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute gives a residential tenant a general right to redeem or reinstate a lease after it has been terminated or after an eviction judgment by paying what is owed. The tenant's chances to cure come earlier, and one comes later in a narrow case. Nonpayment: after your written demand for payment, the lease may be terminated only if the tenant fails to pay within five days. Other material breaches: your written notice must give the tenant ten days to remedy the breach, and a timely remedy keeps the lease alive, but any later breach allows immediate termination on written notice. After judgment: the court's order must let the tenant avoid the writ, cure and stay by paying the judgment, including court costs and attorney fees, by cash or cashier's check within 72 hours, but only where the rent was unpaid because of the tenant's good-faith claim that you failed to supply the essential services the Act requires, and the tenant gave written notice of the claim, or actual notice to your agent for collecting rent, within ten days after the rent was due. Otherwise a motion for new trial (filed within three days) does not stay the writ, and a tenant who wants to stop the writ while appealing may post a supersedeas bond within two days (no more than seven if the judge extends the time), and must keep paying current rent into court while the appeal is pending, or the appeal is treated as abandoned. Accepting rent after termination may be argued to waive it or renew the tenancy, so take payment only if you mean to continue the tenancy. Older statutes outside the Act also let a tenant stop a termination for nonpayment by paying within the ten-day or five-day notice period; for a residential unit the Act's five-day rule governs.

title: No Possession Bond or Confessed Judgment
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute provides a bond by which you can get possession before the eviction trial, or an end-of-term bond with a confessed judgment for possession, and a lease may not authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of it; such a term is unenforceable. Possession comes through the ordinary eviction case, which is set for trial five to ten days after the summons issues. The bond Oklahoma does provide runs the other way: after a judgment for you, the tenant may post a supersedeas bond within two days (a judge may extend this to no more than seven days) to stop enforcement of the judgment while appealing, but must keep paying current rent into the court clerk's office while the appeal is pending, and failing to pay is treated as abandoning the appeal. A motion for new trial must be filed within three days and does not stop the writ. The general ten-day stay on enforcing judgments does not apply to eviction cases.

title: Rent Paid Into Court and Tenant Counterclaims
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute makes a tenant pay rent into court before raising a defense in an eviction, or when a trial is postponed. Rent into court is required on appeal: a tenant who posts a supersedeas bond to stop enforcement of an eviction judgment while appealing must keep paying current rent, with poundage, into the court clerk's office while the appeal is pending; if the amount is disputed the judge sets how much and when; your withdrawing that rent does not stop you from arguing for possession on appeal; and failing to pay current rent while an appeal is pending is treated as abandoning the appeal. That last rule is not worded only for bonded appeals, so treat any tenant who appeals an eviction judgment as having to keep paying current rent into court. Counterclaims: claims for rent, damage to the premises and claims under the Landlord and Tenant Act may be brought in the eviction case, and a right under the Act may be pursued as part of an eviction action, but no statute requires the tenant to raise a counterclaim there, and an eviction judgment does not bar a later suit by either side. The tenant need not file an answer before trial (except to claim title or a boundary dispute). If a jury is requested on the money claims, they are severed and possession is tried separately without a jury. In a small claims case, a defendant who wants to claim a counterclaim or setoff must file a verified answer, delivered to the plaintiff in person, at least 72 hours before the first appearance, and a counterclaim over $10,000 moves the case to another docket unless both sides agree in writing to keep it in small claims. A separate cure applies where rent was withheld on a good-faith claim that you failed to supply essential services (see the redemption row).

title: No Defense for Late Benefit Payments
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute gives a tenant a defense, a continuance or reinstatement in an eviction because rent was late when a Social Security, public assistance or other government benefit payment, or a housing subsidy, arrived late. The ordinary nonpayment rules apply: you may terminate if the tenant does not pay within five days after your written demand. Federal rules differ for Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) tenancies: the family is not responsible for the part of the rent the housing authority's payment covers, the authority's failure to pay is not a lease violation by the tenant, and during the lease term you may not terminate the family's tenancy because the authority did not pay its share. Pursue the authority under your housing assistance payments contract instead. For a tenant who relies on a monthly benefit, agreeing in writing to a due date that follows the payment date avoids the problem.

title: When a Tenant Files Bankruptcy
bodyText: Federal bankruptcy law controls. When a tenant files, the automatic stay generally stops you from starting or continuing an eviction, enforcing a judgment you got before the filing, taking possession, or collecting rent owed from before the filing, until the stay ends or the bankruptcy court grants relief. Two exceptions matter for residential evictions. First, if you obtained a judgment for possession before the tenant filed, you may continue the eviction, but only after a 30-day wait if the tenant files with the petition a certification that state law would let the tenant cure the entire monetary default after the judgment and deposits with the bankruptcy clerk the rent due for the 30 days after filing; if the tenant then certifies within those 30 days that the default has been cured, the exception does not apply unless the court orders otherwise. You may object to a certification, and the court must hold a hearing within 10 days. A tenant whose petition shows a judgment for possession but who files no certification loses the stay for the eviction immediately. Second, an eviction based on endangerment of the property or illegal use of controlled substances there may proceed if you file with the bankruptcy court and serve on the tenant a certification under penalty of perjury that the eviction has been filed or that the tenant, in the 30 days before the certification, endangered the property or illegally used, or allowed the use of, a controlled substance on it; the exception takes effect 15 days later unless the tenant objects, in which case the court holds a hearing within 10 days. Leases: in a Chapter 7 case a residential lease the trustee does not assume or reject within 60 days after the order for relief (or a longer time the court sets within that period) is deemed rejected; in Chapter 11, 12 or 13 the decision may wait until a plan is confirmed unless the court sets a deadline on request. A lease clause that ends the lease because the tenant files bankruptcy or becomes insolvent cannot be enforced after the case begins. No Oklahoma statute says whether an eviction writ may be carried out after you receive notice of the tenant's bankruptcy; Oklahoma's only general post-judgment cure is the narrow one for rent withheld on a good-faith essential-services claim. Because a stay violation can bring sanctions, stop and confirm with counsel that an exception applies, or get relief from the stay, before taking any further step.

title: Who Can Be Served With Eviction Papers
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute provides for a lease to name someone to accept eviction papers for the tenant. The eviction summons may be served as in other civil cases, at least three days before trial, including: personally on the tenant, by leaving it at the tenant's home with a resident 15 or older, by delivering it to an agent authorized by appointment or by law to receive service of process, or by leaving it at an agreed meeting place with a person who lives at the tenant's home; it may also be left with a person over 15 residing on the premises, or, if reasonable diligence fails, sent by certified mail with a return receipt postmarked at least three days before trial. If no one can be served, the summons may be posted on the premises and mailed by certified mail at least five days before trial, but that service supports only a judgment for possession unless the tenant appears. Although the general service statute recognizes an agent appointed to receive process, the library does not offer a lease clause in which the tenant appoints one, because the statutory methods are enough. If the tenant is a participant in the Attorney General's Address Confidentiality Program (for victims of domestic abuse, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking or child abduction), the participant has designated the Attorney General as agent for service of process and for mail, so serve or mail there as well as using the methods above at the rental address, and do not publish the participant's actual address beyond what the eviction requires. Your own side: the lease must identify in writing who may accept service and notices for you, and anyone who fails to disclose that becomes your agent for service (see the landlord disclosure clause). The Attorney General's program rules make its Victims Advocacy and Services Unit the participant's agent for service: any summons, writ, notice, demand or process may be mailed to the participant's substitute address or delivered in person to that unit, which forwards a copy to the participant by first-class mail; mail addressed to the substitute address must show the participant's authorization number, and forwarded mail can take three to five days to reach the participant, so allow for that before the trial date. The rules do not say whether that alone is enough in an eviction, so serve both ways.

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute protects tenants who are federal or state employees or contractors from late fees, termination or eviction during a government shutdown or furlough, or gives them extra time to pay rent. The ordinary rules apply: rent is due when the lease says, and to end the lease for nonpayment you must give written demand and wait five days. A servicemember may have separate federal protections in some eviction cases, depending on military service, the use of the home as a residence and the amount of rent (see the servicemember row). If a tenant tells you pay is delayed by a shutdown, a written payment plan is often cheaper than an eviction, and you may agree to waive a late fee for that period.

title: No Extra Notice-to-Vacate Rules
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a notice to vacate to carry added statements (such as a summary of tenant rights or where to get help), and none specifically forbids alterations or work that make the unit uninhabitable while a notice to vacate is pending. What a notice must say comes from the rule you are using: a notice ending a month-to-month or at-will tenancy must be written and served at least 30 days before the end date (seven days for a shorter tenancy); a nonpayment notice is a written demand for payment, after which the lease may be terminated if rent is not paid within five days; and a notice for another material breach must specify the acts and omissions that make up the breach and state that the lease will end on a date at least 15 days after the tenant receives the notice unless the breach is remedied within ten days. Until the tenancy actually ends, all your duties continue: you must keep the unit fit and habitable and keep supplied facilities in good and safe working order; if you willfully or negligently cut off heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant's remedies apply after written notice; you may not remove or lock out the tenant; and you may enter only on at least one day's notice at reasonable times (except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable) and may not abuse entry to harass the tenant. Each party's duties end only on the effective date of a rightful termination.

title: Lead: No Oklahoma Notice at Signing; Renovation Pamphlet Rules
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute, and nothing in the state's lead-based paint rules (Department of Environmental Quality) or childhood lead rules (State Department of Health), requires you to hand a tenant a state lead notice, certificate or packet with the lease. The federal lead-based paint disclosure and the federal pamphlet are still required for most pre-1978 housing (the federal exemptions cover housing for the elderly or people with disabilities and units with no bedroom unless a child under 6 lives or is expected to live there, leases of 100 days or less where no renewal or extension can occur, units found free of lead-based paint by a certified inspector, and renewals where you made full disclosure before and have learned nothing new since; see the Lead-Based Paint Disclosure clause).

The Department of Environmental Quality's lead-based paint rules say that neither Oklahoma's lead-based paint statute nor those rules require a property owner to inspect or test for lead-based paint, or to reduce or remove it. Oklahoma does, through its Department of Environmental Quality, adopt the federal renovation rules. Before a renovation that disturbs painted surfaces in pre-1978 housing is done for pay, the firm doing the work must give the owner the federal "Renovate Right" pamphlet, and, where the owner does not live in the unit, give an adult occupant the pamphlet too, no more than 60 days before work starts, with a signed acknowledgment or proof of mailing at least 7 days before (if an adult occupant will not or cannot sign, the firm may instead certify in writing that it delivered the pamphlet).

Renovation of common areas in a multi-unit building needs a written notice to each affected unit or posted signs. Minor repair and maintenance is not a renovation, emergency renovations are exempt from the pamphlet step, and work on parts tested lead-free is outside the rules. The state rules reach anyone doing lead-based paint work in pre-1978 housing, and the exception for owners working in their own home does not apply while the home is occupied by someone other than the owner or the owner's immediate family. So if you or your maintenance staff renovate an occupied rental, plan to follow these steps and use certified renovators, and if you hire a contractor, make sure it gives your tenant the pamphlet.

If a child in your rental is found to have a high blood lead level, the State Department of Health may investigate the home; Oklahoma's health rules put the screening and reporting duties on health care providers and laboratories, not on landlords.

title: Contamination: Meth Disclosure and Recorded Cleanup Limits
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute generally requires you to tell a tenant about contamination on the property, with two exceptions. First, methamphetamine: before a rental agreement begins, if you know or have reason to know the unit or any part of the premises was used to make methamphetamine, you must tell the prospective tenant, unless you have had the contamination assessed and it does not exceed 0.1 microgram per 100 square centimeters of surface materials (see the Methamphetamine Manufacturing Disclosure clause).

Second, environmental covenants: where a cleanup approved by the Department of Environmental Quality or another state or federal agency left a recorded environmental covenant with activity and use limitations on the land, a copy must be given to each person in possession of the property, which includes a tenant, by the persons and in the way the agency requires. The covenant runs with the land, so its limits bind your tenant's use even if the lease is silent.

Other recorded cleanup notices also run with the land: DEQ records notices of remediation that can bar activities that damage the cleanup or controls, restrict groundwater use or bar residential redevelopment, and anyone who damages or interferes with the remediation or controls is liable to repair it or for the Department's costs. On a certified brownfield site, knowingly using the land against the recorded land use disclosure is a misdemeanor. If your property has any of these, use the optional Recorded Environmental Covenant clause to pass the limits to your tenant.

Oklahoma's seller disclosure form, which asks about hazardous materials, applies, unless an exemption applies (for example a newly built home no one has lived in, or a transfer to a spouse or lineal relative), to sales of homes with one or two dwelling units, and to a lease with an option to purchase one, when the seller is represented by a real estate licensee or the buyer asks for it in writing; it does not apply to an ordinary lease. A city may restrict occupancy by children of property contaminated by lead or other hazardous substances.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure Rule
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to tell a tenant that a rental contains defective or corrosive drywall. You must still keep the unit fit and habitable and keep the electrical, plumbing, heating and air-conditioning systems you supply in good and safe working order, so if defective drywall damages those systems or makes the unit unfit, the repairs fall within those duties. If you sell the property, or offer a lease with an option to buy, Oklahoma's seller disclosure statement asks about known defects. Telling a prospective tenant about a known defect that affects health or safety is the cautious course.

title: No Duty to Disclose Registered Offenders
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to tell tenants or applicants that a registered sex offender or violent offender lives on or near the property, or to give them a notice about the offender registry. The law says the offender registration acts impose no duty on a real estate licensee to disclose information about a registered offender. The Department of Corrections registry is open to public inspection and may be offered online, and local police and sheriffs must make their registries available on request, so a tenant who wants to know can look. If you choose to mention the registry, point to it rather than describing particular people. Separate rules limit who may live together: two registrants may not share an individual dwelling unless married or blood relatives, and knowingly leasing where they do is a crime (see the Registered Sex Offenders row). It is also a crime for someone who has reason to believe a registrant is out of compliance with registration, and who intends to help the registrant elude arrest, to harbor or conceal the registrant.

title: Property Near Military Bases: No Disclosure Rule; 2027 Rental Bar
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to tell a tenant that a rental lies in a military aircraft noise zone, an accident potential zone or near a military base, or gives tenants a right to end a lease for that reason. Two other laws touch property near military installations. First, a city that lies wholly or partly within an Air Installation Compatible Use Zone, Joint Land Use Study, Army Compatible Use Buffer or Environmental Noise Management Plan area of a military installation (around Altus, Tinker and Vance Air Force Bases and Fort Sill, for example) may adopt zoning that restricts future uses exposing residents to noise above 65 DNL or to accident potential; check your city's zoning before you build or convert property near a base. Second, starting July 1, 2027, a law passed in 2026 bars a foreign principal from a foreign adversary country (including an individual domiciled in such a country who is not a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident) from renting or otherwise controlling real property within ten miles of a military base or installation, a military operating area or other critical infrastructure, and conflicting rental agreements are deemed invalid. Unless you are yourself a foreign entity, you are not required to determine or ask whether an applicant is covered, and you bear no civil or criminal liability under that section; asking applicants about citizenship or national origin carries fair housing risk (see the Foreign Ownership and Leasing of Land row).

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Oklahoma has no ocean coast, and no Oklahoma statute requires you to tell a tenant about shoreline, beach or lake access, or about public access rights along water. If your rental is on a lake or river, access to the water and any dock or shoreline use may be controlled by the agency that manages the lake or by a recorded easement; those are facts about the property, not a state disclosure duty, and if you promise lake access in the lease, describe it accurately.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared Meter Disclosure
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute, and none of the Corporation Commission utility rules reviewed, requires you to tell a tenant about nearby former military ordnance sites, about a plan or permit application to demolish the building, or about a utility meter that also serves areas outside the tenant's unit. Related utility rules do apply. Corporation Commission rules generally bar one customer from separately metering and billing another for electricity or gas, though a landlord may include the cost in rent, and Commission-approved electric submetering systems are allowed; and if you buy electricity or gas from a city and resell it to a residential tenant, you may charge no more than 10% above your cost and your bills must show the per-unit cost and each charge (see the Reselling Electricity or Gas to Tenants row). If a tenant pays a utility account in the tenant's own name that also carries common-area or another unit's usage, say so in the lease and adjust the rent or bill fairly; this is good practice, not a state requirement. If you plan to demolish, give the notice your lease and Oklahoma's termination rules require.

title: No Foreclosure Disclosure Rule
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute requires you to tell a prospective or new tenant that the property is in foreclosure or that a foreclosure case has been filed. Even so, keeping quiet about a foreclosure you know of can expose you to a fraud or deceit claim if the tenant signs relying on a misleading picture, and a foreclosure can end the tenancy early under general foreclosure law.

The cautious course is to tell an applicant in writing before signing when the property is in foreclosure; the optional Foreclosure Disclosure clause records that you did. A tenant who receives notice of a proceeding to recover the property must tell you immediately (see the Foreclosure and Tenants row).

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 warning rules do not apply in Oklahoma, and no Oklahoma statute requires you to post or give tenants a warning about chemicals known to cause cancer or birth defects. Oklahoma's own disclosures that can touch chemicals are narrower: the methamphetamine disclosure, the federal lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing, and any recorded environmental covenant on the land (see the Contamination row).

title: Lease With an Option to Buy
bodyText: Oklahoma has no separate rent-to-own or lease-option statute for homes, but three rules apply if you give a tenant an option to buy. First, the seller disclosure law: for a property with one or two dwelling units, a lease with an option to purchase counts as a contract under Oklahoma's Residential Property Condition Disclosure Act. If you are represented by a real estate licensee, or the tenant asks you in writing, then unless an exemption applies (for example, a newly built home no one has lived in, or a transfer to your spouse or a relative in your direct line), you must give the tenant the Real Estate Commission's disclaimer statement or property condition disclosure statement, signed and dated by you no more than 180 days before the tenant receives it, and the law says it must be delivered before you accept an offer to purchase. When that point arrives in a lease-option has not been settled; the cautious course is to deliver it before the lease-option is signed and to update it if you learn of a new defect. A buyer may sue for actual damages, including repair costs, if the statement is not given or a known defect is left out. Second, the Consumer Credit Code: a lease in which all or a substantial part of the rent is credited toward the purchase price is treated as a sale of an interest in land. If you regularly sell this way on credit to individuals for personal or household use, with installment payments or a finance charge, it can be a consumer credit sale that requires credit disclosures and gives the buyer statutory remedies. Get advice before crediting rent toward a price. Third, the Landlord and Tenant Act still governs the lease, but it does not govern occupancy under a contract for deed by the buyer, unless the arrangement was created to avoid the Act. An option to buy land should be in writing. Because these rules turn on facts and carry their own remedies, the library does not offer an option-to-purchase clause; you may add your own after legal advice.

title: Disclosures Oklahoma Requires
bodyText:
Oklahoma requires these disclosures to a residential tenant, each covered by its own row:
- (1) in every rental agreement, prominently and in writing, the person and address entitled to accept service or notice, and, at or before the start of the tenancy, the names and addresses of the manager and of the owner (or of the owner's agent for service and notices) (Person to Accept Service and Owner and Manager Disclosure clause)
- (2) if you know the premises flooded within the past five years, a prominent written statement in any written rental agreement (Flooding Disclosure clause)
- (3) before the rental agreement begins, any known or suspected use of the unit or premises to make methamphetamine, unless testing shows contamination at or below the state level (Methamphetamine Manufacturing Disclosure clause)
- (4) for most housing built before 1978 (not housing for the elderly or people with disabilities, or a unit with no bedroom, unless a child under 6 lives or will live there; leases of 100 days or less where no renewal or extension can occur, units found free of lead-based paint by a certified inspector, and renewals where you made full disclosure before and have learned nothing new since are also exempt), the federal lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet (Lead-Based Paint Disclosure clause)
- (5) if you hold an Oklahoma real estate license (active or inactive), own the property, and the rental is handled by you or marketed through a real estate firm, written disclosure on all transaction documents that you are licensed, with your license number on the lease, and, if a licensee signs for the owner under a power of attorney, written disclosure on all transaction documents that the licensee is licensed (Real Estate Licensee Status clause)
- (6) if you resell city-supplied electricity or gas, the per-unit cost and each charge on your bills
- (7) a copy of any recorded environmental covenant, when the agency requires it
- (8) if you give an option to buy a one- or two-unit home, the seller disclosure or disclaimer statement in the circumstances described in the Lease With an Option to Buy row
- (9) where a real estate broker provides brokerage services in the lease transaction, each party's written confirmation, in a separate provision in or attached to the lease, of the broker's written disclosure of its duties, or, where the broker did not prepare the lease, the broker's own documentation; including the confirmation in a landlord-prepared lease is the cautious course (Broker Duties Confirmation clause).

No Oklahoma statute requires a state tenant-rights statement or form as the first page of the lease, a notice of whether the unit is covered by a just-cause or rent law (Oklahoma has neither, and cities may not regulate rent), or a warning in a sale-leaseback.

title: Statutory Forms: Eviction and Disclosure Forms, No Lease Form
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute prescribes a lease form or verbatim lease text; you may use your own lease if it follows the Landlord and Tenant Act. Oklahoma does prescribe side documents. For evictions, the affidavit and the summons must be on forms the Oklahoma Bar Association develops in plain language, linked on the Oklahoma State Courts Network, and the summons must be delivered at least three days before the hearing, which must be at least five days after the summons issues. The writ of execution after an eviction judgment, and the small claims affidavit, follow forms set out in the statutes. The Real Estate Commission sets by rule the seller disclosure and disclaimer statements (used for a lease with an option to buy). The Commission's contract form committee also drafts residential lease forms and addenda for voluntary use by real estate licensees; they are not required for landlords. Where a real estate broker is involved, the broker's written description of its duties must be confirmed by each party in a separate provision in or attached to the lease, or, where the broker did not prepare the lease, documented by the broker; whether a landlord-prepared lease still needs the separate provision is unsettled, so include it (see the Disclosures Oklahoma Requires row).

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Notice or Lease Placement Rule
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires an occupancy notice at the top of a lease for a single-family home, presumes a tenant lacks lawful occupancy unless the lease is notarized, or sets the font size or page placement of any lease notice. Oklahoma's fast-track removal of squatters works the other way: a sheriff may remove unauthorized occupants at the owner's request only if, among other conditions, they are not current or former tenants under a written or oral rental agreement the owner authorized and cannot produce a lease signed by the owner or the owner's agent. A tenant must be removed through an eviction case instead (see the Removing Unauthorized Occupants and Squatters row). A signed written lease, with your name and contact address, is the best evidence of who is lawfully in the unit.

title: No Lease Translation Requirement
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to translate a lease, give a translated copy, or use a particular language when you advertise or negotiate in a language other than English. Oklahoma's Constitution makes English the language of official state actions; that rule governs the government, not private leases. If you rent to someone who does not read English well, a translated copy or an interpreter at signing reduces later disputes about what the tenant agreed to; if you do, say in the lease which version controls.

title: No State Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute creates a state "truth in renting" statement or tenant-rights guide, or requires you to give tenants one.
