The Real Estate Commission's voluntary lease forms for licensees list optional attachments, such as "Tenancy Guidelines" and a landlord-tenant "You Need to Know" sheet, but those are broker forms, not a state requirement.

title: No Plain-Language Rule for Leases
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a residential lease to be written in plain language, to meet a readability test, or to be divided and captioned by sections. Oklahoma's plain-language rules reach other documents: the eviction affidavit and summons forms the Oklahoma Bar Association writes, life and health insurance policies, and certain consumer-credit disclosures. Oklahoma's Consumer Protection Act bars deceptive and unfair practices in consumer transactions, but whether it reaches residential leases is not settled (see the Consumer Protection Act row). Clear headings and plain wording still make a lease easier to enforce.

title: No Consumer Restrictions Statement
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a residential lease to carry a statement listing the terms that restrict the tenant's rights, offers Attorney General preapproval of lease forms, or applies a plain-language consumer-contract law to leases. Oklahoma does list lease terms that are unenforceable, such as a waiver of rights under the Landlord and Tenant Act or a promise to pay the other side's attorney fees (see the Prohibited Lease Terms row).

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute sets a minimum type size for a residential lease or any notice in it, or makes small print inadmissible in court. Two Oklahoma lease rules do call for prominence: the person to accept service or notice must be identified prominently and in writing in the rental agreement, and a known flood within the past five years must be stated prominently and in writing in a written rental agreement. Type-size rules in Oklahoma apply to other contracts, such as rental-purchase agreements for goods and real estate wholesaler contracts. Use a readable size and make required disclosures stand out.

title: No Blank-Space Rule for Leases
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires every blank in a residential lease to be filled in before signing, or treats a lease with blanks as a violation by the landlord. Oklahoma's "do not sign if it contains any blank spaces" warning applies to consumer litigation funding agreements, not leases, and the Consumer Protection Act's list of unlawful practices does not mention blanks. Still, fill in or strike every blank before anyone signs: a blank completed later invites a dispute over what the tenant agreed to.

title: What a Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Oklahoma does not prescribe a list of terms every lease must contain, or require the start and end dates on the first page. A lease must, however: identify prominently and in writing the person and address entitled to accept service or notice; state prominently and in writing any flooding within the past five years that you know of, if the lease is written; carry your real estate license status and number if you are a licensee (active or inactive) who owns the property and the rental is handled by you or marketed through a real estate firm, and the license status of a licensee who signs for the owner under a power of attorney; and include each party's written confirmation of the broker's duty disclosure where a broker provides brokerage services. A lease may not contain the terms the Landlord and Tenant Act forbids, such as a waiver of rights under the Act, a confession of judgment, a promise to pay the other side's attorney fees, or a limit on calling police in an emergency; such terms are unenforceable. Where the lease is silent, the Act fills the gaps: rent is the fair rental value, payable at the unit, in full at the start of a term of a month or less and monthly for longer terms; and without a definite term in writing, the tenancy is week-to-week for a roomer or boarder who pays weekly and otherwise month-to-month. Stating the rent, due date, place of payment and term in the lease avoids those defaults.

title: No Rule Requiring Tenant Initials
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a tenant to initial particular lease provisions or notices, and no lease term is unenforceable just because it was not initialed. Having the tenant initial key disclosures, such as the flood statement or the lead-based paint disclosure, is still useful evidence that the tenant saw them. The Broker Duties Confirmation clause uses initials because the law requires each party's written confirmation in a separate provision.

title: Long Leases: Writing, Recording and Both Spouses for a Homestead
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute sets a maximum term for a residential lease. Longer leases do carry formalities. A lease for longer than one year must be in writing and signed by the party to be bound (or an agent or broker with written authority), and to bind later buyers and lenders it must be acknowledged and recorded (see the Leases Longer Than One Year row). If the rental is your homestead (for example, your home that you rent out temporarily without acquiring another homestead), a lease for more than one year is valid only if it is in writing and signed by both spouses, if both are living and not divorced or legally separated. An attorney-in-fact may sign for a spouse if the power of attorney is recorded with the county clerk where the property is, and a court may authorize one spouse to lease a jointly held homestead if the other is incapacitated. A lease of one year or less does not need both spouses' signatures. If you sign as a guardian, court-approval rules for leasing the ward's property apply.

title: No Rule Equalizing Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Leases
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires the same rent or terms for month-to-month and fixed-term tenants, bars terms that are more burdensome for one type, or caps the difference; cities may not regulate the amount of rent. The Act treats the types differently only in how they end: a month-to-month tenancy (or tenancy at will) ends on at least 30 days' written notice, a tenancy shorter than month-to-month on at least 7 days' written notice, and a fixed term expires on its end date without notice unless ended earlier or the parties agree otherwise. If you let a tenant stay after the term ends, a month-to-month tenancy results unless you agree otherwise, so say in the lease or a renewal offer what rent and terms apply to a month-to-month continuation. Any difference in price or terms must still be applied evenly and not based on a protected characteristic under fair housing law.

title: Agreeing on Extra Ways to Give Notice
bodyText:
No Oklahoma landlord and tenant statute sets an "actual notice" delivery standard or lets you and the tenant agree on an extra way, such as a text message, to give a notice the law requires. Where a statute sets the method, use it. A written notice ending a tenancy, and a notice of a lease violation, must be served on the tenant personally; if the tenant cannot be located, on a family member over 12 living with the tenant; and otherwise by posting it on the unit and mailing a copy by certified mail (or the Postal Service's Firm Mailing Book). Serving a written rent demand the same way is the cautious course.

A tenant who cannot serve you personally mails the notice by certified mail to the person your lease names to accept notices. Oklahoma's electronic transactions act lets you deal electronically only with a tenant who has agreed to, lets either of you refuse later electronic dealings (the lease cannot take that right away), and keeps any method another law requires; where you have both agreed, an electronic record the recipient can print or store satisfies a law that asks only for a writing, so treat a tenant's emailed written notice (such as a repair notice) as likely effective, but as the cautious course keep giving your own required written notices on paper.

Federal electronic-signature law does not reach notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for an individual's primary residence. For notices no law requires in writing or by a set method, such as the one day's notice before you enter, an agreed email or text channel works; an optional lease clause sets one up. One statute turns on "actual notice": a tenant evicted for rent withheld over a good-faith claim that you failed to supply heat, water or another essential service may still cure after judgment if, within 10 days after the rent was due, the tenant gave you written notice of the claim or gave actual notice to your agent for collecting rent, and then pays the judgment, costs and fees by cash or cashier's check within 72 hours.

Actual notice means being told the fact, however it is done, so have anyone who collects rent for you pass service complaints on at once, and don't count on a lease term to narrow how a tenant may tell you.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText:
Oklahoma requires these notices in writing. A lease cannot turn the Landlord and Tenant Act's written notices into spoken ones, except where a section itself allows a different agreement (as for the effect of a sale or management-change notice).

From you:
- notice ending a month-to-month or at-will tenancy (at least 30 days) or a shorter periodic tenancy (at least 7 days)
- the demand for unpaid rent (the tenant then has 5 days to pay)
- notice of a lease violation the tenant can fix by repair, replacement or cleaning (10 days, or as promptly as conditions require in an emergency, after which you may do the work and bill it as rent, or for immediate payment if the lease has ended)
- notice that the lease will end for a material violation (at least 15 days, with 10 days to cure), and notice of immediate termination for a later breach
- the itemized statement of deposit deductions, mailed return receipt requested or handed to the tenant
- if your interest ends and you transfer the deposits to the new owner instead of returning them, notice of the transfer with the new owner's name and address
- notice that you sold the property or stopped managing it, which (unless you agreed otherwise) ends your liability for later events and tells the tenant whom to pay
- the certified-mail notice before you treat valuable belongings left behind as abandoned
- as part of the lease, the name and address of the person who accepts notices and legal papers
- in writing at or before move-in, the names and addresses of the manager and of the owner (or of the owner's agent for service and notices)
- plus, in a written lease, any flooding in the past five years you know about.

From the tenant:
- notice ending a month-to-month or at-will tenancy (at least 30 days) or a shorter periodic tenancy (at least 7 days), the same as yours
- notice ending the lease because you did not deliver possession
- notice of a repair, habitability or essential-service breach before any repair remedy arises
- notice within one week after vacating for fire or casualty
- notice ending the lease for unlawful entry or harassment
- the written demand for the deposit (within six months after the tenancy ends, or the deposit reverts to you)
- a domestic-violence, sexual-violence or stalking victim's termination notice with a protective order.

Other writings:
- a tenant with a term of two years or less, or at will, may assign only with your written assent
- a rule adopted mid-lease that substantially changes the tenant's bargain binds only if the tenant consents in writing
- repairs or chores shifted to the tenant need a separate conspicuous writing.

The one day's notice before you enter need not be written. Serve termination and violation notices the way the law requires (see How to Serve Notices).

title: Telling Tenants About Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute requires you to tell your tenant about a foreclosure, lawsuit, tax or sheriff's sale, condemnation or code-enforcement case against the property.

Some proceedings reach occupants directly instead:
- in a city that has adopted the code-lien foreclosure law, the petition to foreclose a code-enforcement lien is mailed to the occupants and notice is posted on the property
- in a mortgage foreclosure, the sheriff serves an occupant with, or posts, the lender's motion to protect property that appears abandoned
- a city that wants to enter for surveys without the owner's and lessee's written consent mails the owner and the lessee notice at least 14 days ahead
- on a public project, to the greatest extent practicable, no one lawfully occupying a dwelling is made to move without at least 90 days' written notice, assuming a replacement dwelling will be available, though the statute says these acquisition policies create no rights or liabilities.

The duty in the statute runs the other way: a tenant who receives notice of any proceeding to recover the property or its possession must tell you immediately and hand you the notice if it is written, and is responsible for the damages you suffer if the tenant doesn't (an existing lease clause restates this). A tenant's attornment to a stranger is void unless you consent or a court orders it. After you sell or lose the property, unless you agreed otherwise, you stay liable under the lease for later events until you give the tenant written notice that your interest has ended.

Cautious course: tell tenants promptly, in writing, about any proceeding you know will affect their possession or whom they pay.

title: No Extended-Absence Notice Statute
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute requires a tenant to tell you before an extended absence, and none gives you extra rights to enter while the tenant is away. You may require the notice in your lease (an optional clause asks for notice of any absence over 7 days, with actual damages if the tenant willfully fails to give it). Treat an absence on its own as not abandonment, and the ordinary entry rules still apply: you may enter without consent in an emergency; otherwise you need the tenant's consent, which the tenant may not unreasonably withhold for an inspection, necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, improvements or services, or a showing to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workmen or contractors, and you must give at least one day's notice of your intent to enter unless that is impracticable, and enter only at reasonable times.

Beyond that you have no other right of access during the tenancy unless the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit, the Landlord and Tenant Act provides it, or a court orders it. Ask the tenant for an emergency contact and for consent to enter for routine checks during a long absence, such as to keep pipes from freezing.

title: Emergency Contacts
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute requires you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour phone number, to put a management website or a social-services hotline in the lease, or to collect an emergency contact from each tenant. Three related rules do apply.

First, the lease must name, prominently and in writing, the person and address for notices and legal papers, and you must tell the tenant in writing, at or before move-in, the names and addresses of the manager and of the owner (or of the owner's agent for service and notices), and keep that current.

Second, if you ask in writing, the tenant must give you the name, address and phone number of a person to contact if the tenant dies, and sign an authorization for that person to have supervised access, remove belongings and receive the deposit refund (see the Contact Person if Tenant Dies clause).

Third, to deal with nuisances and dilapidated property, a city may require the owner's contact information for emergencies and maintenance, or a person to receive notices, without charging a fee, and must keep it confidential; local ordinances are not covered here.

You may also ask each tenant for a general emergency contact by an optional lease clause; collect only what you need and use it only for emergencies. Good practice: give tenants, in writing, a way to reach you or your manager for fire, flooding, gas leaks or a loss of heat or water.

title: Repair Requests and Written Notice
bodyText: In Oklahoma a tenant's repair remedies (ending the lease, repairing and deducting, buying an essential service or moving out, or ending the lease over an uninhabitable unit) do not arise until the tenant has given you written notice; they also do not arise if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a family member, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal there with the tenant's consent. Separately, a tenant must report any defect the tenant has reason to believe you don't know about as soon as practicable, and that report can be made any way. Your lease may ask for repair requests in writing (the library's Maintenance and Repairs clause does), but it cannot take away a tenant's statutory rights, and it probably cannot give up your own right to written notice either, because a lease may not have either side waive rights or remedies under the Landlord and Tenant Act. So don't write that a phone call counts as notice for the statutory remedies; take phone reports for speed, but act on them. If you have agreed with the tenant to deal electronically, an email or portal request that you can print or store is likely written notice, so watch those channels. One deadline turns on knowledge instead of writing: a tenant who withholds rent over a good-faith claim that you failed to supply heat, water or another essential service keeps the right to cure after an eviction judgment by giving you written notice of the claim, or actual notice to your agent for collecting rent, within 10 days after the rent was due, and then paying the judgment, costs and fees by cash or cashier's check within 72 hours. A lease term requiring written repair requests does not remove that actual-notice route, so make sure anyone who collects rent for you passes complaints on.

title: Promises to Repair or Improve
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires your promise to clean, repair or improve a rental to be in writing, to carry a completion date or to be made before the lease is signed, and the Consumer Protection Act does not name a broken repair promise as an unlawful practice. General law still gives promises force. A repair promise written into the lease is a lease term: you must deliver possession in line with the lease, and a material failure to keep it lets the tenant give written notice ending the lease, on a date at least 30 days after you receive the notice, unless you fix it within 14 days; where the failure materially affects health it can open the other repair remedies (repair and deduct only for a repair costing no more than one month's rent); and none of these remedies arises if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a family member, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal there with the tenant's consent. A written lease supersedes the spoken negotiations that came before it, so an unwritten promise may be hard for either side to enforce, but a promise made by a party to get the other side to sign, with no intention of keeping it, is fraud under Oklahoma's contract law. The Consumer Protection Act bars misleading statements that deceive a person before, during or after a consumer transaction, with damages and attorney fees for the person harmed; whether it reaches residential leases is not settled in the statute. A licensed real estate broker or property manager who makes false promises in the conduct of business can lose the license. Cautious course: make only promises you will keep, put each one in the lease or a signed addendum with what will be done and by when, and do it.

title: No Designated-Repairer Rule
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute lets your lease name the person or company that must do a repair the tenant has made at your expense. When you fail to fix a condition that materially affects health and costs no more than one month's rent, and the condition was not caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a family member, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal there with the tenant's consent, the statute lets the tenant, after written notice and 14 days (or as promptly as an emergency requires), have the work done in a workmanlike manner (the statute does not say by whom) and deduct the actual and reasonable cost, or the fair and reasonable value of the work, after giving you an itemized statement. A lease term limiting who may do that work narrows a statutory remedy, and a lease may not have the tenant waive or forego rights or remedies under the Landlord and Tenant Act, so the library does not offer one. The safer route is to fix problems first: name your repair contact, answer written repair notices within the 14 days, and you choose the repairer. Where you and the tenant agree that the tenant will do specified repairs or chores, that agreement must be a conspicuous writing separate from the lease, and it may say who does the work. When you fix a tenant's breach yourself after written notice, you choose who does the work, which must be workmanlike.

title: No Termination Because Repairs Cost Too Much
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute lets you end a lease, or refuse a repair, because the repair would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value. During the tenancy you must make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to keep the unit fit and habitable, and the lease cannot waive that, though a tenant may take on specified repairs or chores by a conspicuous writing separate from the lease. The one cost limit in the statute runs against the tenant: a tenant may repair and deduct only where the noncompliance materially affects health and the reasonable cost is no more than one month's rent. If repairs are not worth making, end the tenancy lawfully: a month-to-month tenancy ends on at least 30 days' written notice, and a fixed term runs to its end unless the lease or the law ends it sooner. For fire or other casualty that substantially impairs the unit, the library's optional Fire or Casualty clause lets you end the lease by written notice, unless the damage was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a family member, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal there with the tenant's consent. The library does not offer a clause letting you end the lease whenever repairs exceed a set cost, because it would let you avoid a repair duty the lease cannot waive; you may add your own term after legal advice.

title: No Rent Escrow for Repairs
bodyText: Oklahoma has no statute letting a tenant pay rent into court or into an escrow account until you make repairs, so there is no escrow program, no exemption from one and no exemption notice to give. A tenant's repair remedies are to end the lease, to repair and deduct, to buy an essential service or move to substitute housing, or to recover damages, each after written notice, and none where the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a family member, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal there with the tenant's consent (see Tenant Remedies for Repairs). A tenant who withholds rent over a good-faith claim that you failed to supply heat, water or another essential service, and who gave you written notice of the claim or actual notice to your agent for collecting rent within 10 days after the rent was due, can still cure after an eviction judgment by paying the judgment, costs and fees by cash or cashier's check within 72 hours. The only rent-into-court rule is for eviction appeals: while an appeal is pending, the tenant pays current rent into the court clerk's office, and failing to pay it is treated as abandoning the appeal. Within two days after judgment (up to seven if the judge allows) the tenant may also post a supersedeas bond; posting one does not excuse current rent.

title: Entry for Regularly Scheduled Services
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute lets you enter without notice for regularly scheduled services such as pest treatment or filter changes, even if the lease says so. A tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry to supply necessary or agreed services, but except in an emergency, or where giving notice is impracticable, you must give at least one day's notice of your intent to enter, enter only at reasonable times, and not abuse your access or use it to harass the tenant. A lease term waiving that notice is unenforceable because a lease may not have the tenant give up rights under the Landlord and Tenant Act.

You may list scheduled services in the lease so the tenant has agreed to them; give notice of each visit at least a day ahead (an optional clause sets this up). A tenant who faces unlawful or unreasonable entry, or repeated unreasonable demands for entry, may get an injunction or end the lease on written notice, and recover actual damages.

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to offer or give notice of a move-in or move-out inspection, so there is no penalty for leaving one out: you do not lose the right to make deposit deductions, and there is no double or triple deposit award tied to inspections. The deposit consequences that do exist are in the deposit law itself. Deductions must be itemized in a written statement mailed return receipt requested or delivered in person, and the balance returned within 45 days after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant makes a written demand; if you fail to comply, the tenant may recover the deposit and any prepaid rent, and either side may still recover other damages the Landlord and Tenant Act allows. Misappropriating a deposit from its escrow account is a crime punishable by up to six months in county jail and a fine of up to twice the amount misappropriated. Without an inspection you must still prove the damage you deduct for, so a dated move-in and move-out condition record, with photos, signed by the tenant if possible, is the cautious practice; an inspection visit during the tenancy needs at least one day's notice of your intent to enter, unless there is an emergency or giving notice is impracticable, and must be at a reasonable time.

title: Changing Lease Terms
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute sets a notice period for changing the rent, a fee or another term of a tenancy, and raising a fee the lease already charges needs no longer notice than raising the rent: a fee you require under the lease counts as rent. During a fixed-term lease the terms stay as written unless the tenant agrees or the lease itself provides for the change. For a month-to-month or at-will tenancy, either side may end it by written notice served at least 30 days before the end date (7 days for a tenancy shorter than month-to-month), so the cautious way to change terms is a written notice, served the way termination notices must be, at least 30 days before the change takes effect, that ends the current tenancy and offers the new terms; no Oklahoma case was read on whether a bare notice of new terms binds a tenant who stays.

Rules are different: you may adopt or change reasonable rules during the tenancy, but a rule binds the tenant only if the tenant has notice of it when it is adopted, and a new rule that substantially modifies the tenant's bargain binds only if the tenant consents in writing. During a declared emergency, increases in the affected area are capped (see Raising the Rent).

title: No Automatic-Renewal Statute for Leases
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute regulates an automatic-renewal clause in a residential lease: there is no reminder notice to send, no required type size or opt-in, and no limit on how early you may ask a tenant to renew. Oklahoma's consumer auto-renewal rule covers contracts to rent goods or rental-related services, not housing, and its unfair service-agreement law covers maintenance and sale services for homes, not leases. Unless otherwise agreed, a lease for a definite term ends on its last day without notice, so a lease may provide that it renews automatically unless either side gives notice (the library offers an optional Automatic Renewal clause).

A lease longer than one year must be in writing. If the lease is silent and you let the tenant stay after the term ends, a month-to-month tenancy is created unless you agree otherwise; an older statute presumes that accepting rent after a lease expires renews it on the same terms for the same time, up to one year, and no Oklahoma case was read on how the two fit, so say in the lease what happens at the end of the term.

title: Owners Who Live Outside Oklahoma: Agents, Companies and Service
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires an owner who lives in another state to appoint an Oklahoma agent, to name an in-state agent in the lease, or to file an agent designation before suing a tenant, and no such rule turned up in the blight, redevelopment or code-enforcement statutes. What Oklahoma requires of every landlord, wherever you live, is this: the lease must prominently identify in writing the person and address entitled to accept service or notice, and at or before the tenancy begins you must tell the tenant in writing the name and address of the manager, and of the owner or a person authorized to act for the owner in receiving legal papers and notices, and keep that information current. Anyone who fails to do this becomes a landlord under the Landlord and Tenant Act and the agent of each owner for receiving legal papers and notices and for performing the landlord's duties, using the rents collected (see the Person to Accept Service clause). The person named does not have to live in Oklahoma, but naming someone here who will actually receive papers and handle notices is the practical course. Living elsewhere does not keep you out of Oklahoma courts: an Oklahoma court may exercise jurisdiction on any basis the state and federal constitutions allow, a summons may be served on you outside Oklahoma (including by certified mail, return receipt requested, delivery restricted to you), and a suit against a nonresident may be brought in any county where you own property. If you own through a company formed outside Oklahoma, company law adds three things. First, a limited liability company formed elsewhere must register with the Secretary of State before transacting business here, naming an Oklahoma registered agent. An LLC that owns income-producing real property in Oklahoma is treated as transacting business, unless it acquired the property by collecting a debt or enforcing a mortgage. Until it registers, it may not bring any action, suit or proceeding in an Oklahoma court, including an eviction; its leases stay valid and it may defend a suit, and by doing business unregistered it makes the Secretary of State its agent for service on claims arising from that business. Second, a corporation formed elsewhere may not do business here through offices, agents or representatives located in Oklahoma (a local manager, for example) until it qualifies with the Secretary of State. If it does business without that authority, it may not bring a case until it qualifies and pays all fees, penalties and franchise taxes for the time it operated unqualified, and it faces a fine of $200 to $500 for each offense (its agent $100 to $500); its contracts stay valid and it may defend. The statute's list of activities that need no qualification does not include owning or renting out real property, so plan to qualify. Third, a corporation, LLC, trust, partnership or other unincorporated business that rents under a name other than its legal name must file a trade name report with the Secretary of State, and a partnership using a fictitious name must file a certificate naming its partners; the partnership statute bars the partnership from suing on contracts made in that name until it files (filing later cures it). Finally, anyone you pay to rent out your property, find tenants, or control the rent of a single-family home needs an Oklahoma real estate license unless an exception applies, such as a resident manager who lives on site at an apartment building, duplex or complex; you may rent out your own property without one. Tax withholding on rent paid to owners abroad and to members of pass-through entities is covered in a separate row.

title: Rent Paid to Owners Abroad and to Out-of-State Members: Tax Withholding
bodyText: Rent paid to an owner who merely lives in another state carries no withholding duty: no Oklahoma statute, and no rule in the Oklahoma Tax Commission's income tax and withholding chapters, makes a tenant or property manager withhold Oklahoma income tax from rent for that reason. Owners abroad are different. Federal tax law requires every person who pays, receives, holds or controls rent from U.S. property owed to a nonresident alien individual (someone who is neither a U.S. citizen nor a U.S. tax resident) or to a foreign partnership, and it names tenants expressly, to withhold 30% of it, and the same rule applies to rent owed to a foreign corporation. That reaches a tenant who pays such an owner directly and a property manager who collects the rent and pays it over. The 30% withholding does not apply to rent that is effectively connected with a U.S. trade or business and taxed as such, and a nonresident alien owner may elect to treat all income from U.S. real property held for the production of income that way; the election continues for later years unless the IRS consents to revoking it. Oklahoma adds its own withholding: in place of the federal 30%, Oklahoma taxes nonresident aliens at 8% and foreign corporations at 4%, and every payer of the amounts covered must withhold that percentage, pay it to the Tax Commission for each quarter by the last day of the following month with a return, and give the owner a written statement of the year's payments and withholding by January 31 of the next year; a payer who fails to withhold or pay is personally liable to the State. The Tax Commission's rule repeats the 8% duty for every payer of Oklahoma taxable income to nonresident aliens. Neither the Oklahoma statute nor the rule says whether the federal effectively-connected exception or election also ends the Oklahoma duty. Cautious course: before paying rent to an owner who is not a U.S. citizen or resident, or to a company organized outside the United States, get the owner's tax status in writing and get tax advice; until the adviser confirms that an exception applies, the payer withholds the federal and Oklahoma percentages. Owners that are pass-through entities: if the owner is an LLC, partnership, S corporation or trust not taxed as a corporation, the entity itself (not the tenant or manager) must withhold Oklahoma tax at the highest individual rate from each nonresident member's share of the Oklahoma income it distributes, pay it by its own return's due date (with quarterly estimated payments when the year's withholding can reasonably be expected to exceed $500), and give each such member and the Tax Commission an annual statement. A nonresident member is an individual not resident or domiciled in Oklahoma, a business without its commercial domicile here, or a trust not organized here. The statute excuses withholding for a member who files the Tax Commission's affidavit submitting to Oklahoma tax jurisdiction, for income the Tax Commission has ruled not subject to withholding, and for a publicly traded partnership that files an annual information return; the Tax Commission's rules add that an entity disregarded for income tax (for example, many single-owner LLCs) is not a pass-through entity, and that no withholding is required for tax-exempt members, on distributions to another pass-through entity (which must itself withhold on what it distributes), or where the entity has elected to pay Oklahoma tax at the entity level. Reporting rent: Oklahoma law lets the Tax Commission require everyone, tenants included, who pays $750 or more in rent to a taxpayer in a year to report the payments to it under oath, in the form and to the extent its rules prescribe. The Tax Commission's rule says persons paying $750 or more a year to taxpayers must file a report, and that the report is to include payments the IRS requires to be reported. Federal law requires information reports on rent only from payers engaged in a trade or business, so a tenant renting a home to live in generally has nothing to report; no case or Tax Commission guidance was read on whether Oklahoma's rule reaches further, and a business tenant, or a property manager that collects and pays over rent, should ask its tax adviser.

title: Police, Crime Reports and Calls for Help
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires or regulates a crime-free lease addendum, requires a landlord to cooperate with police investigations or report tenants to the police, lets a landlord consent to a police search of a tenant's home, or penalizes a property for police or emergency calls. Several rules still reach you. Calls for help: a lease may not waive or limit a tenant's right to summon a peace officer or other emergency assistance in an emergency, and such a term is unenforceable; and you may not deny, refuse to renew or end a tenancy because the applicant, tenant or a household member is a victim or alleged victim of domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking, whether or not there is a protective order. So never count police or emergency calls against a tenant. Reporting duties that bind every person, you and your staff included: anyone who has reason to believe a child under 18 is a victim of abuse or neglect must report it immediately to the Department of Human Services hotline, and knowingly and willfully failing to report promptly is a crime; anyone who has reasonable cause to believe a vulnerable adult is suffering abuse, neglect or exploitation must report it as soon as they are aware, to the Department of Human Services, the State Department of Health's Office of Client Advocacy, or the city police or county sheriff, and knowingly and willfully failing to report promptly is a misdemeanor punishable by up to a year in jail, a fine of up to $1,000, or both; a similar duty covers an incapacitated or partially incapacitated person or a minor suffering abuse, neglect or exploitation; and anyone who has reason to believe a person is trafficking in children must report it promptly to the Oklahoma Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs Control. If you find a tenant dead and no physician was attending, you must promptly notify the medical examiner of a death the law requires to be investigated (for example a violent, suspicious, unusual or unattended death), and the body must not be disturbed until the medical examiner and any investigating police agency authorize it: call 911 and leave the unit as it is. Court orders: a court order authorizing police to intercept communications can direct a landlord to furnish information, facilities and technical help; you are paid at prevailing rates and are immune from liability for complying. Drug activity: it is unlawful for any person to keep or maintain a dwelling or other place that drug users resort to for using controlled dangerous substances, or that is used for keeping or selling them; the penalty is a civil fine of up to $1,000, or a felony where the violation is charged and found to be knowing or intentional. Act promptly on criminal activity you learn of (see the No Criminal Activity clause). Police at the door: the Oklahoma Constitution protects homes against unreasonable searches, so let police into an occupied unit only with a warrant, the tenant's consent or a real emergency, and give tenant records only on a subpoena, warrant or court order, or with the tenant's consent.

title: Who May Appear in Court for an LLC or Corporation Landlord
bodyText: If the landlord is a corporation, limited liability company, partnership, trust or other legal entity (for example, you own the property through one), an Oklahoma statute lets it go to court without a lawyer in two kinds of case: a small claims case (a money claim of up to $10,000, not counting attorney fees and costs, or recovery of personal property worth up to $10,000), and an eviction (forcible entry and detainer) case that is on the small claims docket or assigned to the small claims division. An eviction goes on the small claims docket when the total sought with it (rent, damage to the premises, or another Landlord and Tenant Act claim), not counting attorney fees and costs, is within the small claims limit; a district court may also, by court rule, send any eviction to the small claims division to decide possession, whatever the amount, and then return it to the assigned judge. In those cases the entity may appear through a corporate officer, member, manager, partner, trustee or regular full-time employee, who may sign the affidavits and other filings and otherwise proceed like an individual representing themself. An outside management company that is not one of those people is not on the list, and a collection agency, collection agent or assignee of a claim may not bring a small claims case at all. Small claims can stop being small claims: the tenant may move to transfer the case to the regular docket (the judge decides when the claim is under $7,500 and must transfer it at $7,500 or more, on a timely motion and a $50 deposit), and a claim, counterclaim or setoff over $10,000 filed within the time to answer sends the case to another docket unless both sides agree in writing to keep it. Your small claims affidavit must state that you disclaim a jury trial on the merits, but where the claim, counterclaim or setoff is over $1,500 a party may still ask for a jury (in writing, at least two working days before the appearance date, with a $50 deposit). Attorney-fee statutes apply in small claims only if an attorney appears. Outside the small claims docket (a regular-docket eviction or lawsuit, a transferred case, or an appeal) no Oklahoma statute lets a non-lawyer appear for an entity; the Supreme Court's bar rules say that no person or entity may practice law in Oklahoma unless an active member of the Bar Association, and its own small claims rule lets an entity proceed through a corporate officer or regular full-time employee only in small claims (the 2024 statute adds members, managers, partners and trustees). The Rules for District Courts say nothing on it. Whether a non-lawyer appearing for an entity outside small claims is the unauthorized practice of law is case law, so take the cautious course. Cautious course: in small claims, send an officer or regular full-time employee where you can (the people both the statute and the Supreme Court's rule name), otherwise a member, manager, partner or trustee, who knows the facts and has the lease, ledger and notices; for a regular-docket case, a transferred case or an appeal, use an Oklahoma-licensed attorney, and line one up before filing if a large claim or a tenant counterclaim is likely. An owner who is an individual may always represent himself or herself.

title: Other Rules Oklahoma Does Not Have
bodyText: Rules found in some other states that Oklahoma's statutes do not set. (1) No cap on rent paid in advance: no Oklahoma statute limits how much rent you may collect ahead of time. Rent paid ahead is prepaid rent, not a security deposit, but it must be returned in two situations: if you fail to deliver possession and the tenant ends the lease by written notice, you must return all prepaid rent and the deposit; and a tenant may recover any prepaid rent the Landlord and Tenant Act requires you to return. (2) No rent-to-own or lease-option statute for homes, but Oklahoma's seller disclosure law can reach a lease with an option to buy a home with one or two dwelling units: if you are represented by a real estate licensee, or the tenant asks you in writing, you must give the Real Estate Commission's disclaimer or disclosure statement, unless an exemption applies (for example a newly built, never-occupied home, or a transfer to a spouse or to a lineal relative such as a child, grandchild or parent of an owner); see the Lease With an Option to Buy row. Each of the following is also absent and is explained, with what Oklahoma has nearby, in its own row: no lease type-size or bold-print rule (the No Lease Type-Size Rule row); no rule requiring the tenant to initial lease clauses or notices (the No Rule Requiring Tenant Initials row); no duty to translate the lease (the No Lease Translation Requirement row); no seasonal or vacation-rental regime (the No Special Rules for Seasonal or Vacation Rentals row); no possession bond (the No Possession Bond or Confessed Judgment row); no rent-into-court requirement before a tenant raises defenses (the Rent Paid Into Court and Tenant Counterclaims row); no defense for a late government benefit payment (the No Defense for Late Benefit Payments row); no early termination for age, illness or a move to care (the No Early Termination for Age, Illness or a Move Into Care row); no right to end a lease because repairs cost too much (the No Termination Because Repairs Cost Too Much row); no tenant organizing right (the No Statutory Tenant Organizing Right row); no landlord insurance mandate (the No Required Landlord Liability Insurance row); no hardship stay of an eviction (the No Hardship Stay of Eviction; No Moratorium Law row); no rent-reporting rule (the No Rent Reporting Rule row); no extended-absence notice statute (the No Extended-Absence Notice Statute row).

title: Squatters, Cash Receipts and Registration Outside the Landlord Act
bodyText: Three rules a landlord might expect outside the Landlord and Tenant Act: (1) Squatters: Oklahoma has a specific remedy. An owner or the owner's authorized agent may ask the county sheriff to remove people unlawfully occupying real property, without an eviction case, but only if all of these are true: you are the owner or authorized agent; the people unlawfully entered and remain or live there; the property was not open to the public when they entered; you have told them to leave; they are not current or former tenants under any written or oral rental agreement you authorized; they cannot show a government-issued document or ID using the address within the past 12 months; they cannot produce a lease signed by you or your agent; they are not your immediate family; and no litigation about the property is pending between you and them. You submit a verified complaint on the form the statute sets out; the sheriff verifies it, serves a notice to vacate immediately and puts you in possession, and for an hourly fee may stand by while you change the locks and remove their belongings. A person wrongfully removed can be put back in possession and recover actual costs and damages, three times the fair market rent, court costs and attorney fees, and the procedure may not be used to get around Landlord and Tenant Act rights, so never use it against a tenant or former tenant (use the eviction case instead). Knowingly presenting a fake lease or deed to stay on property is a crime, and an occupant removed this way who intentionally damages the home by $1,000 or more commits a felony. (2) No cash-rent receipt duty: no Oklahoma statute requires a landlord to give a receipt for rent, including rent paid in cash or by money order; receipt duties exist for others, such as money transmitters, hearing-aid sellers, bail bondsmen and public officers. Give a dated receipt for every cash payment anyway; it is your proof too. (3) No registration condition on evictions: no Oklahoma statute makes landlord or rental registration or licensing a condition of filing an eviction or winning possession, and cities may not require registration of real property through fees, civil fines or criminal penalties, although a city may keep a list of owners or their designees and, to address public nuisances, dilapidated properties or other unlawful conduct, may require, without charging a fee, contact information for the person responsible for emergencies and maintenance or the name and contact information of the person who receives notices and legal papers. A different filing can matter: a company formed outside Oklahoma must register or qualify with the Secretary of State before it can bring a case (see the Owners Who Live Outside Oklahoma row).

title: Contractor Liens and Work Your Tenant Orders
bodyText:
Anyone who, under an oral or written contract with the owner of land, does labor, supplies material or rents out equipment used to build, alter or repair a building or improvement on it (or to put up fixtures, plant trees or hedges, or build fences or sidewalks) gets a lien on the whole tract, its buildings and appurtenances, and that lien can be enforced by selling the property. If the person who ordered the work does not hold title to the land (a tenant, for example), the statute allows the lien on the buildings and improvements separately from the real estate.

Oklahoma has no notice-of-nonresponsibility procedure, and no statute decides when work a tenant orders reaches your interest; no Oklahoma case was read on whether a tenant counts as an owner or whether your consent to the work changes that, so assume a contractor your tenant hires could claim against your building. Timing: an original contractor files the lien statement within four months after last furnishing labor, material or equipment; a subcontractor or supplier within 90 days.

Subcontractors and suppliers must usually send the owner a pre-lien notice within 75 days, but not for a residential project of four or fewer units none of which an owner lives in, and not for claims under $10,000, so a small rental can be liened with no advance warning. You will learn of a filed lien by certified mail sent within five business days of filing. On work you order yourself, you owe subcontractors no more than you agreed to pay your contractor, but you carry the risk of what you pay the contractor until the 90 days run, and you may pay a subcontractor directly and count it as payment to the contractor.

To clear a lien, you may deposit cash or a surety bond of 125% of the claim with the county clerk; a lien not sued on within one year of filing is canceled by law; you may sue the claimant to have the lien adjudicated; and in a suit to enforce a lien the winner recovers a reasonable attorney fee. If your lease lets the tenant make alterations, use the optional No Liens for Tenant Work clause, and remember that a tenant's agreement to do repairs, alterations or remodeling must be a separate conspicuous writing (see the Tenant Maintenance Agreement).

title: No Special District Statement in an Oklahoma Lease
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a lease to say that the property lies in an improvement, assessment, fire protection, conservancy or other special district, to have the tenant acknowledge district charges or rules, or to give a tenant a vote or voice in a district because of the tenancy. Districts' petitions, assessments and contracts run to landowners: for example, a petition for a municipal parking-station improvement is signed by owners of land in the improvement district, with co-owners counted by their shares and the owner of a life estate deemed the sole landowner, and a fire protection district may contract with the owner or the occupant of nearby property outside any district for a fixed annual fee. One district type to watch is the rural water, sewer, natural gas or solid waste district. A right to one service connection (a benefit unit) carries the right to take part in the district's affairs, and a participating member, a person owning or having an interest in land in the district who subscribes to a benefit unit, gets one vote at the annual meeting. Whether a tenant's lease counts as an interest in the land for this purpose is not settled by statute, so if your rental is served by such a district, keep the benefit unit in your name and say in the lease who pays for the service. If you want to pass any district charge on to the tenant, the lease must say so plainly; no Oklahoma statute does it for you.

title: Leasing Tribal or Restricted Indian Land
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute makes a residential lease of privately owned land wait for a government officer's approval, and Oklahoma has no communal land tenure of its own: if you own the property outright, the lease binds when you and the tenant sign it (a lease for longer than one year must be in writing and signed by the party to be bound or by that party's agent or broker). Indian land is different. Land the United States holds in trust for a tribe or an individual Indian, and land a tribe or individual Indian owns but can sell or encumber only with federal approval (restricted land), is governed by the federal leasing statute and the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) leasing rules. Under them, anyone who is not an owner of the Indian land needs a lease from the owners before taking possession of any part of it; possession without a required lease is a trespass, and BIA may act to recover possession, including eviction, for the owners. A residential lease of a single-family residence (under the BIA rules, a building with one to four dwelling units) needs BIA approval. BIA approves unless required consents are missing, the rules' requirements are not met, or it finds a compelling reason to protect the owners, and it may not unreasonably withhold approval; once it acknowledges a complete package it has 30 days to approve, disapprove or return the package for revision, and the parties can press for a decision if it misses the deadline. Before approval: the lease takes effect on the date BIA approves it. The lease may set a date for the parties' obligations to each other to begin, before or after approval, but until approval the tenant has no effective lease, so do not let the tenant move in before BIA approves. What the lease must contain: the BIA rules list mandatory terms (among them the tract, purpose, parties, term, ownership of improvements, payment terms and late charges, enforcement by the United States, BIA's right to inspect on reasonable notice, and hold-harmless terms where the lessee may lawfully give them). The federal term limit is generally 25 years plus one renewal of up to 25 years (longer for some tribes, including land held in trust for the Cherokee Nation), and a residential lease cannot be extended by holdover unless it says so. Rent for individually owned land must be at least fair market rental unless every owner waives it in writing or BIA waives it in the cases its rules allow. Where a tract has several owners, owners of a set share of the interests must consent (90% where there are one to five owners, 80% for six to ten, 60% for 11 to 19, and more than 50% for 20 or more). Renting out a home you lease from Indian owners: if you hold an approved residential lease of Indian land and rent the home to a tenant, that rental is a sublease, which needs the owners' consent and BIA approval unless your lease allows subleasing without them and the sublease does not release you from your own liability. If BIA does not decide within 30 days of receiving the required documents, the sublease is deemed approved to the extent consistent with federal law and takes effect 45 days after it was mailed or delivered to BIA. Exceptions: no lease is needed by an Indian owner of all the trust or restricted interests in the tract; a tribe with BIA-approved leasing regulations may approve its own residential leases of tribal land (not individually allotted land) for up to 75 years where its regulations so provide; a life tenant holding a life estate in all the trust or restricted interests may lease for the life of the estate without BIA approval but must record the lease; leases of tribal land by a tribe's federally chartered corporation for up to 25 years, and leases under a special act of Congress that authorizes leasing without approval, need no BIA approval but must be recorded; tribal land assignments and permits fall outside these rules. Multi-family developments and other residential developments that are not housing for public purposes fall under BIA's business-lease rules: those leases also take effect only on BIA approval, and units in such a development may be sublet without landowner consent or BIA approval only if the lease allows it, the developer stays liable and BIA gets a copy of each sublease within 30 days. Which law governs: the BIA rules say a lease approved under them is subject to federal and tribal law and not to state law, except where the tribe or Congress has expressly made state law apply or a federal court has applied it, and that the parties may adopt state or local law where there is no federal or tribal law if the lease says so and the Indian owners expressly agree. So the Oklahoma landlord-tenant rules in this library may not govern such a lease. Restricted land of members of the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee (Creek) and Seminole) is governed by special acts of Congress, and the BIA rules exempt a lease made under a special act that authorizes leasing without approval; whether a residential lease of such land needs BIA approval turns on those acts. Cautious course: if the property is, or may be, Indian trust or restricted land, check its status with the county clerk's records and with the BIA agency or the tribe, get a BIA-approved lease or sublease (or written confirmation from BIA or the tribe that none is needed) before the tenant moves in, and get advice.

title: Leasing When the Owner Holds Only a Life Estate
bodyText: Oklahoma has no civil-law usufruct, but the same problem arises with a life estate: someone who owns a home only for his or her lifetime, with others (remaindermen) taking it at death. A life tenant may rent the property out, and rent from land granted for life can be collected like any other rent; a person entitled to rent that depends on someone's life may still collect the arrears unpaid at that person's death, and an executor or administrator has the same remedies and liabilities for rent as the person who died. The life tenant must keep the buildings and fences in repair from ordinary waste and pay the taxes and other annual charges, and a just share of extraordinary assessments that benefit the whole property, and the remaindermen may sue for waste or trespass that injures their future interest even while the life estate lasts. What no Oklahoma statute says is whether a lease signed only by the life tenant survives the life tenant's death; no Oklahoma case was read on it. Cautious course: if you lease from a life tenant, or are one, have the remaindermen sign the lease too or keep the term short, and as a tenant-facing landlord tell the tenant in writing who will hold title and receive rent after the life tenant dies. After a death, the life estate's end is shown in the land records by a recorded death certificate and affidavit or by a court decree, so check the county clerk's records before relying on who now owns the property.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute says whether a tenant of rented land gets hunting or fishing rights unless the owner reserves them, and no Oklahoma case was read on it. What the statutes do say matters for rural rentals: no one may hunt, trap or take game on another's land without the consent of the owner, the lessee or the occupant, and the same rule applies to fishing (with exceptions such as land no resident occupies, unless the owner posts an objection). So your tenant, as lessee and occupant, can lawfully give friends permission to hunt or fish on the property unless the lease says otherwise.

Consent lasts no more than one year unless a longer period is given, and a first conviction for hunting without consent is a misdemeanor punished by a fine of $500 to $1,500, 30 days in county jail, or both (repeat convictions carry higher fines or at least six months in jail). On land primarily used for farming, ranching or forestry, willfully entering without permission of the surface owner, surface lessee, hunting lessee or lawful occupant is trespass. A landowner or lessee may lawfully forbid hunting, fishing and trapping on its land, and Oklahoma's constitutional right to hunt and fish does not change trespass law or property rights.

Giving someone permission to hunt or fish does not by itself add to your duty of care or your liability beyond what the recreational and farm liability statutes provide. If you want to control hunting, trapping and fishing on a rental (or keep those rights for yourself or a hunting lessee), say so in the lease; the optional Hunting, Trapping and Fishing clause does that. A lease of land used primarily for agriculture is outside the Landlord and Tenant Act (unless it was set up to avoid the Act), so for a farm lease the written lease itself is the main place these rights are settled.

title: No Incentive for Renting to Veterans
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute gives a landlord a tax credit, payment, deposit guarantee or other incentive for renting to a veteran, or requires or regulates a veterans' rent discount or preference in private housing. Oklahoma's veterans' housing help goes to veterans who own homes: subject to available funds, the Department of Veterans Affairs may give a disabled veteran a one-time grant of up to $5,000 toward a specially adapted home the veteran is buying or remodeling, if the veteran is approved for the federal Specially Adapted Housing grant and meets residency conditions. Oklahoma's veteran tax benefits (such as sales tax and vehicle exemptions for veterans rated 100% disabled) are the veteran's, not the landlord's. Federal programs for veterans, such as housing vouchers, have their own rules, which are not covered here. You may offer a veterans' discount if you wish, since no Oklahoma statute bars or requires one; offer it on the same terms to every eligible applicant.

title: Which Code Edition Applies in Oklahoma
bodyText: Oklahoma's statewide building and fire codes are adopted as named, fixed editions, not as whatever edition is newest. The Oklahoma Uniform Building Code Commission adopts the codes by rule, and they are the statewide minimum standards for residential and commercial construction. The current rules, effective September 14, 2026, adopt the 2024 International Residential Code for one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses, the 2024 International Building Code and the 2024 International Existing Building Code for what the rules call commercial construction, and the 2024 International Fire Code for residential and commercial fire prevention and fire protection systems, each with Oklahoma amendments (the electrical, plumbing, mechanical and fuel gas codes are adopted the same way). The Commission expressly chose not to adopt the 2021 editions, and published errata to the adopted IBC, IRC, IFC, existing building, electrical, fuel gas, mechanical and plumbing codes are not incorporated. A newer model-code edition applies in Oklahoma only after the Commission adopts it by rule. Cities, counties and state agencies may enforce higher standards, and local amendments to the adopted codes need the Commission's approval, so check your city's adopted codes too. The Landlord and Tenant Act names no code or edition: it defines building and housing codes broadly as any law, ordinance or government regulation on fitness for habitation or the construction, maintenance, operation, occupancy, use or appearance of a dwelling, says an owner who has someone else act as landlord still must conform with the Act and any other law, code, ordinance or regulation on maintaining and operating the premises, and states your repair duty as keeping the unit fit and habitable and keeping supplied systems in good and safe working order. Which edition governs a given repair or renovation, and how far the codes reach existing buildings, turns on the adopted model-code texts, which are copyrighted, not reproduced in the state rules; ask your local building official before major work.

title: Renting in a Condominium or Homeowners Association
bodyText:
Condominiums: under Oklahoma's Unit Ownership Estate Act, unit owners, their tenants, the owners' and tenants' employees and anyone else who uses the property are all subject to the Act and to the condominium's declaration and bylaws, so your tenant is bound by them even if the lease were silent (the Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance clause says so expressly). The owner must comply strictly with the bylaws, rules and declaration, and the association (or an aggrieved owner) can sue the owner for sums due, damages or an injunction, so you remain answerable for your tenant's violations.

The bylaws set use restrictions and can be amended by unit owners holding 75% of the aggregate ownership interest set by the declaration, effective only once recorded in an amended declaration. If the association forecloses its lien for unpaid assessments, the bylaws can require the owner to pay a reasonable rental for the unit, and the association can have a receiver appointed to collect it.

Planned communities (homeowners associations): members are the recorded lot owners, not tenants; for an owners association formed under Oklahoma's real estate development statute (by a recorded instrument signed by all the owners) after that statute took effect on June 5, 1975, the association can enforce the recorded covenants where they so provide and can lien a defaulting owner's lot for assessments, though no lien may be placed or foreclosed unless the owner was told in writing on joining of the association's restrictions and rules and of the owner's potential financial liability; and any owner in the development can sue another owner to enforce the covenants, with the winner recovering attorney fees.

What Oklahoma does not have: no statute caps an association's lease-approval or application fee or regulates an association-held tenant deposit; none lets an association demand rent directly from your tenant when you fall behind; none limits a new rental restriction to owners who buy later or agree to it; none limits the tenant information or rental fees an association may require; and none protects a home child care business against association rules. Those questions turn on your community's recorded documents.

If they require the association to approve a lease, get approval before the tenant's move-in date: if you cannot deliver possession, rent stops until you do, and the tenant may either end the lease by written notice and get back all prepaid rent and the deposit, or demand that you perform the lease, sue for possession against anyone wrongfully in possession, and recover actual damages. A lease may not take those remedies away.

This library offers an optional Association Approval of Lease clause for such communities: the tenant must apply to the association and cooperate (and pays the association's fee only if the lease says so), and the clause states that the tenant keeps those remedies if approval is refused or delayed. It gives you no right to cancel the lease when approval is refused or delayed, because a lease term letting you do so could cut off the tenant's choice to insist on the lease and recover damages.

title: No Required Association Disclosure in a Lease
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a lease of a condominium unit or a home in a homeowners association to disclose the association's obligations, to include an owner's or tenant's statement about the association's documents, or to give the tenant copies of the declaration, bylaws, covenants or rules, and no statute treats a tenant under a long lease as a buyer entitled to the association's resale documents. The disclosure rules that exist are for buyers: a title company closing a sale must give the buyer a copy of the recorded covenants and restrictions of a planned development, and condominium bylaws are recorded with the declaration and attached to or referenced in each unit's first deed, so they are public. Oklahoma's seller disclosure law reaches a lease with an option to buy a one- or two-unit home only where the seller has a real estate licensee or the tenant asks in writing, with exemptions (see the Lease With an Option to Buy row). Even without a disclosure duty, a condominium tenant is bound by the Unit Ownership Estate Act, the declaration and the bylaws, and the Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance clause makes your tenant responsible for following the association's rules. Since you cannot enforce rules a tenant has never seen, give the tenant a copy of the rules and any restrictions on use, parking, pets and common areas at signing, and keep a signed receipt.

title: Cable, Satellite and Internet Access
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute gives a tenant a right to the cable, satellite, telephone or internet provider of the tenant's choice, requires a landlord to let a provider wire a building, or bars a different rent for tenants who subscribe. Federal rules and the Oklahoma Corporation Commission's telecommunications rules do reach rentals. Antennas and satellite dishes: a Federal Communications Commission rule prohibits any lease provision (like any other private or public restriction) that impairs a tenant's installation, maintenance or use of a covered antenna on property within the tenant's exclusive use or control in which the tenant has a leasehold interest, such as a balcony, patio or yard only the tenant uses. Covered antennas are a dish one meter (about 39 inches) or less in diameter used for direct broadcast satellite service or to receive or transmit fixed wireless signals via satellite; an antenna one meter or less used for wireless cable-type video services or other fixed wireless signals; an antenna of any size used to receive over-the-air television broadcasts; and a mast supporting one of these. A restriction impairs if it unreasonably delays or prevents installation, maintenance or use, unreasonably increases its cost, or precludes an acceptable-quality signal, and any fee must be reasonable. A restriction that would otherwise be barred is allowed only if it is necessary for a clearly defined, legitimate safety objective (stated in the restriction or in a document readily available to tenants, and applied as far as practicable without discrimination to comparable fixtures), or necessary to preserve a property on or eligible for the National Register of Historic Places without treating antennas worse than comparable fixtures, and in either case is no more burdensome than necessary. A landlord who wants to keep a restriction bears the burden of showing it is allowed, and may enforce it only through a proceeding before the FCC or a court; while one is pending, enforcement must be suspended (except for qualifying safety and historic-preservation restrictions), no fine or penalty accrues and no attorney fees may be assessed, and a tenant who loses gets at least 21 days to comply. For your lease, this means: do not ban covered dishes or antennas in areas the tenant alone uses, and do not require approval or charge fees that unreasonably delay installation or raise its cost; written safety rules that meet the test above are allowed. The rule does not reach property outside the tenant's exclusive use or control, such as a shared roof or common grounds, so a lease may require consent before the tenant installs anything there. Whether a particular wall, railing or roof is within the tenant's exclusive use or control, and how far a restriction may go before it impairs reception, are settled by FCC rulings and court decisions. Exclusive service deals: a separate FCC rule makes void any clause giving a cable operator or other covered video provider the exclusive right to provide video service to an apartment building, condominium, cooperative, gated community, mobile home park, garden apartment or other centrally managed residential development (not hotels, rooming houses, dormitories, nursing homes and certain other facilities), and bars those providers from entering into or enforcing agreements that pay the owner more per tenant as more tenants subscribe, or that give the provider the exclusive right to pay the owner for access. Exclusive marketing arrangements remain lawful, but the provider must disclose them in its marketing to tenants. These rules bind the provider, so an exclusive video clause in an Oklahoma apartment owner's service agreement cannot be enforced. Oklahoma Corporation Commission rules: where tenants have a choice of local telephone providers, a provider may not enter into an agreement with a property developer, multi-tenant property owner or manager, homeowners association, or an agent of any of them that would prohibit or restrict a tenant's right to choose a provider, and a provider that learns an owner, manager or agent is restricting that choice must report it to the Commission's Public Utility Division; a carrier receiving universal-service support may not contract with the owner or manager of multi-tenant dwellings to provide its supported services exclusively. If an owner or lessee denies the area's designated carrier of last resort access to the property and the carrier is later asked to serve there, the carrier may ask the Commission to waive its duty to extend service if it considers the cost excessive. In apartment buildings the telephone demarcation point (where the phone company's responsibility ends) may be at each unit or at a central location in the building if adequate security is available. Cautious course: get advice before signing an exclusive or revenue-sharing service agreement with any provider; in the lease, do not ban covered dishes or antennas in areas the tenant alone uses (written, documented safety rules applied to comparable fixtures are the safer way to set limits), require the tenant's written consent before installing anything on roofs, common areas or other areas outside the tenant's exclusive use, and treat any installer as the tenant's guest.

title: Plug-In and Portable Solar
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute gives a tenant a right to install a plug-in, balcony or other solar device, and none voids a lease term or deed restriction that limits residential solar. Oklahoma's solar statutes deal with commercial solar facilities and with wind and solar leases of land and airspace for energy production; the airspace law expressly does not apply to an owner using solar for domestic use only. So your lease's alterations clause governs, and you may require your written consent before a tenant attaches anything to the building. One utility rule matters whoever installs the device: for an electric utility the Corporation Commission regulates, no one covered by the Commission's parallel-operation rule may interconnect or operate generation facilities in parallel with the utility without the utility's prior written approval, and interconnection costs beyond the utility's normal policies fall on the party connecting. (The rule does not cover other utilities, small power producers qualifying under the Commission's separate cogeneration and small-power rule who have not agreed with the utility to operate under it, or parties operating under parallel-operation agreements signed before March 20, 1981 who have not agreed with the utility to operate under the cogeneration and small-power rule; a qualifying producer has its own right to generate in parallel, and, unless that rule or an approved experimental purchase tariff provides otherwise, the utility's terms and conditions of service apply to it.) A solar device that feeds power into a home's wiring while the home is connected to the grid is likely to be operating in parallel, so a tenant who plugs one in without the utility's approval may be breaking the utility's terms of service on whoever's name the account is in. Customers with distributed generation can also be charged a higher fixed monthly charge than other customers in their class. Municipal utilities and electric cooperatives may have their own rules. If a tenant asks to use a plug-in solar device, have the tenant show the utility's written approval and agree in writing how it will be mounted and removed.

title: Electric Vehicle Charging: What Oklahoma Requires
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute gives a tenant a right to install an electric vehicle charger or requires a landlord to provide one, so whether a tenant may charge or install a charger is a matter for your lease (an optional Tenant EV Charger Installation clause is available). What the law does reach: the accepted standards for electric vehicle charge stations are the building codes adopted by the Oklahoma Uniform Building Code Commission, so any installation should be done by a licensed electrician with whatever permit your city requires.

If you let tenants charge and bill them for it, Oklahoma's charging rules may apply to you: a state tax of three cents per kilowatt hour applies to electricity used to charge electric vehicles, but not at stations with less than 50 kilowatts of capacity (which covers ordinary Level 2 chargers), not at stations that do not require payment, and not at a private residence where the owner or occupant pays for the power; anyone who owns or operates a charging station must conspicuously post the rate charged; and a paid charging station that began operating after November 1, 2021 must register with the Oklahoma Tax Commission, a requirement that, unlike the tax, has no capacity exception in the statute.

A charging provider is not a public utility, and selling charging is not treated as reselling retail electricity for the Corporation Commission's rate regulation; the Commission's charging-station rules do not apply to chargers that are not open to the public (including at multifamily dwellings), that are free, or that have less than 50 kilowatts of capacity. If your building's power comes from a municipal utility, Oklahoma also limits what you may charge a residential tenant for resold electricity to 10% over your cost, with an itemized bill, and whether that limit reaches charging sales is unsettled, so stay within it.

See the Shared EV Charging row for the details, and ask a tax adviser before charging tenants by the kilowatt hour.

title: Shared EV Charging
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to provide electric vehicle charging in a parking lot, garage or other shared area, or to let tenants install chargers there. If you choose to offer shared charging, how you charge for it decides which rules apply. Free charging, or charging included in rent with no separate payment: the state charging tax does not apply to stations that do not require payment, and the Corporation Commission's charging-station rules do not apply to free stations. Paid charging: the three-cent-per-kilowatt-hour charging tax does not apply to stations of less than 50 kilowatts (ordinary Level 2 chargers), but if you charge tenants for charging you should post the rate conspicuously at the charger (and on any website or app used for payment), and register the station with the Oklahoma Tax Commission within 15 days after it starts operating, because the statute's registration duty for paid stations has no capacity exception.
