For a station subject to the charging tax, any invoice must state the tax separately. The sales tax exemption for charging-station electricity applies only where the charging tax is collected and remitted, so ask a tax adviser whether sales tax applies to charging you sell below 50 kilowatts. Selling charging does not make you a public utility, it is not treated as reselling retail electricity for Commission rate regulation, and the Commission's charging-station rules do not reach chargers that are not open to the public, such as those at multifamily dwellings; but if your power comes from a municipal utility, keep any charge to tenants within 10% over your cost and itemize the bill, because it is unsettled whether the resale limit reaches charging. In a condominium or homeowners association, the association's documents may control common-area chargers. Put the charging rules (who may use the chargers, how long, and the price or that charging is included) in your lease or posted rules.

title: A Tenant's EV Charger When the Lease Ends
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute deals specifically with what happens to a tenant's electric vehicle charger when the lease ends. A general fixtures rule applies unless your lease says otherwise: when someone attaches property to another's land without an agreement allowing removal, it belongs to the landowner unless the owner chooses to require or permit its removal, but a tenant may remove, at any time during the term, anything attached for trade, manufacture, ornament or domestic use, if it can be removed without injury to the premises and has not, by the way it was attached, become an integral part of the premises. A charger bolted to a wall and wired to a circuit may or may not meet that test, and no Oklahoma case was read on chargers, so the safest course is to decide in writing when you consent to the installation whether the tenant must remove the charger and restore the installation point or must leave it as your property (the optional Tenant EV Charger Installation clause does this). Note that the tenant's statutory removal right runs only during the term; if a tenant leaves a charger behind after moving out, treat it like other property left behind under the Landlord and Tenant Act's abandoned-property rules (see the Handling of Property Left Behind clause) unless it has become part of the premises.

title: Snow and Ice Removal
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute assigns snow and ice removal at a rental, either to you or to the tenant, and none sets a deadline for clearing sidewalks. Two Landlord and Tenant Act rules frame the question. Except for a single-family residence, you must keep all common areas of the building, grounds, facilities and appurtenances in a clean, safe and sanitary condition, so walks, steps and parking areas shared by tenants are yours to keep safe. And if you want the tenant to take on snow and ice removal as a chore, put it in a conspicuous writing separate from the lease, signed on its own; a snow-removal clause inside the lease risks being unenforceable. Use the optional Tenant Maintenance Agreement (separate document) for that, and see the row Chores and Repairs by the Tenant Need a Separate Writing. The tenant's own statutory duties, such as keeping the part of the premises the tenant occupies and uses as safe, clean and sanitary as the condition of the premises permits, need no separate writing, but no Oklahoma case was read on whether they include clearing snow, so do not rely on them for it.

title: Guarantors and Lease Renewals
bodyText:
Oklahoma has no statute written for lease guarantors. No statute written for leases limits a guarantor to the original term or requires a guaranty to state a maximum amount or an end date, and no statute caps a deposit you take from a guarantor (Oklahoma caps no security deposit); the general limits below still apply. Oklahoma's general guaranty and suretyship statutes apply instead, and several matter when a lease is renewed or changed.

Writing and timing: a guaranty must be in writing and signed by the guarantor. A guaranty signed at the same time as the lease, as part of what you receive for renting to the tenant, needs nothing more in exchange; one signed later must be supported by some consideration separate from the lease, so have the guarantor sign with the tenant.

Scope: a surety cannot be held beyond the express terms of the surety contract (no Oklahoma case was read on whether a lease guarantor counts as a surety, so treat the guaranty as reaching only what it says), and the guarantor's obligation can never be larger or more burdensome than the tenant's (if it is written larger, it is cut down to match). Treat a guaranty as covering a renewal, extension or month-to-month continuation only if it says so.

Changes release the guarantor: if you, without the guarantor's consent, change the tenant's obligation in any respect, or impair or suspend your remedies against the tenant, the guarantor is released, except to the extent the tenant has indemnified the guarantor. A new term, a rent increase or a side deal with the tenant can do this. Undoing the change later does not bring the guarantor back. Accepting a partial payment reduces the guarantor's obligation by the same amount. Delay alone in pursuing the tenant does not release the guarantor, and neither does a discharge of the tenant by operation of law that you did not bring about by any act or omission of your own.

Continuing guaranties: a guaranty covering future liabilities under successive transactions is a continuing guaranty, and the guarantor may revoke it at any time as to future transactions unless there is a continuing consideration for them that the guarantor does not renounce. No Oklahoma case was read on whether a lease guaranty that covers renewals is a continuing guaranty, or whether the ongoing tenancy is continuing consideration; if a guarantor revokes in writing, treat renewals that begin afterwards as possibly unguaranteed.

Pursuing the tenant first: a guarantor of payment is liable as soon as the tenant defaults, without demand or notice. But a surety may require you to proceed against the tenant, and if you neglect to, the surety is released to the extent harmed by that neglect. And when a court of record enters judgment on a written lease under which the tenant and a co-signer are jointly and severally bound, and the co-signer is shown to have signed as surety, the tenant's property within the court's reach must be exhausted before the surety's is taken. No Oklahoma case was read on whether a lease guarantor counts as a surety for these rules; if a guarantor asks you to pursue the tenant, do so promptly. A guarantor is not liable if the tenant's contract is unlawful, but is liable despite a mere personal disability of the tenant, even one that makes the contract void against the tenant.

Practical course: use the optional Guaranty clause and choose renewal coverage expressly; have the guarantor sign the lease with the tenant; and have the guarantor sign, or consent in writing to, every renewal, extension, rent change or other amendment. Do not add an attorney-fee or indemnity promise to a guaranty written into the lease.

title: Trying to Settle Disputes Before Court
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute requires a landlord and tenant to try to settle a dispute before going to court, and none sets rules for a lease clause that tries to require it. Two Oklahoma rules make a mandatory pre-suit step risky. First, Oklahoma contract law voids every contract term that restricts a party from enforcing its rights under the contract by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary courts, or that limits the time to do so.

Second, every right, obligation and remedy in the Landlord and Tenant Act is enforceable in any court of appropriate jurisdiction, including small claims court, and may be brought as part of an eviction case unless the provision creating it says otherwise, and a lease may not make either party waive or forgo rights or remedies under the Act. A clause making the tenant (or you) give notice, meet or wait before suing could be struck on either ground, and it would bind you too. Whether a short notice-and-meet step counts as such a restriction is a question for the courts, so this library does not offer a mandatory pre-suit clause for Oklahoma.

What you can do: use the optional Trying to Resolve Disputes clause, which invites written notice and a prompt response but is expressly not a condition of any claim, notice or eviction. A claim disputed in good faith may be settled by agreement without any further consideration, so put any settlement in writing and have both parties sign it. Mediation through a court-supervised program under Oklahoma's Dispute Resolution Act is voluntary: the parties sign a written consent on the program's form before it starts, what is said is confidential, and limitation periods pause while it runs.

In a money-only suit of $250,000 or less handled under the Expedited Actions Act, the court may send the case once to a short alternative dispute resolution procedure unless the parties have agreed not to; a suit that asks for possession is not in that process.

title: Substitute Housing Is the Tenant's Remedy, Not Your Duty
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to provide or pay for alternate housing while you make repairs, after a fire or other casualty, or when a unit is unfit. Substitute housing is a remedy the tenant chooses, and it is triggered by the tenant's written notice, not by you. It applies only when, contrary to the lease or your statutory maintenance duties, you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service. After giving you written notice of the failure, the tenant may, upon written notice, obtain reasonable substitute housing for as long as your failure lasts, and is excused from paying rent for that period. The statute does not say you pay for the substitute housing; the remedy it gives is that rent stops. No Oklahoma case was read on whether a tenant may also recover the cost of substitute housing as damages, so do not assume you never will. The tenant may instead end the lease immediately by written notice, buy the service and deduct its cost from rent, or recover damages for the reduced rental value. None of these rights arises until the tenant has given you written notice, and none arises if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with the tenant's consent. After a fire or other casualty that substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit (unless caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, the tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with the tenant's consent), the tenant may move out and end the lease by written notice within one week, or stay in the usable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value; you have no duty to rehouse. A lease term requiring the tenant to accept housing you choose instead of these remedies would waive the tenant's rights under the Landlord and Tenant Act and is unenforceable. You may still offer another unit or a hotel voluntarily, and the tenant may accept. Relocation-assistance statutes in Oklahoma bind whoever acquires property for public use in a publicly funded project (public agencies, redevelopment trusts and any other person doing so), not a landlord renting its own property.

title: Children in the Household
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires a lease to say anything about children, but fair housing law limits what you may do. Familial status is protected. You may not refuse to rent, make housing unavailable, set different terms or services, advertise a preference, or say a unit is unavailable because a person is pregnant, is in the process of getting legal custody of a child under 18, or lives with a child under 18 as the child's parent or legal custodian (or with the written permission of the parent or custodian). An adults-only rule, extra rent or deposit for families, or rules that steer families to certain units run into this. Oklahoma's familial-status protection does not apply to housing for older persons as the statute defines it: housing the Attorney General's Office of Civil Rights Enforcement determines is designed and operated to assist elderly persons under a federal or state program, housing intended for and solely occupied by persons 62 or older, or housing intended and operated for at least one person 55 or older per unit as determined by that office's rules. The state fair housing law also does not apply to a single-family house rented by an owner who owns (or holds an interest in the proceeds of) no more than three single-family houses at a time, but only if it is rented without a licensed broker or agent (or the services of an owner of a building for five or more families) and without any discriminatory notice or advertisement, and, if the owner was not the most recent resident, for only one rental in 24 months; nor to rooms or units in a building for no more than four families where the owner lives in one of them (the statute makes its whole exemption list subject to the no-broker and no-discriminatory-notice conditions, so treat those conditions as applying to an owner-occupied building too). The federal Fair Housing Act also protects familial status and has its own exemptions and its own, stricter test for 55-and-older housing, so qualifying under state law does not by itself exempt you federally; in particular, the federal advertising ban applies even to an owner who is otherwise exempt, so never advertise or post a preference against families. Occupancy limits: a lease may set reasonable limits on use of the unit by tenants and occupants, and a limit of two persons per bedroom is presumed reasonable in Oklahoma, but that two-person limit does not apply to children born to the tenants during the lease. Fair housing law leaves room for reasonable state or local limits on the maximum number of occupants. Apply any limit the same way to adults and children, and do not use it to keep families out. If a child joins the household during the tenancy: Oklahoma has no separate landlord-tenant rule beyond the born-during-the-lease exception, but refusing to renew, raising the rent or ending the tenancy because of a pregnancy, a birth, an adoption or a custody placement would be familial-status discrimination unless an exemption applies. The statute's exception names only children born to the tenants; as a cautious course, treat a child adopted or placed in the tenants' custody during the lease the same way. Your right to have an occupant removed for breaching the lease does not reach the tenant's own unemancipated minor children, because the Act does not treat them as occupants. List every household member, including children, in the lease's occupant list.

title: Parking Rules and Towing
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute sets special rules for parking regulations in a residential lease. No statute requires you to hand the tenant a separate parking document before signing, to use a particular heading, to state in the lease whether parking is provided or what it costs, to make a parking permit last as long as the lease, or to limit the vehicle information you ask for. Parking regulations are rules about the tenant's use of the premises, so the general rule statute governs them.

A parking rule is enforceable against the tenant only if its purpose is to promote the convenience, peace, safety or welfare of the tenants, protect your property from abusive use, or fairly distribute services and facilities held out for tenants generally; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies to all tenants in the premises fairly; it is explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do or not do; it is not meant to evade your obligations; and the tenant had notice of it when signing the lease or when it was adopted.

A rule adopted after the tenant signs that substantially modifies the tenant's bargain binds the tenant only if the tenant consents in writing. No Oklahoma case was read on what counts as a substantial modification; as a cautious course, get the tenant's written consent before taking away an included space or adding a parking charge during the lease. A required parking fee is rent, so set it in the lease.

Towing: Oklahoma's private-property towing statute requires no posted signs and no advance notice before a resident's vehicle with expired registration is towed, and sets no rule for expired registration as such; it lets the owner, legal possessor or authorized agent have a licensed Class AA wrecker service remove a vehicle reasonably believed abandoned after at least 48 hours on the property, or a vehicle left there without express or implied permission, using the Department of Public Safety's Tow Request and Authorization Form and a joint inventory.

A tenant's car in an assigned space usually has permission, so make clear in the lease and parking rules which vehicles are not permitted, and give the tenant written notice before towing. Posting your lot has a separate benefit: on posted private property, parking without permission from the landowner or person in charge (unless casual or involuntary) is a misdemeanor, a violator who is convicted must also pay the reasonable and necessary removal and storage charges, and the landowner is not liable for damage to the trespassing vehicle while it is trespassing, being removed or in storage.

Local ordinances may add sign or notice requirements.

title: Smart Locks and App-Based Entry
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute regulates smart locks, keypads, key fobs or app-based entry in rental housing, and no statute lets an abuse survivor demand that whoever runs a connected device's accounts cut off another person's access. The general rules still apply to an electronic system. Entry: a code or app that lets you open the unit is still entry. Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give at least one day's notice and enter only at reasonable times, and do not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant. Apart from those statutory occasions, an abandoned or surrendered unit, or a court order, you have no other right of access during the tenancy. Remote logs do not replace these rules. Lockouts: disabling a tenant's code or app access to keep the tenant out is a wrongful exclusion. The tenant may recover possession through a court proceeding, or end the lease after giving you notice of that intention, and in either case recover up to twice the average monthly rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater. Data: if the system stores tenants' fingerprints or other unique biometric data with their names, a breach of that data can trigger Oklahoma's breach-notice duties (see the row on protecting applicant and tenant data). A separate consumer data privacy law takes effect January 1, 2027 but reaches only businesses processing data on very large numbers of Oklahoma consumers. Installation: the sale, installation and servicing of electronic locks and access-control systems is regulated under Oklahoma's Alarm, Locksmith and Fire Sprinkler Industry Act, which requires a license to engage in that business. The sale of systems designed for the customer to install is exempt, and so is an individual who owns and installs locks or electronic security devices on the individual's own property (not as a normal business practice on others' property); the Department of Labor's rules add that a company or its employee doing locksmith work (which covers mechanical and electronic locks) on the company's own property is exempt unless it does that work as a normal business practice on others' property. A management company working on buildings it does not own, and anyone installing a separately defined electronic access control system (card readers, keypads or biometric devices on an outside power source), should use a licensed company or confirm the exemption with the Department of Labor. Good practice: say in the lease how entry codes are issued and changed, give each tenant their own code, change codes between tenancies, and keep a working mechanical key or override for power or network failures.

title: Tenant Security Cameras and Video Doorbells
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute addresses tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells. No statute gives a tenant a right to install one, and none bars you from allowing or limiting them, so your lease's alterations and rules terms decide (a rule must meet the usual tests for rules, and a new rule that substantially changes the tenant's bargain needs the tenant's written consent). General criminal laws set the outer limits for you and your tenants alike. Audio: Oklahoma is a one-party-consent state. Willfully intercepting a wire, oral or electronic communication is a felony unless the person intercepting is a party to the communication or one of the parties has given prior consent, and even then not if the interception is for the purpose of committing a criminal act. An oral communication here means one made by a person who expects, in circumstances that justify the expectation, that it will not be intercepted. A doorbell or camera that records conversations between other people, such as neighbors talking in a hallway, can cross that line; the cautious course is to require audio recording to be off, or limited to conversations the tenant takes part in. Video: it is a crime to use photographic, electronic or video equipment in a clandestine manner, for an illegal, illegitimate, prurient, lewd or lascivious purpose, to watch a person without the person's knowledge and consent in a place where there is a reasonable expectation of privacy, or to publish or distribute such images, and a separate crime to capture images of a person's private areas that way. Cameras, whether yours or a tenant's, should never point into another unit, a bathroom or a bedroom, and should be visible rather than hidden. Tampering: it is a misdemeanor for an unauthorized person to refocus, reposition, cover, disconnect or otherwise tamper with or disable a security or surveillance camera or security system. This protects your cameras from tenants. As a cautious course, do not disable or remove a tenant's camera yourself; require the tenant to remove it under the lease, through notice and, if needed, the courts. Installation: a tenant who installs a camera without charge to protect the tenant's own belongings, or uses a system sold for customer installation, does not need an alarm or locksmith license. No Oklahoma case was read on privacy claims against camera owners.

title: Caring for a Tenant's Animal
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute gives you a special right to enter a unit to care for a tenant's animal, or makes you the animal's owner because you feed or shelter it.

Entry: the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry for agreed services, and you may enter without consent in an emergency. Otherwise give at least one day's notice and enter at reasonable times unless an emergency or impracticability excuses it. The optional Animal Care clause lets the tenant name a caregiver in advance; even then, try to reach the tenant first and give whatever notice is practicable (a call, text and a note on the door), and document why notice was impossible.

Care duty: Oklahoma's cruelty statute applies to any person who deprives an animal in captivity of necessary food, drink, shelter or veterinary care to prevent suffering, or who causes or permits that, whether the animal belongs to that person or to another. Once you take charge of a tenant's animal, feed and shelter it or promptly turn it over to its caregiver, animal control or a shelter. Peace officers and animal control officers can take custody of an abused or neglected animal by court order, and a law enforcement officer may get a warrant to seize an abandoned or neglected animal.

Left behind: abandoning an animal includes vacating a premises and leaving the animal there, and depositing a dog, cat or other domestic animal in a private or public place intending to abandon it is a misdemeanor.

If a tenant abandons, surrenders or is evicted and leaves an animal, the property-left-behind statute requires you to keep the tenant's property in a place of safekeeping with reasonable care; it was not written with animals in mind, so the cautious course is to call animal control or a shelter rather than hold a live animal for the statute's notice period, and still send the tenant the statute's notice by certified mail saying where the animal was taken, since a landlord who deliberately or negligently disposes of property outside the statute is liable for actual damages.

If a sole tenant dies, follow the contact-person procedure for the tenant's property. Service and assistance animals have separate rules (see the Assistance Animals row).

title: No Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute requires you to give a tenant a state fact sheet or other notice about pets and eviction, whether or not you know the tenant has a dog or cat, and no Oklahoma statute sets special pet steps in an eviction. The general eviction rules apply to a household with animals: after judgment, the tenant gets notice (in person, or by posting when personal service fails) that the writ will be executed no sooner than 48 hours later, and you may ask the sheriff or city police to help execute the writ. If animals remain when you retake possession, do not treat them as ordinary property left behind: anyone who deprives an animal in captivity of necessary food, water, shelter or veterinary care to prevent suffering can commit cruelty, even if the animal belongs to someone else, and, for the animal-abandonment crimes, abandoning an animal means voluntarily giving it up, which includes vacating a home and leaving the animal there. Ask the tenant to arrange for the animals before the writ date, and call animal control or a shelter for any animal left behind (see the row on caring for a tenant's animal).

title: Using the Home Only as a Residence, and Illegal Uses
bodyText: Unless the lease says otherwise, a tenant who uses the unit for any purpose other than as the tenant's home breaches the lease, and that breach is grounds for ending it (the Residential Use Only clause relies on this). Oklahoma criminal law voids a residential lease outright only for illegal gambling: every lease under which the tenant uses the premises to violate the gambling law is wholly null and void, and a lease becomes void when the tenant is convicted of allowing prohibited gambling devices or games there; you recover possession through an ordinary eviction case. No statute voids a lease for drugs, prostitution or other crimes; for those, use the criminal-activity termination ground (see the No Criminal Activity clause). Criminal law also reaches owners who knowingly let property for illegal uses: knowingly renting premises to be used for gambling carries daily penalties that become a lien on the property; letting a building knowing it is intended for an illegal lottery or for other purposes punished in the same parts of the criminal code is a crime, and so is an owner knowingly permitting a building to be used to record race bets; and leasing premises with knowledge or reasonable cause to believe the tenant intends to use them for prostitution is a felony. Separately, real property used or intended to be used to commit or facilitate a felony drug offense can be forfeited to the state, but no owner's interest is forfeited for an act or omission that the owner shows was committed or omitted without the owner's knowledge or consent. Act promptly on credible reports of illegal use and keep a record of what you did.

title: Drug-Free and Crime-Free Lease Terms
bodyText:
No Oklahoma statute requires a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum, and none prescribes its wording. Oklahoma law already supplies the core of one: every tenant must not engage in criminal activity that threatens the health, safety or right of peaceful enjoyment of other tenants or is a danger to the premises, and must not engage in any drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises personally or by any household member, guest or other person under the tenant's control.

Such criminal activity by the tenant, a household member, a guest or another person under the tenant's control, and any drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises by any of them, is grounds for immediate termination of the lease. The No Criminal Activity clause states this in the statute's words, with the required carve-out for victims, so a separate addendum adds little.

Limits: you may not deny, refuse to renew or end a tenancy because the applicant, tenant or a household member is a victim or alleged victim of domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking. You may not refuse to lease to, or otherwise penalize, a person solely for being a licensed medical marijuana patient unless that would risk a monetary or licensing benefit under federal law.

You may ban smoking and vaporizing marijuana on the premises, inside its structures and within ten feet of the entry, but you may not deny a patient the use of other lawful, non-smoked medical marijuana products lawfully recommended under the medical marijuana law, so a blanket ban on all cannabis use does not fit Oklahoma law. If you rent to a Housing Choice Voucher family, federal rules require the lease to make drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises by any tenant, household member or guest (or on the premises by another person under the tenant's control) grounds for terminating the tenancy; HUD's tenancy addendum supplies that language.

For these rules a drug is any federally controlled substance, and drug-related criminal activity includes illegal use, so a voucher tenancy can put the federal rule and Oklahoma's medical marijuana protection in conflict; no source read reconciles them, so get advice before acting against a voucher tenant's state-lawful use. Separately, an owner who shows that illegal drug activity happened without the owner's knowledge or consent keeps the property if the state seeks to forfeit it, so act on credible reports promptly.

title: What a Tenant Must Not Do, and Your Remedies
bodyText:
Oklahoma's Landlord and Tenant Act lists what a tenant must do and must not do, and those duties apply whether or not the lease repeats them.

At all times during the tenancy the tenant must:
- keep the part of the premises the tenant uses as safe, clean and sanitary as its condition permits
- dispose of garbage and waste safely
- keep plumbing fixtures as clean as their condition permits
- use electrical, plumbing, heating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances safely
- not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises, or permit any person, animal or pet to do so
- not engage in conduct, or allow anyone or any animal there with the tenant's permission to engage in conduct, that disturbs other tenants' quiet and peaceful enjoyment
- follow valid rules
- not engage in threatening criminal activity or any drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises, personally or through household members, guests or others under the tenant's control.

The tenant also may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry for inspections, repairs, services or showings.

Your remedies:
- for a breach you can fix by repair, replacement or cleaning, you may give written notice and, if the tenant does not act within ten days (or as promptly as an emergency requires), do the work and bill it as rent
- for a material breach, a written notice ending the lease in at least 15 days unless cured within 10
- for a breach causing or threatening imminent and irremediable harm that the tenant does not fix promptly after notice, an immediate eviction filing
- for qualifying criminal activity, immediate termination
- for refused access, a court order or termination.

The optional Prohibited Acts clause repeats the damage, disturbance and access duties in the statute's words. Separately, some acts on rented premises are crimes for the owner if knowingly allowed, such as letting property for gambling or prostitution (see the row on illegal uses).

title: Renting the Same Unit Twice
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute specifically forbids renting the same room or unit to two tenants for the same period, or sets a special penalty for it. The general delivery rules decide what happens. At the start of the term you must deliver full possession to the tenant. If you do not (for example, because you also rented the unit to someone else who moved in), rent abates until possession is delivered, and the tenant may either end the lease by written notice, in which case you must return all prepaid rent and the deposit, or demand performance and bring an action for possession against the person wrongfully in possession and recover actual damages. If a person's failure to deliver possession is willful and not in good faith, the aggrieved person may recover from that person up to twice the monthly rent stated in the lease, prorated daily, for each month or part of a month that person wrongfully remains in possession. You may also bring an action for possession against anyone wrongfully in possession. Keep one signed lease per unit and period, and confirm a unit is vacant and unpromised before signing a new lease.

title: Housing Your Employees
bodyText: Oklahoma's Landlord and Tenant Act has no exception for housing you provide to an employee, such as a resident manager or maintenance worker (a farmhand whose rental agreement covers premises used primarily for agricultural purposes may fall under the agricultural exclusion below). Unless the arrangement was created to avoid the Act, the Act's only exclusions are residence at an institution incidental to detention or to medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar service; occupancy by a buyer under a contract of sale or contract for deed; occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization in its building; transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or similar lodging; occupancy by a condominium unit owner or cooperative proprietary-lease holder; and occupancy under a rental agreement covering premises the occupant uses primarily for agricultural purposes. So if an employee occupies a dwelling unit under a rental agreement, the employee is a tenant with all of the Act's rights. No statute requires a special disclosure for employee housing, an offer of a regular lease when the job ends, or a filing with any agency, and none says the tenancy ends automatically with the job. Ending it follows the ordinary rules: a fixed term expires on its end date; a month-to-month tenancy needs at least 30 days' written notice; a tenancy shorter than month-to-month needs at least 7 days' written notice; and if the person stays, you must bring an eviction case. The Act's notice rules do not apply to an occupant who has no rental agreement with you and with whom you have not consented to create a tenancy, but an employee you placed in a unit is unlikely to fit that description. No Oklahoma case was read on whether rent-free housing given as part of pay is a rental agreement, so the cautious course is to treat it as one. Good practice: put the housing in a separate written rental agreement, not just the employment offer; state the rent or that it is part of compensation; use a month-to-month term (or a fixed term) so you can give the statutory notice when the job ends; and keep housing decisions separate from any dispute about wages. Where the Oklahoma Minimum Wage Act applies, lodging received by the employee may be credited toward the minimum wage, provided you also pay at least the minimum cash wage the statute sets by reference to federal rules.

title: No State Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: No Oklahoma statute or Real Estate Commission rule requires you to give tenants a state-agency statement of tenant rights, attach one to the lease or have tenants sign one, and none bars you from suing until one is given. The Oklahoma Real Estate Commission publishes a voluntary information sheet for owners and tenants ("Property Owners and Tenants - You Need to Know!") and makes the Landlord and Tenant Act available on its website. Its lease forms and addenda are prepared for voluntary use by real estate licensees, and the Commission's rules do not require a licensee to hand tenants a rights pamphlet. Giving tenants that sheet or a copy of the Act is good practice but not required. What Oklahoma does require at or before the start of the tenancy is different: the lease must prominently identify in writing the person and address authorized to accept service and notices, and you must disclose in writing the name and address of the manager and of the owner or a person authorized to act for the owner (see the Person to Accept Service clause), along with the other required disclosures. Federally assisted housing is different. If the unit is in a covered federal housing program (including Housing Choice Voucher units, public housing and Low-Income Housing Tax Credit properties), the owner or manager must give HUD's notice of rights under the federal Violence Against Women Act, with the certification form, to an applicant who is denied residency, at admission, with any notice of eviction or termination of assistance, and in multiple languages as HUD guidance directs.

title: Credit Card Surcharges on Rent
bodyText:
If you let tenants pay rent or other charges by credit card and add a surcharge for doing so, follow Oklahoma's credit card surcharge statute, which applies to anyone doing business in any sale, service or lease transaction. Post the surcharge amount clearly where the tenant pays: at the entry and point of payment for in-person payments, on the home page and the payment page for online payments, and say it aloud for payments taken by phone. The surcharge may not exceed 2% of the payment or your actual cost of processing the card payment, whichever is less. If you accept only credit cards, you may not add a surcharge at all.

You may instead offer a discount for paying by cash, check or debit card, offered to every tenant clearly and conspicuously. No court decision on whether the statute reaches residential rent was reviewed, so the cautious course is to follow it. A surcharge the lease requires is also rent under the Landlord and Tenant Act.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Oklahoma follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Okla. Stat. tit. 12A, § 3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Okla. Stat. tit. 12A, § 1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Oklahoma's landlord-tenant act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the act, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 107). That binds you and the tenant alike. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
